comment_teaching:
Darwin was a very Gen Z and approachable instructor who always answered students’ questions sincerely and thoroughly. Since the class was quite long, he made an effort to keep it engaging by adding interesting jokes and using Mentimeter to encourage student interaction and participation.
He was also very generous and flexible with the quiz make-up policy, which I really appreciated. His English pronunciation was very clear, so it was easy to follow his lectures. He responded to emails quickly, which made communication smooth even outside of class.
Most importantly, Darwin was very receptive to students’ feedback and was willing to adjust his teaching accordingly.
comment_grading:
Participation Weight 10% / Mean 9.84: Done by Canva class quiz once a week (so five times throughout the entire course). Only 4 out of 5 quizzes would be graded so if you miss one quiz or didn’t get a good quiz grade in the previous one, you still have one more chance.
Poster Presentation Weight 30% / Mean: 78.77: Poster exhibition style. Can team up with max. 4 people. Had to create a new bioengineering related product and make it as a poster. Graded by TA (70%) and peer assessment (30%). Your team has to explain the context, how the product works, limitations etc. 
Midterm exam Weight 30% / Mean: 71.33: You can have 1 double-sided cheatsheet. Half of the course contents (Intro-Chapter 5: Bioimaging). Basically 5 presentations for mid term.
Final exam Weight: 30% / Mean: 72.75: Same as midterm. Other half of the course contents (Chapter 6: Biomolecular engineering-Bioinformatics)
comment_workload: Doable compare to other UST CC courses. Since it was summer term course, it was quite burdensome to prepare all presentation and finals at the same time. (Final was two days after final poster presentation) Also, the class is 3 hours 20 minutes long so it was hard for me to concentrate until the end, but Darwin gave us some breaks in between and he always finished class early.

comment_content: The first half of the course is about BioInstrument and bioimaging (blood pressure, pulse oximetry, X-ray, MRI, etc). The second half of the course is Biomolecular Engineering(Drug Delivery, Tissue Engineering,etc). It is ok if you have no biology or chemistry or physics background, the content is not hard.
comment_teaching: Prof Wong always make the class so interesting. He encourage student to talk and thinks. Everyone is so active in the class.  Unlike other course that most of student just sit and listen.
comment_grading: The content is not too hard, both midterm and final are open books. Therefore it is not hard to get a good grade in the exam. However, most of the people will do well in the exam, getting A might be challenge.
comment_workload: 4 set of homework and a project, not much. The homework set are very easy, usually you can find the answer on the lecture slides. The project is to choose a technology related to biomedical engineering, make a poster and have a presentation to explain this technology to other student. After that, write a two page report. Not much of workload.

comment_content:
Syllabus of the course: 
Lecture 1: Atomic Structure

Lecture 4: Crystallographic Planes
Lecture 5: Crystalline Characteristics and Imperfections
Lecture 6: Imperfections and Diffusion

Lecture 9: Strengthening Materials
Lectures 10 & 11: Failure of Materials I/II
Lecture 12: Phase Diagrams
Lecture 13: Phase Transformation
Lecture 14: Polymer Structures
Lecture 15: Polymer Properties
Lecture 16: Semiconductors
Lecture 17: Electrical Properties
Lecture 18: Optical Properties
(Thermal Properties and Advanced Materials are originally included. But they are later removed as the professor can't finish the complete syllabus.)
Overall speaking, this course is particularly difficult among the engineering introduction courses. Some knowledge inside is pretty abstract, especially those in the first few lectures, and of course, requires some time to understand them. If you are 
not an enthusiast in Chemistry and Physics, you will also find them quite boring. I strongly do not recommend you to attend this course if you are not good at these subjects. If you have studied DSE Chemistry, Physics Elective 2 and the course CHEM 1020 before, they will be beneficial for you.
comment_teaching:
Prof. Nyein is a new professor in UST so I will try to be less critical. Actually, Prof. Nyein's teaching is quite good. She can explain the concepts quite clearly with good reasons. The logic flow is still easy to follow and understand. Sometimes, when she is explaining, she will demonstrate some related examples. She is also willing to answer questions during the lecture. 
One thing I have to mention is that she refused to upload the lecture videos and include some important concepts in the PowerPoints. She said that she wanted to encourage students to join the lectures more regularly. I can understand her intentions, but it is not quite good for students to revise, in my opinion. If she can upload the lecture videos and improve the PowerPoints, then her teaching can be said to be really remarkable. 
Every week, there will be a tutorial session. However, the TAs will just briefly recap some knowledge and show assignment answers during it. Sometimes they will also give out some easy questions for us to work on, but they are only just better than nothing. By some means, the tutorials were quite useless, and I did not attend most of them.
comment_grading:
Assessment plan of the course: 
Assignment x 6 (18%)
Mid-Term Exam x 2 (50%)
Final Exam (32%)
Statistics: 
Assignments x 6: Mean: 13.42/18, My score: 17.67/18
Mid-Term 1: Mean: 61.5/100, Median; 62.5/100, My score: 70/100
Mid-Term 2: Mean: 62.2/100, Median: 67/100, My score; 75/100
Final: Mean: 64.1/100, My score: 79.5/100
My final score is 79.36 and I got an A-. The grade is quite out of my expectations. Probably my assignments and the final exam saved me. It somehow shows that the cutoff of A range in this course is not very high. I don't know what are the cutoffs of B and C ranges, but for me, it's not bad.
comment_workload:
Perhaps the craziest thing about this course is that there are 2 mid-terms. So, you will find yourself spending more time studying this course. 
Assignments will be given every 1 to 2 weeks. Apparently, they are very difficult as they are mainly about some advanced conceptual things. Even if you attend all the lectures, you might still not be able to answer the questions. You have to spend quite a lot of time searching for answers and explanations on the Internet. They are quite time-consuming, but I have to say that they are some good practices. 
For mid-terms, you can bring a 3" x 5" cheat sheet but can only be written on one side. For the final exam, it is just the same but the cheat sheet can be two-sided. According to Prof. Nyein, the exams will focus more on applications and practical things. So, if you can truly understand the concepts, and complete the assignments on your own, you should be able to get some acceptable scores in the exams.

comment_content:
I honestly took the course due to the lenient grading policy. Once I am actually enrolled though, getting a good grade is not as easy as all the reviews here make it seem. The PowerPoint presentations are a bit too superficial; the professor will usually annotate them quite heavily to convey a multitude of things that are not contained in the actual presentation, which makes it impossible to predict what will come out in the final exam and midterm. I recommend you to make your cheat sheet as detailed as possible, copy & paste everything there (formulas, definitions, graphs, everything) and try to really understand the concepts, such as the Streeter Phelps oxygen sag curve, e.t.c., because the final exam will not be as straight-forward as the midterm and will require detailed understanding of these concepts far more than what the lecture notes provides. Midterm was kinda simple though.
You may consult the textbook if you want to (some midterm questions came from there). The professor also entertains questions in the lecture and through emails.

You need to form your own group for labs and project (same group). You can choose your topic in a wide range of choices (basically related to food science will be fine). You need to do literature review in the project. Most students choose to debunk a food myth as their topic. Although the presentation is only 5-minutes long, it takes a lot of time to do research on the topic if you want to achieve a high score.

Final exam (60%)
No attendance taken. No mid-terms.
I initially took the course because my SENG advisor told me she's heard many people wax lyrical on the course's grading leniency. After completing it myself, turns out this wasn't a myth after all.
The rubrics for the group project sounded a little intimidating to us, but I do believe that so long as both the report and video are relevant to the given themes, you'll do just fine. The grade deviation mostly came from students' performance on the final exam. Heck, we even put Spongebob music & transitions in our video and weren't punished for it lol.
Ben kept mentioning how the final exam would be extremely easy. Ngl, at first we all thought he pranked us. The exam comprised 55 MCQs and 40 short answer questions. Nearly 100 questions and they only give you 2 hours. Some MCQs were tricky and unpredictable as well, so to some extent Ben did lie to us on the difficulty level. However, after the exam me and a few of my groupmates intentionally approached Ben while he was leaving to say our thanks (for gifting us an enjoyable course - perhaps for the final time) and to reproach him at the same time for lying to us HAHAHA. I told him I didn't have enough time to finish the exam: left some 4-5 short answer questions blank and was unsure of quite a few of the MCQs. Wanna know what he said?

title: Worth taking
comment_content: CIVL 1160 provides a broad, high-level overview of civil infrastructure systems. It's conceptually interesting and very light on workload compared to typical engineering courses. However, the delivery and resources have significant drawbacks. Expect a manageable course for breadth, but be prepared to work around the lecture and tutorial structure to grasp key concepts.
comment_teaching:
Lectures: The professor(s) are generally knowledgeable and enthusiastic about infrastructure. However, a major weakness is the difficulty in distinguishing crucial information from interesting but irrelevant tangents or anecdotes. Important case studies, key definitions, or examinable concepts are often delivered with the same emphasis as fun stories or background fluff. This makes effective note-taking challenging.
Lecture Slides: A significant drawback. The slides provided are typically extremely bare-bones, often just containing bullet points, titles, or single images without sufficient context or explanation. They are not understandable in isolation and serve poorly as revision material. Attending lectures is essential simply to get the explanations missing from the slides, but even then, filtering signal from noise is hard.
Tutorials: Largely unhelpful ("basically useless"). They often lacked clear structure, meaningful practice problems, or effective engagement with the lecture material. TAs frequently seemed unprepared or unable to clarify complex points beyond what was (minimally) covered in lectures. Time felt unproductive.
comment_grading:
Quiz 1 (20%): Covers material from Chapters 1-5/6. Usually MC/short answer.
Quiz 2 (20%): Covers material from Chapters 6/7-10. Format similar to Quiz 1.
Group Project (10%): A relatively simple project, often involving a basic case study analysis, feasibility study, or system overview related to one infrastructure domain. Focus is more on applying concepts lightly than deep technical work. Group dynamics are the main variable here.
Final Exam (40%): Comprehensive, covering all chapters (1-11). Heavily weighted, so performing well here is crucial, especially given the curve. Format typically MC and short/long answer questions.
Curve: Grading is explicitly on a curve, meaning your final grade depends significantly on your performance relative to classmates. Aim to be above average, particularly on the final exam.
Be careful midterm and final have negative marking, all MCQ, Correct is +3 points Incorrect is -1 point, Blank is 0 points
comment_workload:
This is arguably the course's biggest positive. The workload is minimal compared to core engineering courses.
Lectures are the primary commitment. Readings are suggested but rarely essential for assessments.
Assignments are infrequent, short, and straightforward.
The group project (see grading) requires coordination but isn't overly demanding content-wise.
Studying for quizzes and the final is necessary, but the scope is manageable. Definitely one of the lightest engineering courses workload-wise.

title: A terrible introduction to computer science, an alright introduction to Python. (OLD)
comment_content:
When one looks to take an introduction to computer science course, they hope to be introduced to computer science. As such, it is a huge shame that COMP1021 does not introduce you to computer science, it instead places you in the middle of the Python programming language where you have to piece everything together yourself. 
Exploring the content, the following topics are covered:
- Installing python, the python shell, print(), input(), variables, type casting, the random module, python files.
- Turtle graphics, moving, colours, etc.
- Selection/decision statements (if, elif, else), comparison operators, indentation
- Looping (for, while)
- Python sequence types (List, tuple, string)
- The modulus operator (%)
- Functions
- Slicing, 2D/3D structures (with lists)
- Data types
- Turtle shapes, click and drag events, key events, the turtle coordinate system
- The RGB colour system
- State diagrams
- Dictionaries
- Objects
- Recursion
This is a pretty compressive list of topics if you aim to become acquainted with Python. But therein lies the major problem: these topics, while useful for basic scripting, are woefully insufficient for understanding the fundamentals of computer science. 
Nothing about how computers work, nothing about computer history and paradigms, nothing on anything to do with foundational computer science. Such as disastrous and ill-fully narrow course this is. Computer Science classes at high school teach this stuff yet the university level course couldn't think to include it.   
First time students are left with a mountain of content and no idea how it works at any level below the surface. Students complete this course only knowing how to construct bare Python scripts.
It is also very important to bring up the unnecessarily extensive use of Turtle graphics. It is clear the designers of this course imagined that the fun interactivity of Turtle graphics might make students interested in the course. However, what starts off as a playful learning tool turns into an overused gimmick. Students are guided into using this heavy object-based module from the start, only covering objects in small detail right at the end of the course. Turtle Graphics becomes less of a tool for learning and more of a colorful distraction, a facade masking the course's lack of depth.
If the content of this course is bad, the examinations are certainly terrible. Never have I seen such devilish and unreasonable examination questions in my life. One question from a midterm read as follows:
"A quadrillion is one followed by 15 zeroes. What is a quadrillion divided by 2? Use Python to work it out."
Only a true genius could conjure up such a work of art. How could this actually be testing anything useful? This just tests a student's ability to type out 15 zeroes under the stress and pressure of the examinations. Ridiculous. 
While some exam questions are intuitive and interesting, the majority stand to bring you a deep sadness. You are constantly second guessing yourself as the questions are riddled with gotchas. It is as if those who wrote the exam sat laughing, smugly taunting students as they put these questions together.
In the end, this course is a true disappointment at an opportunity to ignite curiosity and wonder in the computer science field. Many assume a science and technology university to have a truly captivating computer science course, but this just isn't the case. It feels that many students take this course, finish it, and have no further interest to pursue computer science.
COMP1021 demands your respect, claiming to introduce computer science but instead delivers an accelerated Python bootcamp, over-reliant on Turtle Graphics to mask its lack of substance. It's playing us for fools.
comment_teaching:
I can only speak to Gibson Lam's teaching. I have heard stories that David Rossiter's teaching is great, but I've never attended his sessions.
Course and grading aside, Gibson Lam is actually a pretty good teacher. There definitely seems to be a strong passion for teaching within him and it shows well during lectures. 
He himself categorizes his teaching style as a style which "Teaches using other things instead of slides" and "Uses new illustrations and examples". But we must be real and ground ourselves in reality, he most definitely makes extensive use of slides.
A first-time learner of computer science may struggle understanding Gibson Lam as he goes into an internal monologue during his teaching, covering important novel concepts incredibly quickly and without much afterthought. That being said, if you can understand his fast spoken English and swift topic switches, learning from Gibson Lam can be both rewarding and interesting.
comment_grading:
An area this course redeems itself a little is the grading. The grade weightings chosen are your best of:
- Midterm 24%, Lab projects 36%, Final exam 40%
- Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%
This does mean that, if you do poorly in the midterm, you can override it with a much better final performance. 
The higher weighting of lab projects is also definitely a bonus to this course. It is completely realistic to achieve full marks in all 3 of the hand-in lab projects. This does reduce the stress of having to perform excellently in the midterms and finals.
However, all of this doesn't quite matter if this course is graded on a curve, for which it is. Despite being an introductory course, you are against the full range of students. There will be students who have never studied computer science and students who have been programming since they were 5. This makes it difficult to achieve top grades in the course and feels to be demotivating for new students who actually were interested in computer science.
comment_workload:
The workload in this course is perfectly reasonable. Only 3 of your 6 lab projects are required to be handed in. You can definitely get away with only ever doing those 3 but do beware of the possible reference of the non-hand-in labs in the exams. 
It would be difficult to severely mess up your labs if you put in any ounce of effort into them. Depending on your understanding of the course, use of AI, etc. the labs should take you anywhere from 20 minutes to 2 hours. You are also able to attend lab session to receive some guidance.
In addition, the course is also open book. You can refer to course material and personal notes during the exams. This can reduce the strain on studying for the exam and does mean the exam covers more computational thinking and logic than memorization. 
In all, COMP1021 may not consume much of your time, but it also won’t ignite your interest in computer science. Thankfully though, it does seem to only be uphill from here.

comment_content:
B-
*Spring 2025 update: I took COMP2011, and added a section about it in grading*
Background before the course: knew pascal (outdated dse language), C#, Unity, (some) C++, (some) Python
Didn't take the C-placement test (which allows one to go directly to comp2011 programming with C++) since I want to secure GPA for CS major. Thus, I am here.
Feels more like a programming intro course suited for novices (can't really complain: I was supposed to be in COMP2011):
-Topics (python): operators, if else, while and for loops, enumerable (list, tuple, string), using modulus for sequence, function, slicing (enumerable[x:y:z]), boolean logic (limited to and, or, not), data type, text file handling, finite state, dictionary, class and object, recursion
-Topics (turtle): basic control, application of loop in graphics, handling input (click, drag, key press), using multiple turtle objects, color coding
Topics are taught in a high-level manner. By high-level, I mean more surface-level (how things behave) than in-depth (how computers cause things to behave). I guess it is for good as this approach doesn't scare off those who know less about programming prior.
While CS concepts like finite state, color coding are introduced, most topics are just programming.
I can't say that this course is entirely unrelated to CS though, since the lab projects introduce students to different fields of CS: 
-Fields: digital art, game developing, digital music, and AI
-Projects: "getting started" (circle art), guessing game, sketchbook, fireworks, lava game, music system, robot thinking
The projects do look appealing, I was quite drawn in to the music one that I made some extra functions like modulating the music. On top of that, the projects aren't too tedious to complete.
However, (kinda hot take) the instructions are sometimes too hand-holding, where they gave too much hints for certain tasks (e.g. straight up the pseudocode for the part). This may hinder students from learning the mindset needed when working on the fields.
I think they should add more optional tasks for students to try out, which can put a stronger emphasis on the fields while not making the course too stressful, hence, doing a better job at introducing CS.
That being said, they provide many useful materials, including example codes, interactive examples, and most importantly previous midterms/finals with video explanation, helpful for those with less advanced background to catch up.

title: Introduction to Turtle (and a bit of Python)
comment_content:
Disclaimer: I am definitely not the intended audience for this course. I have some experience with Python in the past, am taking COMP 2711 as a freshman (which is arguably the better course to be named Introduction to Computer Science), and in the end I got full marks on all content in this course.
This course is intended for total newbies to programming in general, which is a good thing. The course title, however, is a misnomer. I would personally call it "Introduction to Turtle Graphics (and a bit of Python) (and little to none about Computer Science)".
As you can guess, this course focuses mainly on the use of the Turtle module in Python (drawing to the Turtle window, getting text and mouse input from Turtle, and a light introduction to classes by learning to use multiple turtles). It also covers a bit of Python 3.11 (loops, tuples, slicing, functions, and file handling), and barely any Computer Science topics (recursion and state diagrams).
I personally would've hoped for more about list comprehension and less about Turtle in general, since Turtle is rarely used if ever in the real world and list comprehension is 90% of what makes Python useful for all majors (yes, even business majors). The ability to just write 10 lines of code and be able to process and analyze most data you come by on a regular basis is what makes Python invaluable to learn as a beginner, and that's sadly just not covered in this course.
If you are a beginner who wants to learn Python using this course, go for it, just know that there's more to Python than turtle.forward(). If you are familiar with other programming languages and want to learn Python, this course fails to teach what makes Python stand out compared to other languages. And lastly, if you are someone super familiar with Python and programming in general, take this course for a free GPA boost lol

Something I've come to realize in this course is that they assume the absolute minimum in terms of your knowledge in programming, and that's a good thing. The professors would explain concepts in a really high level (high as in more abstract and less about how the computer actually processes instructions), yet also go to such detail and would provide many examples of where you might make mistakes and how to fix them.
The course website has a bunch of useful material for you to practice Python on, including a bunch of interactive examples. The lab assignments contain guided videos for literally every step of the process, and if you still have trouble with the assignments, you can go to the lab sessions where the TA guides you even more. comment_content:
Very easy and fun course for beginners. It teach you about basic Python, including turtle as well. Turtle is covered probably as an interactive way to show how the language works, like loops, functions, if-else statement, etc. Notice it'd probably be useless for later courses though, so if you aim for practical use, you should probably apply for COMP1023 available in recent years.
Laptop is a MUST, especially for exam. They don't allow pen and paper exam format. If you plan to enrol, buy a laptop.

comment_grading:
Good grading. I got perfect 100% grade and A+, but heard that the course is very competitive. Single mistake probably make you miss the A+. 
One thing nearly ruined my midterm: my exam monitor program failed to run due to the antivirus program. One pop up appeared but disappeared quickly. I emailed Rossiter for this after exam and he requested me to his office. But at that time I did able to log in to exam monitor program due to I switched off and on the laptop. I tried different things to replicate the bug, like opening 20 chrome tabs of pdf notes, re-extracting the exam monitoring program exe file from the zip, but they didn't work. Eventually I renamed the exam monitoring program (from "exam-monitor-win.exe" to "exam-monitor-winx.exe") and successfully replicate the bug and pop-up. I immediately captured screen as proof and sent to Rossiter. 
Rossiter is a very strict person, so if you encountered the same situation with me but didn't find the solution, you would eventually get a 0 mark. Be careful with that.
comment_workload:
Very light workload, if you aim for a pass or a reasonable grade. But I practice a LOT for the exams, by grinding past paper problems repetitively and time myself to build up my consistency, accuracy and speed. 
How I train? Skip lectures and read notes. Once exam practice problems (midterm/final) were released, I tried to grind through them one by one. Time limit for each problem is calculated by: 
((problem point) / (total point)) * time limit * 80%. This ensure you're able to do all problems using 80% of time and use remaining 20% to check your work. For those I failed to solve within time limit or got the wrong answer, I'll simply redo it the next day.
Understanding concepts is NOT ENOUGH!! Problem grinding is a MUST!! Since as mentioned, the exams are accuracy and speed oriented. They require deep complex thinking over a narrow curriculum within time pressure. Imagine, can you win grandmaster on chess by just knowing chess rules? Can you AP+ lv15 song in maimai by just knowing now notes work? This explain the importance of repetitive training.
Now about the exam problem type. There's too much of it so I won't waste time here. Basically if you watch all solution videos available, you'll eventually understand how to solve. But I need to mention some things that are not mentioned in solution videos: this course is often joked as a "typing test". When you're doing your exam on your laptop, some code are not copyable and you're expected to dry run it. Sometimes it'd be faster and more accurate and reliable if you just type the whole thing out on Python IDLE. This is allowed in exam. For longer un-copyable code you may need to shorten it yourself, only contain the critical parts and test run it.
Math is required of course. Expect DSE-levelled math. One dry run problem I can remember is to evaluate the final graph drawn by a randomly moving turtle which coordinates are constrainted by some mathematical relation, and that's equivalent to solving some inequalities to find the shape of the region representing the solution set of some simultaneous inequalities.

title: Candid review of COMP1021
comment_content:
COMP1021 is an introductory Python programming course rather than a true introduction to computer science. It's like a Coursera course. Topics include variables, conditions, loops, functions, lists, dictionaries, recursion, basic objects, and extensive use of the Turtle graphics library. Turtle, turtle, turtle and turtle. 
Lectures are engaging and beginner-friendly. Gibson is really chill.
Workload is light. Only a few labs are graded, and assignments are straightforward and can be completed with reasonable effort.
Midterms were manageable but finals are much more difficult, featuring lengthy questions, tricky wording, and significant time pressure. You gonna speed up like really. Exam performance depends heavily on careful reading and avoiding careless mistakes.
I'd say this course is suitable for students with little or no programming background who want to learn Python basics. Students seeking deeper computer science concepts may find the material somewhat superficial.

A well-structured introductory programming course covering Python fundamentals, basic data structures, functions, recursion, object-oriented programming, Turtle graphics, PyGame, and simple user-interface concepts. The course does not cover every Python feature, but its scope is appropriate for beginners.

comment_workload: The overall workload is moderate. Reviewing the lecture slides, practising the example code, and completing the lab exercises should be sufficient for most students. High grades mainly require regular coding practice rather than extensive memorisation.

comment_content: The course provides a broad introduction to Computer Science by covering multiple areas such as game programming, web programming, user interface design, and computer graphics. The variety of topics keeps the course interesting and helps students understand how computing can be applied in different contexts. Using Python as the main programming language makes the content accessible for beginners while still allowing meaningful problem-solving.
comment_teaching: The teaching approach is generally clear and structured, making complex ideas easier to understand for students new to computer science. comment_content: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Python programming, starting from basic syntax and control structures (if–else statements, loops, functions) and gradually moving on to data structures such as lists, tuples, and dictionaries. The use of Turtle and PyGame libraries helps students understand graphical programming, event handling, and basic UI concepts, which makes the learning process more engaging. More advanced topics, including recursion, file input/output, and basic object-oriented programming, are briefly introduced toward the end. While not all Python features are covered, the scope is appropriate for an introductory-level course.
comment_teaching: Lectures are conducted entirely in English, using relatively simple language, although the speaking pace can be fast at times. The quality of teaching materials is high, especially the lecture PowerPoint slides, which are clear, well-organized, and closely aligned with the examinable content. The course website is well maintained and updated weekly. Lab instructors explain concepts step by step and often demonstrate code directly, which is particularly helpful for students with little or no programming background.
comment_grading: Grading is based on a mid-term exam, a final exam, and two assignments. Exams are open-book but still require a solid understanding of program structure, syntax, and data structures, especially list operations. Assignments are generally graded fairly and generously if the required functionality is correctly implemented. Overall, the grading scheme is reasonable, and students who consistently follow the course materials and practice coding should be able to achieve good results.
comment_workload: The overall workload is moderate and manageable. Most learning comes from reviewing lecture slides and understanding the provided code examples rather than extensive memorization. Labs are held weekly and are mostly ungraded, but they are useful for practicing core concepts and preparing for assignments. As long as students keep up with the weekly materials and do not leave assignments until the last minute, the time commitment required for this course is reasonable.

- Midterm 0%, Lab projects 42%, Final exam 58%
This does mean that, if you do poorly in the midterm, you can override it with a much better final performance.
The higher weighting of lab projects is also definitely a bonus to this course. It is completely realistic to achieve full marks in all 3 of the hand-in (marked) lab projects. This does reduce the stress of having to perform excellently in the midterms and finals.
comment_workload:
This course does not have too big of a workload. As mentioned previously, only 3 of your 6 lab projects are required to be handed in. You can definitely get away with only ever doing those 3 but do beware of the possible use of lab concepts in the final exam.
It would be difficult to severely mess up your labs if you put in any ounce of effort into them. Depending on your understanding of the course, use of AI, etc. the labs should take you anywhere from 20 minutes to 2 hours. You are also able to attend lab session to receive some guidance.
In addition, the course is also open book. You can refer to course material and personal notes during the exams. This can reduce the strain on studying for the exam and does mean the exam covers more computational thinking and logic than memorization.
So, COMP1021 may not consume much of your time, but it also won’t ignite your interest in computer science—leaving you with little more than a handful of Python scripts and a lingering sense of disappointment.

Well it is an introduction course so don't expect much from it. In the course, you basically learn how to write Python with turtle, a Python drawing/GUI tool. It basically teaches you variables, if/while/for control flow, a little bit object oriented programing, and other basic things without getting TOO technical. If you already have basic programming skills, you will find this course VERY boring (personal experience).
If you are confident about your programming skills, you can just skip all the lectures and only attend the lectures before the exams just so you know how the online exams work.
===
I just noticed the course description says "students will experience a range of fun and interesting areas from the world of computing, such as game programming, web programming, user interface design and computer graphics". 
... yeah that's complete bs. This course teaches, quite literally, none of that. You could argue the course does *involves* computer graphics and a bit of game programming, but you won't actually *learn* much about those things. I don't know how that gets approved.
comment_teaching: Gibson tries to be engaging, but because the course is so boring, I didn't listened to most of what he teaches. However, I think he didn't give students enough time to think about questions he asked in the class. Because of this, you might find it challenging to acquire the type logical thinking skills you need for the exam (unless you already know programming or you took ICT for the DSE).
comment_grading:
I got an A+ but I heard that the grading is pretty unforgiving if you want to get A or A+. If you make a little more than 2-3 careless mistakes (such as spelling mistakes), your A+ would be gone. However, if you are not aiming for A, the grading can actually be good, because if you messes up the midterm but nails the final, they will automatically discard your midterm result, basically giving you a second chance. 
In the end I got 96 something which is an A+.
Note that, many people found the final exam this semester very difficult, and this is also evident by the mean score of *53.8*. The exam difficulty definitely varies year by year so good luck on that.

There are two different calculating grades system. 
1. Mid-term Exam (open-book, 1 hr) = 20%
   -- Week 7 進行，考試範圍至約全個課程的 40% - 45%
   -- 若不赴考，或將 Mid-term 分計入後會令整體分數更低的話，佔分將變為 0%
   Final Exam (open-book, 2.5 hr) = 40%
   -- 考試週進行，考試範圍為全個課程
   -- 若之前未有赴考 Mid-term，或將 Mid-term 分計入後會令整體分數更低的話，佔分將變為 60%
  Assignment 1: Music System = 20%
   -- Python command-line 文字 program，讀取代表一段音樂的 plain-text file 以輸出 MIDI 音效
   -- 20% 中：Lab 3 & 4 基本完成部分 = 15% + 15% = 30%；額外進階功能 (列出音符及樂器資訊、倒轉音樂等) = 70%     
Assignment 2: Game Project = 20%
   -- Python Turtle 視窗介面的 Space Invader 遊戲，由 user 輸入敵方數目，並就每個 keyboard 及 mouse events 作出回應
   -- 20% 中：Lab 7 & 8 基本完成部分 = 16% + 18% = 34%；額外功能 (遊戲設計主題、自訂音效及 sprite 材質、cheat mode 等) = 66%
Assignment Point = 2% (只適用於 Assignment 1 & 2 總共得分 < 40% 的情況)
   -- Lecture 期間，lecturer 會請學生答問題；同學每次若被選中並答中，將得到一個乒乓球以作記認，下課後可憑球申請取得 2% 的 Assignment Points
   -- 若本身 Assignment 1 & 2 總分已夠 40%，將不會額外得到 2%
   -- 若本身 Assignment 1 & 2 總分不足 40%，將只會為 Assignment 總分最多增至 40%

comment_grading:
Lab gradings are based on strict marking scheme. No room for argument mostly. Not difficult to get full mark for all the labs if you follow through the instructions and tested the code before submission. No late submission allowed.
Midterms and finals are both pretty difficult this year (judged from mean score and SD). The reading-load during exam is extremely huge and the time is VERY tight. No breathing moment definitely. Both of them are divided into two sections (no significant difference in difficulty). Also, both open book, feel free to read any downloaded PDF sources or Python files from your computer, as well as the course website).
Midterm: 25 mins per section, approx. 9 questions per section.
Final: 40 mins per section, approx. 10 questions per section.
Each question may have the length of up to a page or two (for final even THREE!) and you NEED time to digest what the code is trying to do. Most questions are about filling a gap in the code so it works as intended or something like that. Not difficult if given enough time but you just don't have that luxury. All in all I find it a reading comprehension and common sense exam undercovered as Python.
Midterm CAN be omitted as there are two formulae for grading but not recommend to skip midterm since final could be even harder. Just don't bet.

(Lab + Midterm + Final)

36%+24%+40%

42%+0%+58%

title: Introduction to python turtle graphics
comment_content: While turtle graphics can be an engaging way to introduce beginners to programming concepts, placing too much emphasis on it in an introductory Python course may have several disadvantages. First, it limits the scope of learning by focusing primarily on visual and geometric tasks, which may not appeal to students interested in more practical or real-world applications of programming. This narrow focus can lead to a lack of exposure to essential programming concepts such as file handling, data structures, and algorithms, which are more broadly applicable. Additionally, turtle graphics abstracts away key elements of Python syntax and logic, meaning students may struggle to transition to text-based problem-solving or larger coding projects. Overemphasis on graphics might also unintentionally foster a perception that programming is more about drawing than solving diverse problems, potentially alienating students with non-visual learning preferences or career aspirations in data science, web development, or other fields.

title: Very Introductory Turtle Graphics Course
comment_content:
This course offers a preliminary introduction to Python programming, with a particular focus on turtle graphics. Topics covered include:  conditional statements, loops, lists, tuples, dictionaries, turtle graphics, turtle event handling, the RGB color system, text file handling, the turtle coordinate system, objects, functions, and recursion.
While the course content is well-structured for absolute beginners, offering a satisfactory introduction to basic python programming and especially turtle graphics, it might be underwhelming for those seeking a solid foundation in programming.
1. The course does not cover advanced Python features and libraries,  which are crucial for data analysis, scientific computing, and more complex programming tasks. This omission leaves students without knowledge of essential tools that do have wide applications.
2. The course lacks the rigorous training in program design, writing and testing. Although the labs are suitable examples of how to create a small program for beginners, the way they are assigned ruins the opportunity for students to practice and demonstrate programming skills.  The lab only requires creation or modification of a few lines of code in the skeleton code given, which is almost like spoon-feeding. The course simply lacks the rigor university-level courses should have.
3. The course overly emphasizes the use turtle graphics. While turtle graphics might be a fun, intuitive way to introduce beginners to programming, it is not what computer science is really about. Real programming is not just drawing stuff with turtle graphics. Interestingly, turtle as an object is introduced in the beginning of the course, yet the concept of classes and objects are introduced in the last couple of lectures. This arrangement makes the logic of the course incoherent. 
4. The course name is deeply misleading. Computer science is not playing around with turtle and python. Instead, it should cover various different topics such as data structures, algorithms, computer structures, etc.
comment_teaching: Teaching quality for beginners is not bad. Cecia is nice and explains basic concepts in an engaging way.
comment_grading:
Very lenient grading in this year in terms of what percentage of students get good grades. 
The course offers 2 ways of assessment and the final grade will be the higher of the two scores:
1. 36%labs+24%midterm+40%final
2. 42%labs+0%midterm+58% final
While the two ways of assessment might make it seem like the course is tolerant to mistakes, it is completely the opposite. The course is graded on a curve and many students get high scores in the exam, which means that the competition to get good grades is fierce and any unintentional mistake might kill off your A+. 
The reason I still gave the grading a C despite the lenient grading this year is because I'm a little disappointed by the assessments of this course. The labs simply don't require a reasonable amount of work to get full marks. Also, the test does not really reflect coding and problem-solving skills. Instead, it is like a test on reading comprehension and familiarity with turtle. The exams are tough, but the main difficulty is not from designing and writing programs, but is from understanding many very long questions and getting them all correct within very limited time.  Be VERY CAUTIOUS in the exams and the labs. Each mistake can set you back quite a few points. The ways of assessment do not really reflect coding ability.
Here's the statistics for this year's exam:
midterm: mean:54.6, sd: 25.1
final: mean: 55.5, sd: 19.6
You are guaranteed at least an A if you get full marks in labs( be careful don't make any mistakes!) and score mean+ 1SD. Scoring a little above mean (mean +0.5 sd) in exams will get you a B+, and a little below mean is C. This is pretty good grading and the grading is indeed better than previous years, where 1 mistake in exams will approximately cost you a sub-grade, i.e. full marks=A+, 1 problem wrong=A, 2 problems wrong=A-.

comment_content:
Format:
Lectures: 2 sessions per week, around 1 hour each; attendance not counted.
Lectures only use PowerPoint slides from the course website, which are updated weekly.
A textbook written by the lecturer (《Interactive Python Programming for Beginners》, September 2016, around $190) is recommended but not required to complete the assessments.
Labs: 1 session per week, around 2 hours each, attendance not counted.
Labs only use materials from the course website, with a lab task for each session.
Except for the labs required for assignments, no other labs need to be submitted or graded.
Course Coverage: (textbook chapter numbers in brackets)
Programming fundamentals and basic Python functions (03,05,07)
Basic conditional statements (if...elif...else), loops (while, for...in) (05,06)
Basic drawing functions in the Turtle library (02)
Drawing with Turtle using loops (06)
PyGame library's MIDI functionality and time control (time.sleep())
Data Structures: List, Tuple, Dictionary (08)
List and String: Slicing and basic functions (append(), insert(), remove(), extend(), reverse(), ...) (08)
Function structure and operations, global vs local variables, stack, recursion (09)
type(), file read/write (04,13)
Dictionary structure and operations (10)
Dynamic Turtle operations and settings: speed(), tracer(), reset(), shape(), shapesize(), ontimer(), update(), ... (11,12)
Turtle mouse and keyboard event control (12)
Class and Objects (14)
As an introductory course, it is reasonable not to cover all Python features comprehensively (e.g. with..., lambda, exception)
comment_teaching:
Pros:
All-English instruction, though vocabulary is concise and pace is relatively fast
Independent course website (http://course.cse.ust.hk/comp1021)
Course materials including PowerPoint PDFs (color and grayscale versions), code examples are published a week in advance on the website
Lab instructors explain each step and its significance in detail based on website materials, providing actual code when needed, so students who don't understand the code can copy it during labs
Cons:
The first few lectures did not complete the content for that session, causing the teaching progress to lag behind
Lecturers are accustomed to using English, and their pronunciation is sometimes inaccurate

Syllabus of the course: 
- Fundamental functions of Python (variables, Booleans, loops, lists, tuples, strings, slicing, functions, dictionaries, text and file handling in Python, objects)
- Turtle graphic (basic drawing codes, creating new "turtle", dragging and clicking processes, key presses processes, coordinate system, colour changing)

Formula 1: Labs (36%) + Mid-Term (24%) + Final (40%)
Formula 2: Labs (42%) + Final (58%) (Mid-Term not included)
Statistics: 
Lab 1 Mean: 94.4/100
Lab 5 Mean: 90.9/100
Lab 6 Mean: 92.4/100
Mid-Term Mean: 47.2/100
Final Mean: ~66/100
My score: Full mark in all the 3 labs, 41/100 in Mid-Term, 82/100 in Final, 89.5/100 in total (using formula 2)
They will use the highest score from one of the formulas as your final score. It means that you don't have to worry if you get a bad grade in the Mid-term. 
I don't think that this course really gives out good grades. I could only get a B+ with this total score. I got some statistics from others that 91 could only get an A- and you had to have 98 to get an A+. Perhaps there are too many smart students in this course. 
Don't make careless mistakes in the exams anyway. They can really cost a lot in this course.

David教得很好，节奏很舒服。赞！
comment_grading:
# Course grading policy #
There are two ways of grading, and they will choose the one that gives you the higher score. This means that if you didn’t do well in the midterm, you can all in final. For this semester, it seems that the midterm is almost useless because it was much harder than final and most people use the second grading scheme.
Scheme 1: midterm 24% + labs 36% + final 40%
Scheme 2: midterm 00% + labs 42% + final 58%
# Some statistics #
Almost everyone can get full in labs, including me.
Midterm : mean = 47.2/100 || sd = 21.2 || mine = 100
Final : mean = roughly 66/100 || mine = 94
Overall : mine = 97.6% -> A
I’m definitely not satisfied with this letter grade because I only got ONE question wrong in the final exam. In this semester, it seems that only those who get full in overall can get A+. Bad grading.
Labs are easy because there are clear instructions and grading schemes. You can follow the instructions step by step and easily receive full marks.
Midterm is much harder than final this time. As a result, for those who don’t have programming background, all in final is not a bad choice in this semester. However, I think the exam actually does not test your programming ability. The important thing is to avoid careless mistakes. I think they could have designed the exam problems more properly. What’s more, online exams brought many problems. Be careful, otherwise you may get a penalty.

comment_grading:
Two grading methods. 
24% midterm + 36% lab + 40% final 
42% lab + 58% final 
Lab: The lab component consists of seven labs in total, with three of them requiring hand-in submissions. While the labs are not particularly difficult, they can be time-consuming, and it is essential to ensure that everything works correctly and matches the marking scheme before submitting. A single error can significantly impact your lab grade, and the mean score is typically above 90.
Midterm: The midterm consists of two parts, with 25 minutes allotted for each section. However, the midterm in this semester was challenging, with tricky questions that resulted in a mean score below 50. The time is limited, and students cannot think deeply about the questions since they only have an average of 3-4 minutes per question.
Final: The final exam is also divided into two parts, with 40 minutes allotted for each section. The final exam is generally less challenging than the midterm, with a mean score above 65. The final exam includes longer questions that allow students more time to think about their answers.
Overall, it is relatively easy to achieve a normal grade in this course, but it can be challenging to earn an excellent grade (A/A+). A simple mistake can result in losing the entire mark for a question, and the competition among students is fierce.

comment_content:
COMP1021 is generally an introductory course in computer programming or computer science. Here are some key aspects and comments on such a course:
### Course Content
- **Programming Fundamentals:** Introduction to programming concepts, including variables, data types, control structures (loops, conditionals), and functions.
- **Problem-Solving Techniques:** Emphasis on algorithm development and debugging skills.
- **Introduction to Programming Languages:** Often focuses on a specific language (like Python, Java, or C++) to teach core principles.
- **Basic Data Structures:** Understanding arrays, lists, and possibly introductory concepts of object-oriented programming.
### Comments
- **Hands-On Learning:** Practical coding assignments help solidify theoretical concepts and encourage experimentation.
- **Challenging Yet Rewarding:** While some students may initially struggle with programming logic, the satisfaction of solving problems can be highly motivating.
- **Supportive Resources:** Many courses offer tutoring sessions, online forums, and collaborative projects to foster a supportive learning

The course covered some basic concepts in computer science, but I felt it was a bit too focused on turtle graphics. While it was a fun way to learn, it limited the depth of other topics. We touched on important concepts like if statements, for loops, lists, dictionaries, functions, and recursion, but I think there could have been more variety. It would have been great to explore additional programming paradigms or real-world applications of Python to give us a broader understanding of the language and its capabilities. Overall, a more balanced approach would enhance the learning experience.
comment_teaching: You can definitely manage in this course without attending lectures. I didn’t go to any of them and just worked through the PowerPoint presentations and completed the mandatory labs. The materials are pretty well organized, so if you ever feel like you need clarification, you can always watch the lectures later. As long as you stay on top of the labs and engage with the content, you’ll be fine. It’s a flexible approach that allows you to learn at your own pace.
comment_grading: The grading scale in this course feels a bit off. The gap between the B and C ranges is quite wide, making it challenging to get a solid grade. Achieving an A is tough since many students already have a good grasp of the concepts before starting. The mean score for the midterm was around 50-55, and the final was similar, with a mean of about 50. On the bright side, the labs are pretty straightforward, you can usually tackle most of them in just a few hours, and some can even be finished in an hour. Overall, while the labs are manageable, the grading can be pretty competitive, especially for those aiming for top marks.
comment_workload: The course had a pretty light workload, with only 3 mandatory labs out of a total of 6. I’d definitely recommend doing the optional labs as well, since the final exam referenced some of them. If you skip those labs, you might find yourself struggling to answer some of the final questions. Overall, the labs are manageable and a great way to reinforce what you've learned, so taking the time to complete all of them will really pay off in the end.

Contrary to the course title, this course is ACTUALLY NOT an introduction to computer science. Computer science is NOT about writing programs in Python, playing with turtles (pun intended), and call it a day. Computer science IS about analyzing and designing algorithms, optimizing them, and getting to know the low-level details of your computer and how it works (instruction sets, registers, ALU, data bus, programming paradigms).
You say you teach Python, okay, I would at least expect you to teach some of the useful builtin-functions like map, filter, sum, prod (all very functional programming-like), yet, none of these were covered. At least if you cover these, I'd say the course is remotely and weakly related to computer science at all.
Multiplication of sequences by an int to repeat them probably wasn't mentioned.
Don't get me started on useful Python features. WHERE DID LIST COMPREHENSIONS GO? WHERE DID DICTIONARY COMPREHENSIONS GO?
And are you kidding me, turtle graphics? Parts of mid-terms and finals are just geometry problems disguised as Python programming problems. If you want to plot a graph, use matplotlib; if you want to play with multi-dimensional arrays, numpy's got you covered.
For context, I am also taking COMP2711 this semester (yes, and as a year 1 freshman), and it is MUCH MORE appropriate to be the PROPER introduction to computer science. More context will be in my following COMP2711 review after its final exam on 20th.
COMP1021 gives an illusion of what computer science actually is and its difficulty. This should have been a common core course instead. Yes, I'm saying computer science is difficult and it is. You'll know what is actually happening in computer science when you understand what happens further down the road of COMP, namely COMP2012, COMP3711, etc.

The course is called introduction to programming, but in fact the people taking the course typically already know Java or another programming language. If you are truly looking for an introductory programming class, I recommend COMP1021 instead.
The exam papers are far too easy, but there are many tricks that make you lose points. I find these tricks rather pointless, as any free IDE should be able to catch such errors with ease. They include:
- Hidden curly brackets or syntax errors in the LQs
- Poorly phrased questions (eg. how many times is a function called?)
- Easily testable things not taught in lectures (eg. float multiplied by an integer)
None of the content is particularly hard. The course will cover basic variables, conditional statements, expressions, looping, recursion, classes and inheritance, 1D and 2D arrays, and basic data structures (stack and queue). 
If you want to do well, just make sure you do not make any careless mistakes. I have heard that even a 90% is B range in this class.
Overall, I learned very little from this class, and the exam was more focused on trying to trick you rather than testing your ability to think like a programmer.

comment_grading:
Two pathways for grading:
10% labs, 5% written assignment, 20% programming assignment
If midterm score > final score: 25% midterm, 40% final
If final score > midterm score: 0% midterm, 65% final
Most people got 100%s in the labs and programming assignment. In general, people did worse on the written assignment, where the median was 41/50.
Midterm:
LQ: 68.75/100 Median: 77.5/100 UQ: 90.5/100
Final:
LQ: 74/100 Median: 86.5/100 UQ: 92.5/100
In general, people did better on the final than the midterm for 2 reasons. First, the final was arguably easier than the midterm. Second, due to the existence of pathway 2, your midterm score does not matter if you do well on the final, so we were more incentivized to revise for the final exam.
I scored 92/100 on the midterm but 97/100 on the final. Through pathway 2, my weighted score was around 98/100, and I scored an A+.
The reason I rated the grading for this course so low is because I have heard many negative things about the grading. As everyone is competent at programming in this course, the median is naturally very high. As such, even a few marks is enough to knock you down a grade.

Recursion is the hardest across all papers, e.g. recursion with a stack ADT, subset sum problem, and generate permutations. Solving these problems becomes formulaic since they involve iterating through the array/string ONCE and doing recurrence relationships with each item.

Raymond is an exceptional teacher. After each lesson, he stays to clarify any confusion regarding the course material, ensuring that every question is answered before the session ends. If any questions arise after class, students can easily reach him via email, and he responds with detailed and thorough explanations promptly.
A unique aspect of the course is the "coupon" policy, which has two main uses:
Assignment Waiver: The coupon can be used to waive one question on an assignment, granting full points regardless of whether the answer is correct or even submitted. This is particularly useful if you're struggling with a specific question or if you're racing against the deadline and can't complete all the tasks (not that anyone would have personal experience with that).
Project Advantage: It can also secure full marks on one part of a project, which might otherwise be challenging to achieve without utilizing the coupon.
Coupons can primarily be earned in two ways: by answering questions posed by Raymond during lessons or by providing solutions for the "in-class exercise" (which will be further discussed in the 'workload' section). However, if you’re hesitant about answering questions quickly or feel unsure about completing the "in-class" exercises, there’s no need to worry. As the semester progresses, Raymond will inquire whether students have coupons. For those who do not, he will offer opportunities to answer questions, making it highly likely that everyone will earn at least one coupon, which is especially encouraged for use in projects.

The workload for this course is manageable, comprising only two homework assignments and one project over the semester.
Homework
There are two homework assignments: one before the midterm exam and one afterward. Each assignment consists of four to five questions that assess your understanding of the course material. For someone like me, who tends to learn the material while doing homework, it takes about five hours to complete each assignment—roughly one hour per question. This is relatively light compared to the two-month deadlines for each assignment.
Project
The bulk of the course workload is centered around the project, which can be completed individually or in pairs. The project consists of three phases, and as long as you follow Raymond's guidance, achieving a full score is quite feasible. In fact, the average score for the project is over 90%. As a solo participant, I spent about three days on the project, which may sound like a lot, but is actually quite light given the generous deadlines.
In-Class Exercises (Optional)
Raymond offers in-class exercises during lessons, which are discussed in the following class. If you feel confident, you can arrive a bit early to show your answers to Raymond. If your answer is correct, you can earn a "coupon." However, participation in these exercises is entirely optional; I personally never participated in them before exam revisions.
Attendance
During lessons, there are iPRS questions that grant you marks simply for participating, regardless of whether your answers are correct.

comment_content:
1.Association: Apriori and FP-growth

5.Data Warehouse: find out which data to enquire with lowest cost
6.Web Databases: HITS and PageRank
Midterm exam covers topic 1,2 and 3 except neural network and accuracy measurement. Final exam covers all topics. 1 past paper and solution is provided for each exam. Some questions in the exam are the same as past paper, it is a good idea to print some past paper answers on the cheatsheet. A calculator is required for the exam. Paper checking session is held after each exam. The exam format is determined by a poll in class. Number of multiple choice questions, time, difficulty, whether there is bonus question that is extremely difficult and whether he allows a cheatsheet change every year.
Topic 2 and 3 are same as COMP2211. These topics introduce different models that observe the pattern of some data and make predictions, it shows you how artifical intelligence works. I find these topics useful and interesting. COMP2211 focuses on programming and math while this course focuses on drawing diagram, memorize how an algorithm works and less math. Do not take this course if you are bad at math. If you took COMP2211 before, you will study 2 less topics. If not, you can attend COMP2211 lectures in addition to this course to have a better understanding on these topics.
The class schedule for this course is Monday 1.30-2.20pm, Friday 9-10.20am at LTB in 2025 and 2026, 280 students enrolled with no one in the waitlist, it is possible that the class schedule remains the same so you should expect 9am classes if you take this course.
This course is a technology common core course. Even SENG students do not need technology common core, they can take this course to substitute CTDL or UROP. I would like to compare this course with other technology common cores.
ELEC1010 counts tutorial attendance while this course doesn’t. The teaching from its instructor, Guan Isabel, is worse than this course. Students who study physics or ICT in secondary school should take ELEC1010 while students who have good math, study math extended module 1 or 2 should take this course.
COMP1945 requires group presentation. It has no midterm exam, its final exam covers everything so you need to revise more materials, it has higher workload than this course.
MECH1905 has less workload than this course but the teaching from its instructor, Lee Yi-Kuen is worse than this course.
ENVR1030 suits students who are bad at math. It requires less calculation and more writing. The waitlist is long and is hard to enroll.
comment_teaching:
In the lecture, Raymond introduces the algorithm, writes some notes that he shows it under the projector and uploads to canvas after class, distribute in class exercises, ask 1-3 questions on iPRS and ask challenging questions that he will give a coupon to the one answered. He teaches well, he provides explanation on algorithms and demonstrate how to complete the exercises. Lecture videos are available.
If you look for excellent teaching, for topic 2 and 3, you can attend COMP2211 lectures in addition to this course. The instructor is Desmond Tsoi, I believe you like the teaching.
You are required to answer 20 iPRS in order to obtain the full score (10%) for the in-class participation, it counts no matter whether you answer it correctly or not. In 2026 Raymond asked 26 iPRS questions in class. For students who hate 9am classes, you can skip around 4 classes while obtain full attendance, only 7x 9am classes remains. I think the workload is actually pretty manageable.
To be honest, there are just a total of two homework and one project to be submitted in this course.

If you are uncertain about some challenging questions, you can simply consult the professor or find the TA during the tutorials. There is no reason to think the workload is very heavy.
The project contains three phases, with each phase requiring you to complete certain tasks. The first two phases are pretty easy because it only requires you to collect data and test the model. comment_content:
There are 3 assignments: The first one getting us familiar with video editing, the second one focusing on the use of greenscreen & the 3rd one on music remix. comment_workload:
This is my own subjective opinion only, because my experience in video editing is little to none :p
The workload for this course is extremely intense, if you're not familiar with video editing beforehand, and are aiming to get good grades. For each of the submissions, you have to make a 1~2 minute video (2~3 for the final project), and a commentary video on what you have created. Basically:
-You better have some creative ideas, and don't be afraid to express them. Otherwise, picking the right topic for each video may be quite exhausting & time-consuming!
-The professor values the level of detail in your videos quite a bit, stuff like matching the BGM frame-by-frame, how you apply greenscreen/other techniques to make the video that much funnier/realistic...so if you want to get the good scores, prepare to work sleeplessly/over a few days on the videos : ) I didn't sleep AT ALL the day before each submission.
-Get yourself a teammate. The work can be done by a group of 2, so find a friend & you'll half the workload. I sure relied on my friend quite a bit, couldn't have gotten this far without my bro. (Sike, both of us still went sleepless working on it, so yeah)
-The main video is important, but the commentary may be even more important. The commentary can be a pretty fun video filled with memes or a bit more serious (like an actual commentary), but whatever your style is, you'll want to pick out some of the most important/overlooked details from the main video & explain how those moments were made, instead of just replaying the entire video with some subtitles going over it :p
TL;DR, if you want to enjoy a common core with light workload, this is NOT the place for you. If you like video editing & are willing to either spend 15~20+ hours on each assignment on average, or is OK with getting a lower grade, then this will be a fun course for ya :)

comment_grading:
In this course, you have to hand in 4 works in total, also some research ratings, here's the composition:
3 Assignments (45%: 10, 20, 25%), 
Project (35%), 
Peer & research ratings (10%)
The research rating would come from the research released by the TAs in Canvas, just follow the instructions and submit them on time. Then you could get easy full marks on this part.
For each assignment/project (what we called "MIA"), you had to submit:
1. a 2-3 minute work ("masterpiece")
2. a directory commentary video of your work, "includes inspirations, creative process, storytelling, video and music magic tricks, and other cool secrets." according to the source.
Your MIA's grade would come from 3 factors:
1. Professor Horner
To be honest, grading from Prof. Horner is kinda biased: he has a strong preference in so-called 'wacky-twists', in which does not favor in any really slow-paced or 'plain' work. Please have some mental preparation.
2. TAs.
3. Your peer grading:
It's done by Canvas quiz in every lecture: it would count toward your attendance so please do the quizzes. 
All you have to do is to grade everyone's work out of 5 (refer to the following rubric) and leave your comments.
However, there's some students that just leave the comments empty and randomly give marks so that they could fake the attendance :(. It could strongly affect the totals marks given to everyone.
So, please do attend, enjoy the lecture, and do grade and comment your peer's work :) That would be helpful to everybody.

Wow-factor of creation video (and behind-the-scenes video), count out of 5:
5/5: Super inspired
4/5: Very inspired
3/5: Inspired

1/5: Uninspired

title: Not recommended for people who solely take Broadening CC's for the credits requirement
comment_content:
3 assignments and 1 final project. The first assignment is making a mash-up of the audio from one source with the video of another. The second is using green-screen techniques to combine characters from different media into one setting. The third is making a music video mashup incorporating elements from multiple songs or remixing a given song. The final project is basically do whatever you want, there are no rules (except be really creative). Each submission requires a 1-2 minute video of your work, and a corresponding 1-2 minute commentary video describing your creative and technical choices (except the final project, which is 2-3 minutes for both the video + commentary). You can work on the video yourself or in groups of 2 people (if you want to have a more manageable workload highly recommend you find someone to work with). 
I can totally see people submitting the same types of content for all 4 assignments, as the criteria for all of them were pretty loose and are generally quite friendly towards whatever your passions or interests are.
comment_teaching:
A course that rewards those who self-learns everything and/or already have a developed hobby in music and video making.
Almost no in-class teaching was done. Prof. Horner does enthusiastically go over other people's creations (from this semester + previous semesters) in class and gives out a lot of artistic and a few technical suggestions, but these largely do not really help that much beyond video ideation. The comments he gives you after you submit your video are all just positive remarks like "Great techniques!" or "Amazing idea!", don't expect to receive actual feedback for your video (courtesy of the TA's) until after your video is shown and peer-reviewed.
Other people previously claimed that there were tutorials provided which help students who don't have that much experience get started. My opinion is that this is only to a small extent; these tutorials aren't really that helpful if you want to really impress them and get a decent grade, they either just suggest a few techniques and tools or they're way too esoteric for most people to understand, and many of them really are only for one purpose (ex. they provided a lot of deepfake AI tool tutorials for the final project, which wouldn't be that useful if you don't want to do something like that). Especially noteworthy if you aren't coming from a field or profession where sound/video design is researched or video editing is used, or you aren't a graphics design major at heart, most of the tutorials also use apps and features which either are pretty finicky to use or turns out are behind a paywall. In fact, in my opinion it is really difficult to obtain a decent grade in this course without spending several hundred dollars on video and audio editing software/AI tools (ex. video editing tools: Final Cut Pro is a one-off 2300 HKD purchase, the standard subscription for Capcut premium is 60 HKD/month which you have to purchase to do literally anything (seriously, even splitting audio and video from a clip requires Capcut premium), Davinci Resolve is free but most advanced techniques besides plugins require a subscription that costs 230 HKD/month, the full range of adobe software requires at least a 400 HKD/month subscription to use etc., iMovie is free to use if you have a Mac but I do NOT recommend it for this course as it is so basic and there are so little features). 
Of course, you could have a really creative premise that compensates a lack of technology with either a really good storyline or clever artistic choices, but this is HARD to do especially without making it look or sound like it's "low-budget".
As I am only taking this to complete my last Broadening CC requirement and I have some basic experience in video editing (due to some random stuff i did for a university club a few years ago), the only two subscriptions I purchased was a standard plan for Runway ML (so I could survive assignment 2) and Capcut Premium, both of which I swiftly cancelled after I finished my final project (Audacity, GarageBand (for Mac users), and the base version of Davinci Resolve were free). Even then, I had to rely on my experience on playing an instrument for several years and having a decent knowledge in music theory for assignment 3 and the final project to get a good grade. I recommend you take this course if you're already passionate in video editing and music creation and have or know how to use several of the tools recommended by this course, if not RUN AWAY.

comment_workload:
4 video projects only, seems light right?
NO.
Firstly, the assignment due dates are absolutely atrocious. Assignment 1 due in the middle of add/drop period, assignment 2 right before midterm period, assignment 3 in the middle of midterm period, final project right after midterms end. I constantly found working on these videos got in the way of a ton of other stuff I was doing (for a year 4 student working on postgraduate/job applications, and I anticipate most people taking this course is year 4 given how fast COMP1943 turns from available to waitlist during the first day of course reg, this is borderline hellish). 
Also, one only realizes how much effort you need to put into each video when you actually do it. Having the idea is one thing. Executing it is a whole other situation. Prof. Horner and his TA's value quantity AND quality, videos that approach the 2 (or 3) minute limit and are full of artistic details and techniques. Even if you spent a massive amount of time and energy on your assignment, or you have a really good idea, they won't judge you on your idea alone if it looks like you had trouble achieving what you wanted to do.
Don't sleep on the commentary video either, to get a higher grade its not really that suggested to just add subtitles to a running clip of your workspace, instead a separate edited video that explains every important thing you did. The first two assignments I just added subtitles to a video recording of my Capcut workspace for my commentary (because I ran out of time) and neither were received very well. Some people went above and beyond and made their commentary video seemingly more amusing and detailed than their actual assignment, especially if their original video revolves around a theme/subject that isn't very well known by many people (ex. certain sports like F1 or football), but this obviously takes a lot of time. 
(also, quick PSA but please do not just throw a ton of prompts into GenAI tools and make slop videos, it gets extremely boring and repetitive after several watches)
I only spent around 8 hours working on Assignment 1, as the prompt wasn't too difficult to achieve and I already knew before the class began what I wanted to do. However, I had to spend almost 20 hours for Assignment 2 to learn Davinci Resolve, masking, green screen etc., and the TA's still thought my video was pretty mediocre. To make up for this, I spent a bit more time (~25 hours) composing and remixing the song for my Assignment 3, which paid off. Finally, I spent around 30 hours total for the final project making both my audio and video components. This course ain't for you if you don't have any free time or if you value your sleep schedule (although during midterm season most people probably don't value it anyways), I had to pull near all-nighters for these assignments.

comment_grading:
The grading scheme is a ridiculous patchwork: Participation (attendance) 15%, Quizzes 10% (four at 2.5% each), AI news presentation 5% (individual), Reading response 15% (individual) plus 5% peer review, Case study analysis 15% (individual) plus 5% peer review, Debate (group) 15%, and Debate review (individual) 15%, total 100%. 
Anything that has a peer review means that 20% of that item’s weight comes from an anonymous classmate while the TA accounts for the other 80%, so your final mark on a task can be dragged down by one random student’s whim. For example, if the TA gives you 10/15 but a classmate gives 5/15, your weighted score suddenly becomes 9/15. They say you can appeal anonymous reviews only for “obvious inconsistency” or “unreasonable/unrelated” comments, but who decides what’s unreasonable?
These tiny percentages seem insignificant on their own, but they pile up and can wreck your final grade. I was pretty much average on everything (except the debate, where my team got crushed because one single "smart" person hogged two minutes in the free-debate slot and half our team score evaporated), and even being near the mean didn’t spare me from the system’s hair-trigger penalties.
comment_workload:
The grading scheme is a mess. Tons of little sections and one real pain: a formal debate. Yep, an actual timed debate with multiple speakers. In the free-debate bit everyone gets 5 minutes total, but you must swap every ~30 seconds. If your teammate can’t read a timer and hogs 2+ minutes in one turn, congratulations! You just lost half the 15% debate mark.
Quizzes are “open book” but you get only 10 minutes. Three questions are based on a ~10‑page PDF and expect quick, precise answers; the fourth asks you to respond to a Netflix documentary shown in class. Good luck doing that well in 10 minutes.
There’s also a 30-minute “news” presentation at the start of many lectures that must cover AI news from the previous 14 days only. If you present on Nov 20, you can only use items from Nov 6 - 19, which makes finding relevant AI news a matter of luck some weeks.
This is treated as a common-core course, but the workload and micro-requirements feel totally inappropriate and needlessly strict.
