In terms of difficulty, (in my opinion) they would be arranged (from easiest to hardest)
Logic < Graphs < Algorithms < Number Theory < Combinations < Probability 
The topics taught in:
Logic-- are relatively easy, just make sure not to make careless mistakes for these questions
Graphs-- are mostly "proof" questions. They won't ask you much about graph theory as it will be discussed more in year 3
Algorithms-- understand clearly what big O,theta, and omega are, and you're good to go
Number Theory questions are usually about decrypting texts and stuff like that, which are things that you can memorise. So these questions are practically free marks (unless you're careless)
Combinations and Probability-- now these questions are always tricky. A particular TA named Arman always creates creative and tricky questions. You cannot do these questions through sheer memorisation. You have to use your brain and aimlessly think of methods, which is why it is the hardest.
Comp2711 has a telegram group where you can ask questions to the TAs, and usually get an instant response, which I love.

comment_content:
The following key topics are taught:
- Propositional Logic: Including operators, equivalences, proofs using laws (without truth tables), and rules of inference.
- Predicate Logic: Including quantifiers (∀, ∃), expressing statements with predicates, negation of quantified statements, and formal proofs.
- Sets and Functions: Including set operations (intersection, union, complement, subsets), proofs (direct and contrapositive), countability/uncountability of sets (e.g., natural numbers, functions from N to N, binary strings), and bijections.
- Counting Principles: Including permutations, combinations, binomial coefficients, arrangements with restrictions (e.g., adjacency, no two alike adjacent), unordered pairs, palindromes, and paths in graphs (without reusing edges).
- Combinatorial Proofs: Proving identities using combinatorial reasoning (e.g., involving subsets and distinct elements).
- Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: Applied to counting problems (e.g., digits in numbers with specific constraints).
- Pigeonhole Principle: Applied to grid-based problems (e.g., colored cells sharing corners).
- Probability: Including basic probabilities, binomial distributions, and scenarios with independent events (e.g., catching flies).
- Random Variables: Including expectation (E), variance (var), linearity of expectation, independence, and comparisons (e.g., E(X^2) vs. E(XY) for dice rolls).
- Graphs
- MOD
- Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT)

2. Remember some important concepts even it is open-book. It saves your time on finding concepts in your note during final.
3. Don't simply print all powerpoint slides. Try to summarize the content in the slides as your own note documents and print your own note during final. It helps you to have better understandings on concepts and reduce the number of pages of your notes.

comment_content: The course is mainly based on Principles of Microeconomics (10th edition) by N. Gregory Mankiw, published by South-Western, Cengage Learning. The material itself is very basic microeconomics. The lectures do not strictly follow the order of the textbook, and by the end of the semester we roughly reached the chapter on monopoly. As an introductory course, the content is actually quite thought-provoking and sometimes interesting, especially if you have never formally studied economics before. That said, as a core business school requirement, you do not really have a choice about whether to take it or not.
comment_teaching:
Li Xuan’s lecturing is honestly not very effective. She tends to look down while speaking, and although her pronunciation is fine, her pauses and sentence breaks can be quite confusing during lectures. However, her understanding of the subject is strong. When you ask questions after class, she explains concepts very clearly and in a fairly intuitive way. The issue is more about in-class delivery than ability.
In contrast, Victor’s tutorials are very well structured. He does a great job highlighting the key points, walking through examples step by step, and making the logic behind each concept very clear. Concept comparisons and distinctions are explained thoroughly. After the first midterm, I stopped going to lectures and only attended tutorials. My personal approach was to go through the lecture material on my own and then rely on tutorials, which turned out to be quite efficient for me.
comment_grading:
The grading is very student-friendly, and there are two different schemes you can choose from.
Scheme (1): Two midterms
Problem Sets: 10%
1st Midterm: 15%
2nd Midterm: 15%
Final Exam: 60%
Scheme (2): One midterm counted
Problem Sets: 10%
Higher Midterm: 25%
Final Exam: 65%
Personally, I scored 54/60 on both midterms, 84/100 on the final, and got full marks on all problem sets, which resulted in an A+. Overall, the grading is quite generous, and the instructor clearly tries to help students perform well.
comment_workload:
The workload is relatively light. There are ten problem sets in total. If you complete them on your own, each usually takes around 1.5 to 2.5 hours, depending on your background. Of course, if you simply look up answers online, half an hour is probably enough. Personally, I do not think the problem sets are very helpful for the final exam.
Both midterms are multiple-choice. Before the exams, I did as many past paper questions as I could find, probably over two hundred in total, which helped a lot with exam familiarity. The final includes both multiple-choice and written questions, and there are no past papers available. My approach was to use AI to generate concept comparison questions, since Li Xuan’s exam style is quite textbook-based and focuses heavily on definitions, concepts, and some logical extensions. The written questions are relatively challenging. My suggestion is to fully understand the provided sample questions. Even though the actual exam questions are not very similar, working through the samples helps you get used to the question types.

comment_content:
Microeconomics is the branch of economics that focuses on individual agents, such as households and firms, and their interactions in markets. Here’s an overview of the key concepts and topics typically covered in microeconomics:
1. Basic Principles of Microeconomics
Scarcity and Choice: Understanding the fundamental economic problem of limited resources and the necessity of making choices.
Opportunity Cost: The cost of forgoing the next best alternative when making decisions.
2. Supply and Demand
Law of Demand: As prices decrease, quantity demanded increases, and vice versa.
Law of Supply: As prices increase, quantity supplied increases, and vice versa.
Market Equilibrium: The point where supply and demand curves intersect, determining the market price and quantity.
3. Elasticity
Price Elasticity of Demand: Measures how much quantity demanded changes in response to price changes.
Price Elasticity of Supply: Measures how much quantity supplied changes in response to price changes.
Income and Cross Elasticities: Understanding how demand changes with consumer income and prices of related goods.
4. Consumer Behavior
Utility Maximization: The concept of consumers seeking to maximize their satisfaction from goods and services.
Budget Constraints: How consumers allocate their income to various goods and services.
Indifference Curves: Graphical representation of consumer preferences and trade-offs.
5. Production and Costs
Production Functions: The relationship between inputs (labor, capital) and output.
Short-Run vs. Long-Run Costs: Understanding different cost structures and their implications for firms.
Economies of Scale: The cost advantages that firms experience as they increase production.

Content: A

Part 4: The medium run (AS-AD model) - Ch6-7 (6th edition) 
Textbook: Macroeconomics, Global Edition, written by Olivier Blanchard (and David R. Johnson), published by Pearson Education Inc. (6th edition preferred)
The content of this course is much more difficult than ECON 2103/ECON 2113 (microeconomics) as macroeconomics looks at the economics at a broader perspective. Therefore, even the diagrams may look the same as the microeconomics diagrams like supply and demand, the reasons behind the diagrams are totally different from one another, so you need to put much more time to understand every logical approach and concept.
The lecture notes are pretty comprehensive and include most of the essential concepts, logics and details for the exams and homework.
However, you should be aware that you need to combine the content from different lecture materials to get the whole picture of a model, like AS-AD model, in order to answer the difficult questions in the exams.

comment_content: It's quite interesting how relevant macroeconomics is to our lives, allowing us to study the overall functioning of the economy, including how interest rates impact output (GDP), how government policies influence economic conditions, and the relationship between output and price levels through various models. It’s certainly more complex than microeconomics, with many more factors to consider. The course outline begins with Part 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics (Ch. 1-2), which introduces key concepts such as GDP, inflation, and unemployment. Part 2: The Short-Run Closed Economy (IS-LM Model) (Ch. 3-5) explores the goods and financial markets, combining them to construct the IS-LM model and applying it to predict and explain the effects of fiscal and monetary policies, both individually and collectively. These first two parts comprise nearly half of the course, making it crucial to fully understand these concepts as they are foundational for the remainder of the material. Part 3: The Short-Run Open Economy (IS-LM-UIP Model) examines trade, exports, and imports, revisiting concepts from Part 2 while introducing new ideas like real depreciation, interest parity conditions, and flexible versus fixed exchange rates. Part 4: The Medium Run (AS-AD Model) (Ch. 6-7) discusses the labor market and the AS-AD model, integrating it with the IS-LM model, while Part 5: The Long Run (Solow Model) (Ch. 10-12.1) explores the interactions between output and capital, the effects of the savings rate on capital, output, and consumption, as well as the concept of balanced growth. For me, Parts 3 and 5 are the most challenging, while many find Part 4 the hardest; perhaps my lack of DSE economics background makes it easier for me to grasp new concepts that diverge from the DSE syllabus.

title: Essential course for life! (See the questions/answers to some of sample final exam questions)
comment_content:
This is a common core course for HKUST business school students. In this introductory course to
macroeconomic theory and policy analysis, we will introduce the ways economists look at
economy from an “aggregate” perspective. We will start by introducing key macro variables that
measure aggregate economic performance. The relationship among these key variables will then
be studied under three timeframes: the short run, the medium run, and the long run.
In the short run, we will analyze the goods and financial markets, which form the foundation of
the IS-LM model. A closed economy will be examined first, followed by an open economy in the
short run. We will then move on to the labor market and put all three markets together to derive
the AS-AD model in the medium run. Lastly, if time permits, we will further examine key aspects of
economic growth in the long run. Altogether, the theoretical framework presented in this course
will enable you to predict and analyze the impacts of government fiscal and monetary policies on
the economy. The basic teaching materials closely follow the textbook and lecture notes.
I will use real world examples as much as possible to enhance your understanding of the course
materials. We always hear news and commentaries regarding economic growth, unemployment,
inflation, interest rate, national debt, and financial crisis, etc. Upon completion of this course, you
should be able to understand some of these views and concerns, and to perform your own
analysis in your daily life.

Interesting course but way harder than microeconomics. Step by step way of teaching where each topic adds on previous understanding making models more and more complicated but easy to follow.

II. The Short Run

b. Financial Markets and The LM Relation (Chapter 4): Week 4

Week 5

comment_content: This course provides an introduction to macroeconomics. Be honest, the workload is heavy. If you expect to work hard only before midterm and final, then you may not get good results.

What you should do before midterm and final is NOT understanding concepts, but immerse yourselves into practice questions, in which I will mention in the later part. You should understand the concepts much more early than that.
TAs prepare many self-practice questions. It's nearly impossible to do all of them since it's too much and we still have other courses. If you're not pursuing good grades, you may simply neglect them. If you want to get As, then you should try to read all questions, and understand the answers in case you have no idea on any particular questions (Some questions is not well-designed, you have to identify them and prevent wasting time on them).
Talking about the midterm and final, it is a combination of MCQs and LQs, and more calculation-oriented and diagram-oriented. You need to make sure you understand how to calculate and how to draw diagram in both midterm and final. Well, there is some question like "What is GDP", but the grading is quite lenient, and is not like you must give a formal definition in order to get full mark. To sum up, make sure you understand the calculation and PRACTICE ALL POSSIBLE DRAWINGS of diagram before midterm and final.
My recommendation is: If the ppt shows how to draw the dynamics of, let's say, AS-AD model, under an increase in G, then you can practice to draw the dynamics of AS-AD under a decrease in G and check whether the consequences of all economic variables are opposite to the one on the ppt.

(Latest : READ GRADING SECTION for the stupid rant)
Before I start with this review, I would like to be clear:
This course is now ELEC 1150. The majority of the course remains the same, except for several changes here and there. The reason I'm writing a new review here, is... well, frankly, I'm having my ELEC 1150 final in... around 13 hours. And I have a COMP 2011 final the next day. But I really don't want to revise and just wanna give up. Plus I wanna rant about this rubbish course and inform anyone who comes across my review about what this course is actually like.
When (if) the USTSPACE course page for ELEC 1150 shows up, I will copy this review there.
---------- CONTENT ----------
This course introduces various concepts in the world of IT, from its historical breakthroughs to computer components and how they work, to the rise of the Internet and how data is transferred, and to how modern-day AI works in general. Basically, to anyone who is familiar with the HKDSE ICT subject (though, admittedly, my knowledge is from the "old" ICT curriculum, before they changed it in the 2025 HKDSE exams), this course's content will seem quite familiar to you, for instance in places like computer architecture (ALU, CU, etc.), protocols and how they transfer data packets, and data encryption (public keys, private keys, etc.).
The following list details what the course covers, across 10 lectures:
- Dawn of The Information Technology Revolution
- The Mystery of Electricity
- Digital Age: The Power of 0 & 1
- The Amazing Chip
- The Silicon Revolution
- Five Generations of Computing
- Claude Shannon and Information Theory
- Wired and Wireless Communications
- Cryptography and Secrets of the Web
- Coding World
- The Internet and World Wide Web
Now that I've listed it out, actually they did change quite a few parts of this course from the previous years.
The content itself, is... fine. Honestly, the syllabus is fine to me. Not too bad. Kinda boring and kinda useless. They could've gotten more in depth for numerous topics, perhaps, but owing to the fact that this is a common core course (and being in the "Technology" area, meaning students from SENG, I believe, aren't even supposed to take courses like this, unless they took this as a free elective or to replace UxOP/CTDL... which is what I opted for), the instructors were probably limited on what they could do.
I mean, yes. I personally enjoy reading about scientific and technological discoveries and whatnot, but I'd typically just search all of this up on Wikipedia in my own time.
I had thought that this course, with all these topics, should appeal to my weird brain quite a lot, and thus decided to enroll into this course, ignoring the comments saying not to (that, and because it didn't seem like a difficult course to get good grades in). Well, HAHAHAHA. More on this in the TEACHING section (the majority of my issues with this course are with the teaching).
(I'll admit...as of typing this line, it's 4 in the morning and... I don't wanna do an all-nighter just to type out a review. So, I'm going to write down really short, general ideas of what I had wanted to express, and come back to this review in a week or so, after I finish my final exams. I will also attach resources to this review when I return.)

comment_teaching:
App Design:
App design refers to the process of creating the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) for mobile applications. 
1. User Research: Before starting the design process, it's essential to understand the target audience and their needs. User research helps in identifying user preferences, behaviors, and pain points.
2. Wireframing and Prototyping: Wireframing involves visualizing the app's layout and structure. It helps in planning the app's navigation and functionality. Prototyping involves building interactive mockups to test and validate design concepts.
3. UI Design: User interface design focuses on creating visually appealing and intuitive interfaces. It involves selecting colors, typography, icons, and other visual elements to create a cohesive, user-friendly design.
4. UX Design: User experience design focuses on enhancing user satisfaction and usability. It involves creating seamless user flows, optimizing interactions, and ensuring the app meets the user's goals.
5. Usability Testing: Usability testing involves evaluating the app's design by observing users' interactions and collecting feedback. It helps identify usability issues and refine the design accordingly.
3D Modeling:
3D modeling is creating a three-dimensional representation of objects or scenes using specialized software. Here are some areas where 3D modeling is widely used:
1. Animation and Visual Effects: 3D modeling is extensively used in the entertainment industry for creating animated films, video games, and visual effects. It involves creating realistic characters, environments, and special effects.
2. Product Design and Prototyping: 3D modeling is used in product design to create virtual prototypes and visualize concepts before manufacturing. It enables designers to test different variations and make necessary modifications efficiently.
3. Architecture and Interior Design: 3D modeling is employed in architecture and interior design to create virtual representations of buildings, interiors, and landscapes. It helps architects and designers visualize and present their ideas to clients.
4. Medical and Scientific Visualization: 3D modeling is used in the medical field to create anatomical models for surgical planning, prosthetics, and medical education. It is also used in scientific research for visualizing complex data and simulations.
5. Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR): 3D modeling plays a crucial role in creating immersive experiences in VR and AR applications. It involves building virtual environments and objects that users can interact with in real time.
By learning about app design and 3D modeling, you can acquire valuable skills that can open up exciting career opportunities in industries like software development, gaming, multimedia, architecture, and more.

title: Interesting Course-- From Critical Review of Everyday Environmental Choices to Responsibilities of Different Groups Towards Sustainability
comment_content:
This course examines how everyday lifestyle choices—such as food, clothing, and product use—impact sustainability in the context of climate change and resource limitations. While many individuals aim to consume responsibly, unclear environmental claims, complex product compositions, and hidden production processes often make it difficult to assess the true sustainability of goods and services.
Using a product life-cycle approach, the course investigates what makes products sustainable or unsustainable. It also explores the psychological, social, and economic factors that influence consumer behavior and how these behaviors can be shifted toward more sustainable patterns. Through interactive exercises, discussions, and local case studies focused on consumption in Hong Kong, students gain insight into how businesses and governments can support informed and responsible consumer choices.

comment_content:
Professional yapper, that's what the lecture notes are. So many specific words without explanation, and intentionally using unpopular words. It almost feel like a secondary school student writing where they forcefully use difficult word to yap, but in fact nobody actually use those words. For example, "anthropogenic", guess a more popular word, "human-made". Idk what's the point of using such words. Also, Idk what I have learnt except for memorizations.
Edit: Some contents of the lecture notes are contradicting, but no TAs nor the professor seemed to care nor explained, leaving us in confusion. And the the contradiction was not due to our perception, but literally in the way of "Statement A is false" in slide1, and "Statement A is true" in slide 2. It was 2 consecutive slides, so IDK how they didn't catch that.

comment_content:
In the first 10 lessons, Alexis did a great job covering important topics such as the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, the Hong Kong Climate Action Plan, and other fundamental concepts in environmental science. These discussions on current issues added value to the class and provided beneficial insights.
However, the format of the lessons changed afterwards and became challenging. Each lesson involved three groups giving presentations, followed by IPRS where we had to provide feedback on what we learned, suggestions for improvement, ask questions, and rate their performance. The unexpected aspect was that our comments were graded by the instructor/TAs, something that was not clearly communicated during class or when explaining the logistics. Furthermore, we were unaware of the marking criteria, which added to the confusion. Additionally, the IPRS for the big topics seemed more reliant on luck rather than actual study material.
Overall, I found the course to be uninteresting. Most of the content was presented by students who seemed to recite information they found online or in books without genuine enthusiasm.

comment_workload:
4 online quizzes on Canvas, group assignment, group presentation, midterm, final.
If you've paid attention in class, the online quizzes should be relatively easy. You just need to keep aside a list of the formulae (if any) and a calculator in case you come across a calculation-related question. Each quiz only takes about half an hour.
The group assignment is about finding an article and a short video about a certain topic you are assigned to. There is no need to analyse or study them. Only 2 links are needed per group. This takes about a few minutes to possibly half an hour depending on how well you know your assigned topic.
The presentation is done with the same group as the previous assignment. 3 minute presentation about market news and a short Q&A. Not everyone needs to speak, but everyone needs to be present. This should take a total of about 1-2 hours to prepare (if you are preparing both the slides and the Q&A, and your team members aren't doing much work).
Midterm and final exams are non-cumulative. The midterm is about the first half of the syllabus and the final about the rest. You are allowed to bring as many paper notes as you want (written, typed, screenshotted...). I would recommend being familiar with your notes or have some sort of system to quickly find the info you need since there is no time to go through each page of your notes for each question. They don't take too long to prepare, especially since most of the questions come from the quizzes.

comment_teaching:
The course content is delivered through lectures. There are also biweekly writing workshops which guide you in writing your essay.
LECTURES
The professor is clearly very passionate, but honestly I spent most of the lecture doing other stuff because I wasn't that interested in the content. If you are interested in the content, then I think you will enjoy her teaching, as I saw many people in the front were very engaged and always answered her questions.
WRITING WORKSHOPS
The writing workshops introduce you to argumentative techniques which you will use in your essay. They also teach you how to write an introduction, body paragraphs, do citations and more. It is quite interactive as you talk to your workshop tutor and the other students a lot.
My workshop tutor Suzan Stamper was quite good and encouraged interaction among students. Unfortunately, she always left giving feedback on our homework until the last minute. To illustrate, I only got my first homework while walking from the LC to the classroom. I guess in UST, everyone is a deadline fighter, even the faculty :P
comment_grading:
The essay basically determines your grade.
10% Workshop attendance
10% Online discussion x3
    Discuss course topics in a forum-like environment with your peers.
10% Workshop homework
20% Lecture quiz
    Covers everything discussed in the lectures.
50% Essay
[BONUS] 3% In-class iPRS
--
WORKSHOPS
Workshop attendance and homework is self-explanatory. Just attend the workshops and do the homework reasonably and you will get the score. The quality of your homework is not assessed, but I advise you to try your best to get more useful feedback from your tutor. There are some homework quizzes, but you have unlimited attempts.
My score: Full
--
ONLINE DISCUSSION
For online discussions, I just created one moderately long post (300-400ish words) for each topic, and replied to a few of the others' submissions.
My score: Not released
--
LECTURE QUIZ
The lecture quiz is annoying for people like me who aren't interested in the content, because it forces you to revise stuff. The actual questions themselves don't look difficult, but it is easy to get them wrong because there's always multiple answers which feel correct, and the smallest detail determines the correct answer.
Low LQ Med. UQ High | Mean
0 14 16 18 22 | 15.56
My score: 14.5/22
--
ESSAY
900 - 1100 word argumentative essay discussing your viewpoint on a given essay prompt. There are 3 prompts to choose from this semester and you have to take a clear for-or-against stance.
You write the introduction and body paragraphs throughout the semester as part of your homework and you will get feedback. You then submit a draft essay, which is only graded on completion, but points will be deducted if certain criteria are not met. These criteria include:
- Outside word limit
- No humanities citations, DOI not included for journal entries
You then receive feedback on this draft and revise it. 1/3 of your essay score is based on how you respond to feedback, so take it seriously.
--
BONUS (iPRS)
Just attend the lectures and do the iPRS and you'll get the sweet bonus score.
--
Even though I got below mean on the lecture quiz, I still got an A, probably due to my essay. This shows that, as long as you perform decently on the lecture quiz (above LQ), your essay basically determines your score. The essay score is not released.
comment_workload:
Moderate. 
The online-discussions and homework take around 1-2 hours per week.
There are "required" readings which are quite long, but they're not really needed. Use them as reference material if you're unsure about certain lecture content.
Revising for the quiz is annoying if you're like me and didn't pay attention all semester.
The time needed for the essay depends on how much you like/know about your topic and your past experience. Thus, your mileage may vary.

title: do you have the prerequisites?
comment_content:
before taking this course, you need to ask yourself: do you have the prerequisites?
roughly in the order of importance:
- some level of mandarin AND cantonese (spoken): if you aren't proficient in both, you'll struggle a lot in the phonology section, because the questions are roughly split half and half between mandarin and cantonese. if you only know mandarin, go take huma 1060. if you only know cantonese, go take huma 2031.
- good sense of "白話文" structure: this one's for the morphology and syntax parts. good luck if you're just bad at chinese like me, because you'll fall behind there no matter how hard you study.
- ipa: everything's in ipa, so you'll need to learn it, but if you've already learned it, you'll be way ahead of everyone else in phonology. you don't need to know all the symbols by heart, but you should know how to use the ipa in general, not just in english. knowing english ipa is helpful though, because there are somehow questions asking that even though it's "structure of chinese"...
- jyutping and pinyin: both of them translate pretty well into his system. it's not ipa, but it does mean that you only need to learn the symbols themselves, not how to transcribe your speech.
if you wanna do well in this course (think A/A+), definitely study ipa between semesters.
actual course outline:
1. introduction
2. chinese phonology: speech sounds and tones, romanization systems (never tested?), syllable structure
3. chinese morphology: morpheme and word, word formation process
4. chinese syntax: word classes, word order, sentence structure
5. topics in language situation and dialects across china: linguistic neighbors of the chinese language, defining language and dialect, major chinese dialects
6. brief evolution of different dialects
7. basic knowledge about chinese writing system

title: Very funny professor ! leng grade ( for music learners )
comment_content:
Basically a history of Western classical music course, going from ancient/Medieval music all the way to the Renaissance, Baroque, Classical, Romantic and 20th century.
You learn what music sounded like in each period and why it changed, together with some historical events, cultural ideas, famous composers and their more important pieces.
No music background is really needed. There are music terms and theory to remember, but nothing super technical like actually composing or playing music.
There are quite a lot of forms and terms to know, like sonata form, rondo, fugue, opera seria/buffa, leitmotif, Impressionism, Expressionism etc. You also need to know roughly when they appeared and which composers/styles they are related to.
There is a listening part in the tests, where they play part of one of the pieces covered in class and you have to recognise the piece/composer. Definitely listen to the playlist a few times beforehand because some pieces become really easy to recognise once you've heard them enough.
For the normal test questions, it's mostly stuff from the lecture slides: history, composers, definitions, musical forms and characteristics of different periods. There are quite a lot of little details, but it's not too bad if you revise the slides properly.
The professor also plays quite a lot of music and opera during class, so it's not just sitting there reading music history for the whole lecture.
Overall probably my favourite course this semester. Pretty chill and genuinely interesting, especially compared with more technical courses. I didn't expect to enjoy classical music history that much, but by the end I could actually recognise different styles and understand why the music sounds the way it does.

comment_content:
The course offered a deep dive into the history of Western art music, covering everything from the medieval era up to today, with a special focus on the Late Middle Ages (14th century) through the Romantic period (19th century).
It explored a wide range of music from the last five hundred years, aiming to change how students listened to and understood music. The course examined the basics of music cognition and acoustics, discussed how different pieces fit into their historical and political contexts, and highlighted the interactions between music and other art forms.
Additionally, it helped develop analytical listening skills and deepened understanding of various musical instruments and genres across different eras.

The grading in the course is structured as follows: quizzes on reading assignments account for 25%, while there are cumulative mid- and end-of-semester quizzes that each make up 12.5%, totaling 25%. The term paper is particularly important, so it’s a good idea to start preparing early. The professor doesn’t require that all concepts be applied perfectly, but they should mostly be relevant. I’ve found that the quizzes can be quite competitive, and the average scores tend to be high most of the time.

Getting A or A+ is very hard. A- is obtainable if you study hard and don't make too much careless mistakes in exams. B range is manageable if you study even the cut off seems to be high because the questions are not that hard in exams. And getting (almost) full marks in quizzes is not hard if you know what you are doing or just use AI to help you.
Grading on video essay is very generous. Most people got 16-18 out of 20.
Grading:
1. Attendance: 10%
Cannot miss more than 2 lectures. Otherwise, deduct 1% per lecture. He will take attendance via Canvas at the end of each lecture.
2. Quizzes: 20%
Two types. First is review quizzes (asking facts). It is open-booked and completed via Canvas. Second is listening quizzes (matching between pieces and composers from the piece). The scope of each quiz will be given out about a week.
Not hard to get full marks. You may use AI and Google voice secretly if you want :)
3. Video Essay: 20%
Make a 10-12 minutes video analyzing a classical piece. Although it requires you to attend a concert and talk about the experience, he won't check any record at all, so you can definitely make up the experience and choose any piece you want.
I personally chose Winter 1st movement from Four Seasons, Vivaldi. Not hard to complete. Just take some time.
4. Mid-term Exam
60 MCQs (similar style to review quizzes) + around 5 listening questions (same style as listening quizzes)
Not too hard, but definitely need a week of revisions to remember all those terms and facts, and distinguish different pieces.
Usually professor will play the pieces from the beginning. But occasionally he will trick us by playing the middle part, so please listen the whole piece because you will never know what will happen :)
5. Final Exam: 30%
~26 MCQs + 5 matching questions (matching composers and related musical periods) + ~5 listening questions (you have to write the name of composer and genre of music for each piece) + 3 short questions (asking characteristics and facts)
Difficulty is higher than midterm exam. And the exam is CUMULATIVE (Though focusing more on content after the midterm exam)
My result:
1. Attendance: Full marks
2. Quizzes: Full marks
3. Video Essay: 17/20
4. Mid-term Exam: 65/70
5. Final Exam: 59/70
Final score: 90.1%
Grade: A- (almost B+, so close!)

comment_workload:
[Warning: A Bit Long]
TERRIBLE and HORRIBLE. That’s my final answer for answering the topic of this post. 
According to USTSPACE, MATH 1014 is rated as having a workload of C. If that rating is accurate, then the workload of this course deserves an F—or even a G—assuming C truly reflects the workload of MATH 1014.
I genuinely believe the professor does not respect students. The assessments consist of:
1) Weekly Assignments  
A student posted one of the weekly assignments on USTSPACE—please refer to their comment. Based on my experience, each assignment takes 6–7 hours per week (if you skim ALL the materials and use GenAI slightly). Without GenAI, it can take more than 10 hours. Yet each assignment is worth only 2%.  
Reading materials are posted just a few days (around 3) before the deadline.  
-Marks are graded in increments of 0.1, meaning every decimal can affect your final grade.
2) Book Reviews ×2  
You must read the books thoroughly to write something meaningful, which takes another 6–7 hours. These often overlap with weekly assignments.  
- Graded with 0.1 mark precision (e.g., 11.2/15), but feedback is vague—just “Great job!” or “Nice work!”  
The grading criteria are unclear—possibly based on subjective impressions.
3–5) Final Deliverables During Exam Week  
- Rough Cut and Timeline
- Video
- Paper
Although the course claims to have no final exam, many students enroll expecting a lighter workload. Ironically, the instructor scheduled a film competition during the exam period, worth 1 mark.
- You must attend for 3 hours during exam week to earn it.  
- Assignments 3–5 are also due during the examination period.
Actually, all of the above is just a piece of cake, as it’s written in the syllabus and the instructor kept reminding us during the add/drop period. So if you chose to stay in the course, you should accept it.
What’s truly terrible is that the professor keeps adding “extra bonus marks” activities and assignments.
“Bonus” Marks That Aren’t Really Bonus  
These were not listed in the syllabus, but became essential for anyone aiming for an A-range grade:
6) Two extra weekly assignments (Syllabus said 10, ended up with 12) → 4 bonus marks
7) Three talks with written feedback → 3 bonus marks  
8) In-class questions (0.5 marks each, but students rarely answered, I guess you can ignore it)  
9) Film competition attendance → 1 mark  
Total “Bonus” Marks: At least 8 marks, added without prior notice.  
One talk was announced via email on the same morning it was held. If you want an A-range grade, these “bonuses” are not optional—they’re compulsory.
Personal Reflections
1) The Darkest Day
When I received the Canvas notification titled *“The First Book Review and Weekly Assignment”*, I cried near Canteen II. I even considered ending my life. That’s a true story—I was overwhelmed with quizzes and felt hopeless. I’m deeply thankful to my friends who supported me. That was my darkest day at HKUST.
2) The Film Competition
During exam week, I attended the film session. When the professor announced that attendees would receive 1 bonus mark, the class cheered. I couldn’t. I felt like a poor soul following the professor’s unreasonable demands. I couldn’t feel happy.  
I don’t understand why HKUST students (myself included) are so marks-oriented. One girl spoke up during (other official) class to challenge the professor—but no one supported her. We all stayed silent, myself included.
I really agree with the comment of teaching in one of the posts of HUMA 1430 -  "Unable to understand students' concerns worries or questions."
Final Advice  
Believe me—you’ll regret enrolling in this course. The fast-moving waitlist was a warning. The course enrollment system is a market. Trust the market mechanism. Save your time. Don’t enroll.

comment_content: 自大明崇祯十六载朱由检同学吊死在煤山老歪脖子树，嫂子爱好者多尔衮入关开始讲。期间，你将会学习到大清帝国的政治、文化以及与洋鬼子们的来往等历史的一些十分甚至九分有意思的事物。于历史爱好者言，你将如鱼得水、如鸟归林，有胜于亚当伊娃伊甸园之乐的快乐。随后，你将会学到中国近代史，应该说，作为超级无敌文科战士，一切简单到爆炸。当然，其中的一些站在外国视角审视中国的内容亦有趣矣。至期中，你将会被要求根据一部美国洋鬼子于上世纪六十年代拍的招笑至极的关于义和团的电影攥写评论（没错，如果你经常刷B站的话，你会发现就是那部“棒棒棒棒棒，五十五天在北京”那首歌的电影。）随后就会来到民国，除去体系内讲的一些东西外，还会涉及一些民国时期的民俗文化之演化变迁。教授时不时会掏出一些奇妙小道具。随后，便到了共和国时期，你将会学习毛主席时代的一些有趣的政治历史。假如你是老布尔什维克，比如笔者，你或许能从一个新的角度审视中国社会主义的发展。随后，你会被要求写一篇对比孙大炮和毛主席理念之间差异的paper。在此之后，课程会以改开初期的历史结束。当然，作为”现代中国”，老师会谈及很多有趣的问题——何为现代；何为中国？对了，假如你是我们万恶的P社玩家，你或许会在谈及白莲教时会心一笑，毕竟引用了世界上最伟大的游戏EU4的事件截图（虽然原版的中国dlc很垃圾就是了）

title: Great gateway for China Studies
comment_content:
Haha, I survived this so-called "bad grade" course. 
To be honest, as a fan of modern Chinese history, it wasn't that hard for those who did previous research on it.
The course covered the history of China from early Qing to the reform & open-up in the PRC era. Besides historical facts, Prof Cheung did a great job of inspiring students to think beyond those written facts by historians. Knowing "WHY" and "HOW" China came to today is an important gateway for your China Studies.
More importantly, for new year 1 GCS students, this is a crucial opportunity to develop the necessary essay writing and information processing proficiency. Through the course assignment, you will learn how to modify your essay framework, identify the key factors, and more.
I was not a history student back in my high school time, but I got a pretty good grade at last. Therefore, don't worry too much about the course! As long as you make your effort (and more personal research), you should be able to get a good grade

Conducting personal research is highly recommended if you want to perform better! Purchasing a DSE Chinese History Notes book (also known as 雞精) is truly helpful. Additionally, consider using AI tools to help process the reading material he provides.

The first 5 topics are more focused on eras between the New Stone Ages (新石器時代) and the Han Dynasty (漢朝) and the remaining topics are more focused on eras between the Northern-Southern Dynasties (南北朝) and the Qing Dynasty (清朝).
I believe a fair portion of people (including me) take this to avoid taking C-LANG courses (and hence the famous 400+ waitlist). However, the course itself is interesting, instead of just being a "less-awful" C-Comm course option.
Get yourself eligible for reserved HUMA quota if you want to take this course, or pray that you are in the first group for course enrollment in year 4.

comment_content:
1. Critical thinking and creative thinking

4. symbolic logic
5. categorical syllogism
6. classification and fallacies
edit: Thank yall for pointing out, its Lewis not Alex
Warning: *THIS IS A HUMA COURSE, ITS HUMA1710 NOT MATH1710.*
Only 6 modules, over a whole semester. The course significantly references a book by 李天命. The first module is useless for quizzes. 
The content ideas could be interesting, but course designs skims over the surface and fails to connect underlying dots and drains intricacy, leaving only surface values precipitating as boring memorization of specific examples and special cases, rather than built on solid theoretical foundations and rigor.
If you want to sign up for the course for enrichment of the soul, you might wanna think again. This is a game of "Simon says" (calling it Lewis says is more appropriate) HUMA course disguised as a rigorous study of logic and linguistic elements. Judging from other reviews, you *might be tempted into believing* the course is about juggling with logic operators, and formalising statements and pinpointing fallacies using rules of syllogism and inference. In reality, you are dealing with scattered, unfocused and frail-structured materials littered everywhere, most of these cannot be derived from first principles. 
Not to mention the lecture notes are practically useless (they are only an inch long and does not contain materials relevant to exams at all) and it is by intentional design that you must spend dozens of hours going through every second of the lecture videos trying to find hints (if any) which Lewis drops seemingly at random to "reward those who listen to his lectures". Mind you it is not possible to know the solutions to a good number of the quiz problems without the hints. 
Directly reading the book by 李天命 is a substantially more fulfilling experience.
comment_teaching:
I only watched some of Lewis's lecture videos. Lewis portrays his humour uncensored, and could be fun to listen to. As other reviews pointed out, you can definitely listen to his classes as something like a radio when you are on 91M. But why would I do that if I can enjoy a symphony by Beethoven, or a Stanford lecture on abstract algebra? Surely, you can argue that I brought bad grades upon myself to not extensively attend lectures. But I merely mean to highlight design choices, regardless of personal attendance habits.
As pointed out in the content section, I appall the fact that the crucial intel for quizzes are embedded deep within lecture recordings and trying to find those is more difficult than mining for ancient debris under lava by an unenchanted diamond pickaxe. The architecture of this infrastructure has a Homelander mentality for sure.

title: Ear Training > Theory in terms of "prerequisites"
comment_content:
The content is friendly for students learning music from scratch. It might be boring for the first few topics if you have a music background. 
Topic 1: Rhythm Notations
- Notes and Rest Durations
- Meter (Simple and Compound Meters)
- Barlines (and Pick-up Bars)
- Tempo (BPM and common markings)
- Dotted and Tied Rhythms
- Upbeats and Downbeats
Topic 2: Pitch Notations
- Staves and the grand staff
- Clefs (Treble, Bass and Alto Clefs)
- Accidentals ((Double) Sharps, (Double) Flats and Naturals)
- Enharmonics
- Steps (Diatonic Half Steps, Chromatic Half Steps and Whole Steps)
Topic 3: Rhythm Phrase Composition
Topic 4: Keys and scales
- Major Scale
- Neutral, Harmonic and Melodic Minor Scales
- Circle of Fifths
- Relative and Parallel Keys
Topic 5: Intervals
- Interval Numbers
- Qualities (Perfect, Major, Minor, Diminished, Augmented)
Topic 6: Major-key Melody Composition
- Motives and Themes
- Phrase Structure
Topic 7: Analytical Listening
- Meter (Duple, Triple)
- Tonality (Major, Minor)
- Texture (Homophonic, Polyphonic)
Topic 8: Triads and Seventh Chords
- Major, Minor, Augmented and Diminished Triads
- Major-major, Dominant, Minor-minor, Minor-major Seventh Chords
- Half-diminished and Fully-diminished Seventh Chords
- Chord Inversions
- Figured Bass
Topic 9: Minor-key Melody Composition
Topic 10: Harmonic Analysis
- Major and Minor Harmonic Scales
- Cadences
- Harmonization
- Voice Leading
Some musical notations (e.g., articulations, dynamics, breaks and repeats) that are not in the topics above will also be introduced during teaching, but they are not the focus in this course.
comment_teaching:
Ilari is a great instructor, and he is very passionate about teaching. Although he has some restrictions on using electronic devices during lectures, the sessions are very engaging, apart from his lessons being quite early, and I often fall asleep. I have taken HUMA1102 and HUMA2104 taught by Ilari, and both courses offered me new perspectives on music.

comment_workload:
Perhaps the highest workload for me was attending morning lessons (lol).
Assignments are mild annoyances, but they only take half an hour to complete (or 1-2 hours if you are learning from scratch).
The term paper and final project are due the day before the final exam, so you should have enough time to tackle them.
Although Ilari himself claims the pace of this course is fast and labour-intensive, I find the workload relatively low for me for a few reasons:
1. Having a music background
2. Interested in music
3. Having other courses with higher workload/annoyance
However, as a person with zero knowledge of "music theory" before this course, I did need to learn official musical terms and concepts. Intervals, circle of fifths, chords, harmony, and cadences are items that took me time relating to what I had listened to in the past.
Therefore, having an ABRSM Grade 5+ in Music Theory may save you from the workload, but it isn't the only way to be good in this course.
The workload may be higher (say C) for people without a musical background, considering some people learn music from the absolute beginning. In that case, I believe more listening practices and analyses help bridge the gap. So you are not screwed and can yield a good performance even if you learn music from scratch.

comment_content:
(大概)課程大綱, 我自己寫左一份(中英對照) 下面可以download。
想要份完整既可以喺其他review度搵
1. 小小引言
------------------------------
一如以往, 我為文章篇幅過長而致歉(英文差所以寫中文)
樓下位仁兄isonngky基本上都表明左我對呢個Course既睇法，可以參考下佢既review
對音樂無興趣/感覺的話我就*強烈不建議*去take 呢個course
最大功夫並不是花喺要讀明白D theory度，而係去做ear training
以中小學music 堂為基礎，如果你不是音痴(sorry)，可以哼到D音出黎其實都有大幫助
唔好理人地既身世背景，做好自己，攞A range唔係無可能
------------------------------
2. ABRSM music theory
------------------------------
我自己本身無讀樂理/無玩任何樂器，所以exactly 對應ABRSM 既grading我唔清楚(可以參考樓下其他review)。
不過我報個HUMA2104之前download過ABRSM幾份past paper(grade 5)。我覺得唔係難得好誇張。
以我幾份past paper既小小經驗同睇過官網syllabus，HUMA2104同ABRSM grade 5 不同之處就係*唔需要背*一堆 德文，意大利文 既術語(e.g. Vivace, langsam, largemente, sostenuto, etc.)
------------------------------
3. 除左讀music theory外，呢個course仲要作曲
------------------------------
(*參考*!!)大約地Music theory佔 80% - 85%, 作曲佔 15% - 20%
主要係一曲(Final project, sem尾交)
放心，幾短下，得24小節。一般中等速度(Moderato)大約一至兩分鐘
整個sem, 2-3個月時間會有2份作曲功課係GUIDE住你，慢慢堆疊份final project出黎(雖然佢地都計homework分)
*唔洗擔心*要寫份好似 貝多芬交響曲 咁既世紀大作，只要跟足佢畀你既指示，攞高分唔難。若果做小小畫龍點睛，應該都可以到top甚至滿分。D TA幾好人下
------------------------------
4. 進度chur唔chur既問題
------------------------------
每堂得50分鐘，而且你可能要3個月(一個sem)讀人地半年一年既theory(雖然可能無咁深入)，係的確會緊湊。
大約每一(到兩)堂叫新野，而且都會stack上去，近final會較辛苦。
所以平時無mud時間研究上堂D resource, notes都好，
有聽開歌既，除左聽歌詞以外，都留意下首歌/樂曲既 調性，節奏同配樂，尤其是教左chord(和弦) 之後，尼D都算係ear training既一部分。
------------------------------
5. 要識聽D咩？
------------------------------
最基本既12個音 (C, C#, D, ..., Bb, B)
分辨節奏 (頂多16分音符)
chord(和弦): triads(三和弦), seventh(七和弦)
因為考試會有Rhythm dictation 同melody dictation(我簡稱Melodictation)：打節奏 + TA彈旋律，你負責默寫番出黎放心會彈(幾多次下), 好似50%就當嗰part滿分。亦都有要分辨chord既題目
上堂同tutorial會同你practice, train, 但自己都要落D功夫(上網自己train下)
尼度有個日本網站可以train 節奏: 
https://www.senzoku-online.jp/solfege/rhythmn_js/
考試既level大概會有個網站8級左右
Melodictation 小小tips: 集中寫曬D音，或者係個rhythm先，再處理剩低既手尾，多數都係音階同broken chord，*絕對*唔會好似 ‘忐忑’ 咁痴線😂

comment_workload:
If you have studied ABRSM music theory before, congratulations, this is probably one of the lowest workload course you'll ever take in HKUST. Even if it's a long time ago and you may think you've forgotten everything, it'll be very easy to pick up the contents again.
You do still have to put some effort in the final composition, which you will slowly develop through smaller assignments (major key composition -> major+minor key composition -> final project, which is basically harmonization if your previous work is good enough. You may choose to harmonize only the major/minor section or the whole piece). You do not need to be very creative with the composition as they only assess the technical aspects, i.e. use chords that make sense and add some form of texture, no need to think out of the box. I was very fortunate to have friends with experience in compositions and received some feedback from there.
Term paper (min. 350w) is fine as concert recording was provided.
If you have never studied music theory before, good luck. You'll probably have to compete with other students who have already studied music theory before, which is probably over half the class). STEM students may have an easier time with it as most of the stuff are pretty systematic (like intervals, chords, etc.). Some content must be memorized (circle of fifths -> identify key, inversions), and the rest will become much easier.

comment_content:
Good course for people with previous music theory background, although certain terms used are from American English (though this may be due to my instructor, e.g. "Half note" US vs "Minum" UK, "Authentic Cadence" US vs "Perfect Cadence" UK). Does not include any component of music performance.

The final project is a 24-bar composition consisting of 8-bar major and minor parallel period in an ABA (which are already composed during the previous homework from before). 
Shaw Auditorium is also a very nice place to study straight after the lecture since it would be earlier with less people.

comment_workload:
The level of workload on this course is highly subjective depending on prior knowledge and ability. 
Some may find the 1 to 2 homework assignments per week doable within 30 minutes if they have at least a few years of experience in performing classical music; others may take more than an hour per homework. 
A lot of the composition in this course depends also on how well you adhere to the composition guidelines to create tonal music (so basically it's not just about making nice-sounding music, there are guidelines outlined by the instructor that should be followed to receive a high grade).
Attendance is also counted towards 15% of your final grade, if your assigned lecture session is early in the morning and you know that you won't be able to make it on campus or wake up that early, avoid this course. 
The difficulty of the midterm and final exam is generally not hard if you listen properly to the lecture content, with our midterm average being a bit higher than 80%. 
You will also be required to attend a concert to write a concert report which is worth 10% of your final grade. 
To summarise, the main difficulty in this course is purely to do with putting preparation into learning about the course requirements and making sure you meet them.

- Accidentals and enharmonic equivalents

- Construction of major scales
- The Circle of Fifths (Major and Minor keys) and the placement rules for accidentals
- Devices for determining keys in a musical score
- Minor scale forms: natural, harmonic, and melodic minor (and their practical applications)
- Concepts of relative keys vs. parallel keys
5. Intervals
- Interval numbers (numerical distance)
- Interval qualities (Perfect, Major, Minor, Augmented, Diminished)
- Harmonic vs. melodic intervals

- Writing and analyzing short parallel period phrases *
7. Triads, Seventh Chords, & Figured Bass

- Introduction to seventh chords *
- Chord inversions and the reading/writing of figured bass notation *
8. Harmonic Analysis
- Roman numeral analysis in major and minor keys
- Voice-leading principles and textural distribution *
- Analyzing chord progressions from standard classical repertoire *
9. Cadences & Musical Form
- Introduction to cadences (e.g., Perfect Authentic, Imperfect Authentic, Half, Plagal)
- The relationship between harmonic progressions, cadences, and formal boundaries *
10. Analytical Listening & Ear Training *
- Recognition of musical textures, meters, and overall tonality *
- Aural dictation and singing exercises (intervals, triads, seventh chords, scales, and cadences) *#

comment_content:

comment_grading:
Absolute Grading(?), 90%+ is A range. 
If you have prior knowledge of music theory, you will be able to get a nice grade easily. (As long as you don’t accidentally botch something.) 
If you don’t have prior knowledge, it’s challenging, but very doable. 
[ Grading ] 
Final Exam 25% 
Midterm         20% 
Homework 15% 
Final Project 15% 
Concert report 10% 
Attendance/participation  15% 
-----------------------------------------
More details:  
[ Midterm and Final Exam ] 45% 
Definitely pay attention to the midterm exam, I didn’t have enough time to check my paper and got kicked out of A range. Meanwhile you will have more than enough time for the final exam. 
Both the midterm and final will have written section (majority%) and music dictation (about 25-30%). 
[ Written ] 
Based on homework. Study and re-do the homework, then practice online, such as: https://www.musictheory.net/exercises 
[ Music Dictation ] 
For midterm, it will be {1.} analytical listening and {2.} rhythm dictation. For final, it will be {1.} analytical listening, {3.} melody dictation and {4.} “Triads”. 
I don’t remember anything for the midterm, but for the final, the listening part accounts for 57 out of 198 points (28.8%). {1.} is worth 27 points, {3.} is worth 20 points, {4.} is worth 10 points. 
{ 1. Analytical Listening } (midterm & final) 
You will need to determine the texture (major or minor), meter (duple or triple) and tonality (homophonic or polyphonic) for about 3-4(?) songs – they are “supposed” to be easy but (ahem ahem). 
A pdf homework with a list of youtube links will be released before the midterm for practice. 
{ 2. Rhythm Dictation } (midterm) 
There is some leeway, you only need around 75% accuracy (? I don’t remember) to get full marks. The tutorials before midterm will be for practicing rhythm dictation, but it is nowhere near enough. 
I spent A LOT of time on this part. It is completely normal to go insane at first, but it will be more manageable over time. 
I used this website for additional practice: https://tonesavvy.com/music-practice-exercise/14/rhythm-dictation-game-eighth-notes/ 
Haven’t tried this website, but it seems to be a good starting point if you are really struggling: https://www.musicca.com/exercises/rhythms 
It is VERY important to establish how you want to write down what you hear from the rhythm. Instead of replacing what you have already written down, it might be better to write it below for the next iteration. Also, filling your blanks with some random gibberish might help you count the beats better. 
{ 3. Melody Dictation } (final) 
There is leeway for this one too, around 50% accuracy (? I have poor memory) to get full marks. 
The rhythm for the melody dictation is easier than the rhythm dictation in midterm, and I think I did pretty well only because of that. I most certainly did not get or barely got the note pitches right. 
I did not study for this part. 🙃 
{ 4. “Triads” } (final) 
This part is to determine the quality of triads by ear (major, minor, diminished, augmented). However, I believe this part is subject to change, as in this could be determine the intervals, chords, or key and scales. 
In the (final?) tutorial, I believe you will have a chance to practice whatever it is that will appear in the final exam. 
I also spent a lot of time on this (arguably too much for a mere 10 points). It is extremely normal to get absolutely everything wrong at first, but practice makes perfect. 
I used this website for practice: https://tonedear.com/ 
[ Final Project + Composition Homework ] 15% 
There are three composition homework, which guides you to your final project. The first is rhythm composition, the second is major melody composition, and the third is minor melody composition. (the first one serves as an introduction separate from the second and third) 
You will get feedback for the homework, and it is very important to ask if you don’t understand. 
The final project is just a harmonization of your composition homework. So long as you do well in your composition homework, your final project shouldn’t be too far off. 
Definitely use a music notation software to help you. I highly recommend using MuseScore 4, it’s lightweight and free. 
[ Concert Report ] 10% 
Attend a concert, then a concert recording will be sent to you. Pick your favorite song and listen to it a few dozen times, then write about it. The concert report is very simple, just write about what you feel when you hear the piece, supported by why (analyze the structure: ABA’ structure? substructure? motifs?; analyze the melody: stable? jumpy?; analyze the quality: loud? soft?) 
p.s. I got ~89% = B+ 🙃🙃🙃 
the mean is 84.50% (might not be the most accurate)
comment_workload:
Speaking from someone who had no prior music theory knowledge (except how to read basic music notations). 
[ Homework ] 
The workload is reasonable. At first it will take quite some time to do the ~2 homework per week (and check it), but you’ll speed up eventually with more practice. 
[ Midterm and Final Exam ] 
There are only a few simple things you need to memorize: the order “FCGDAEB”, placement of sharps and flats in G-clef + F-clef + C-clef, harmonic and melodic minor, Circle of Fifths, notation for harmonic analysis (roman numerals, in major or minor, inversions), and 4 different cadences. It may seem a lot at first glance, but it really isn’t. 
The most time-consuming part of this whole course would be ear training. I spent more time doing ear training than studying the contents, even though the music dictation section doesn’t account for a lot. The rhythm and melody dictation done in the tutorials are much harder than in the actual exam, so don’t dwell on it too much. 
The most effective way to train your ears is to do many short sessions each day (20mins to 1hr each session), instead of jamming everything together in one long session (your brain will get fried), and especially not right before the exams. You WILL feel your brain melting for the first 3-5 days, but if you persist and after a few good nights’ sleep, you will notice substantial improvement. 
The rest of the exams are based on homework, so just study those, do some exercises, and you’re good to go. 
[ Composition Homework + Final Project ] 
Since the final project is based on your composition homework, it doesn’t have much extra workload. 
[ Concert Report ] 
Nothing too difficult. Write 1-2 pages, minimum 350 words (but write more than that, I recommend ~500 or more). 
-----------------------------------------
Don’t be discouraged to take this course. Contrary to other reviews, even if you haven’t studied music theory before, this course is worthwhile. The more time and effort you spend, the more you will learn and transform your ears.

comment_workload:
The workload was absolutely horrible; I was the scriptwriter for the play and it was constant stress. Completely unnecessary!
I came up with the whole story and was genuinely excited to make it with the rest of the class who shared the same enthusiasm as me. However, this excitement quickly turns into disappointment and resentment for this course and for some classmates who made my semester a living hell.
A group of them tried helping me writing the script, however they proceeded to completely rewrite my entire script after I worked a long time on it, thinking very carefully about the dialogue, timing and pacing. The story was all over the place; they didn't care about the message of the story to the audience and instead focused too much on parts of the story that were unnecessary. One of the writers had the role of the main character and made sure that her role was always the center of attention and overly dramatic.
I have encountered way too much drama in this course; the teachers were very absent during those times, despite seeing us confront each other during a meeting, where I complained about the heavy workload that was put on me and other students because of those who ruined the script.
When we finished the play, I felt very relieved to be done with this nightmare. I was mentally and physically tired, and the worst part was that I had to worry about my final exams right after, since we performed on the day the study break began.
However, I can fairly say that I have learned a lot from this course, and you will too if you choose to take it. This course will help you gain confidence in yourself through the art of performing (I can say from experience I also played a character in addition to scriptwriting). In the midst of the drama (in a musical drama, how ironic), I was able to speak up for what I believed was right, so did other students. Many of us will have to face such confrontation in our everyday lives in the future, and this course enables you to get a taste of it with meeting some really obnoxious and arrogant people (hopefully your class won't have bad apples), having to work under constant stress and taking charge of a project when it's going down the wrong path.
If you take this course, I wish you the best of luck. Do not take the role of scriptwriter alone; work with some people who respect your story and you as the creator. Make sure you all agree on the overall strong message you want to convey to the audience and do not get sidetracked by making it look "super dramatic" and "emotional". Think of the core first. That will carry your play, it doesn't have to be impressive! Everyone has priorities, and musical drama is going to be at the bottom of the list so keep it simple.

overall it is not a so call "good grade course", if some enroll it only because they want a good grade, without any passion in composing music, i believe it would be super suffering for them

comment_content:
20th century China, but not through documentary films. It covers gradually from 1900s all the way up to 1989.
There's a lecture every week for 3 hours, covering:
1. The end of the Qing Dynasty
2. China's participation in World War I
3. KMT-CCP civil war
4. The Second World War

I wanna highlight on the professor himself. He's liberal with swearing, to say the least. comment_grading:
You've probably seen the marking scheme already, but just in case, here it is again:
1. Attendance and Participation: 5%
2. Weekly timeline, biographies, notes for readings and documentaries: 20%
3. Film Reviews: 30%
4. Research Paper Outline and Timeline: 10%
5. Research Paper [of someone/thing relatively unknown to most people]: 25%
6. Rough Cut/PPT Presentation of Draft Documentary Film: 5%
7. Final Documentary Film based on the Paper: 5%
Here are my grades:
1. Attendance and Participation: Don't know, he actually only took attendance 3 times in the middle of the lecture, so attend all lectures and stay until the end. I probably got full marks.
2. Weekly Timelines: 22.3%
3. Film Reviews: 13.8% + 13.5%
4. Research Paper Outline: 8.5%
5. Research Paper: 25%
6. Rough Cut: Don't know. He went by it really fast. I actually don't know.
7. Final Documentary: 5%
Final grade: A
Some of these reviewers said they did the requirements and still got a D. Just doing those requirements are not enough, they actually go through all of the things in detail.
For instance, in point 2, if you do the same biographies, they will deduct marks. If you copy other people's notes, you get points knocked off. In point 4/5/6/7, if your group is doing someone most people know about, like Mao Zedong, Chiang Kai-shek or others, you're not getting a good score.
It's VERY possible to get a good grade. Even saying pretty random stuff in your film reviews net you an above average score. While points 1 and 6 are never explicitly revealed, those only account for 10%. Doing the essay and the weekly notes well can already net you a great score. Those are just the cherry on top. You have to be insightful and well-researched to get a good grade. Again, just fulfilling quota is not nearly enough.
The professor quite literally showed the ExCel sheet where he kept the marks in the first couple lectures. How are you gonna say it's not transparent at all? Self reporting perhaps?

HE WILL CHECK.
Finally, do not commit to this course if you're an engineering student looking for a good grade like me. It's suffering, but if you're willing to give your 100% it will be worth it.

In addition to reading scholarly books, articles, and historical documents, we will closely study several films made by journalists and filmmakers of the time and in recent years. comment_teaching:
I will try to stay objective in this part, although I really dislike this professor.
Fairly speaking, he has deep insights in Chinese history, and he encourages us to think critically. He also like to share his opinions on recent news. Every lecture he would spare around 30 minutes giving opinions about latest news, which I really enjoy.
However, I don't like the way he interact with some of us. For those who engage actively in class, he is always patient and kind. But for others like me, he seems a bit mean. I have wrote some emails to ask him questions about grading and my project, and he answered quite unkindly, using very mean words. I am wondering why he is doing that. Also, he requires full attendance despite his lecture lasts 3 hours. But I have other classes before and after that, which means if I do take all the attendance, I will have to study 6 hours in a roll without break or lunch. So I skipped second half of his course, and maybe that's one of the reasons why I had bad grade.
Moreover, he has his own preference in history interpretation. There is no "right or wrong" in this class. You have to speculate what kind of comments he like, and applying them to your projects. That's the best way to score high. And I really hate that.
comment_grading:
BADDD!!!

Groupmate A: D

comment_teaching: His teaching is good, and he provides plenty of details to help you understand the material. He is also friendly and willing to answer your questions.
comment_grading:
Every lecture counts toward attendance (15%), and you have to raise your hand to answer his questions during discussions at least once during the whole semester to get full credit for that part. 
There is also a group project worth 20%, and the professor will randomly assign you to a group. 
As other comments mention, he is quite lenient with the grading; as long as your answers make sense and are relevant, he will award you credit. There isn't much to worry about here.
comment_workload: There are around 50 to 70 pages of reading every week, and you are expected to read them beforehand to participate in class discussions. The reading materials are also covered in the midterm, final exam, and group project, so you should expect to spend a fair amount of time each week keeping up with the readings if you take this course.

title: Remove LANG, GPA Strong!
comment_content:
As suggested by the course name, this course devotes all of its content to traditional Chinese painting, particularly artistic critique.
Don't worry if you can't draw proper painting or if you didn't take visual arts in high school at all: I can only draw stickmen, and this don't affect my grade at all. That said, you should try to reach out for students who have visual art background, or at least a person who understands Western art. This would be useful in your later project.
Course outline:
1. Introduction
2. Early Figure Painting
3. The Rise of Landscape Painting
4. Monumental Landscapes
5. Search for Realism
6. Literati Painting
7. Southern Song Academy Painting
8. Southern Song Chan Painting
9. Early Yuan Masters
10. The Four Great Masters of Yuan
=====Quiz 1=====
11. Ming Academy Painting and Zhe School
12. Ming Suzhou Literati Painters
13. Late Ming Painting
14. Qing Orthodox and Individualists
15. Early Qing Individualists II
16. Qing Court Painting
=====Quiz 2=====
*The last lecture was reported to be about the Eight Eccentrics of Yangzhou, but apparently Professor Fu didn't have time to mention them.
*There were also 2 guest lectures by Professor Wu Hong (not from HKUST) on late Qing self-portraits and an painter from Hong Kong Baptist University who demonstrated Chinese painting techniques. Their contents were not examinable in quizzes.
Also a kind reminder for those who want to enroll in this course in the future. As a non LANG course that can fulfil Chinese language common core requirement, this course is extremely popular among students (or "C-LANG refugees"?)
*If you are not in year 4 (and if you are not HUMA student, who have their own quota), please GIVE UP: you'll probably end up in the waiting list at some 100th or 200th position.
*For year 4 students who really want to get into this course, your chance to get into this course entirely depends on careful preparation, mouse clicking speed on SIS and luck.
*I was placed at the 6th place of the waitlist initially, and I only get into the course near the end of the add-drop period. Hopefully this can serve as a useful reference when you are waitlisted.
comment_teaching:
Professor Fu Li-tsui's teaching is probably one of the best in UST, much better than the consistently roasted Chinese LANG instructors. A Taiwanese, her Mandarin/Putonghua accent is impeccable, though you may want to pay extra attention to pronunciation of artist names, like for the artist Guo Xi, I often heard it as "Boxi" (Persia)... Never mind...
Answering questions was encouraged and required (for at least 5 times) during lectures. Don't worry about wrong answers: as Professor Fu would guide you (and the class) to the correct answer nicely and kindly. When Quiz 1 was about to begin, she also calmed us down by suggesting us that "we should probably appreciate these paintings as if they were shown the last time".
Lectures were lively with frequent interactions, though the lecture hall is dark to show the lecture slides containing paintings. Professor Fu was also willing to answer questions after lectures, and I did enjoy discussing some historical backgrounds with her.
For the guest lecturers, Professor Wu Hong delivered his bland lecture in awful Kinabatangan MP English, while the HKBU painter delivered her guest lecture in understandable Mandarin. To be honest, the second guest lecture was much more interesting, as we did see how a Chinese painting was created from abstract elements to a recognizable object.
comment_grading:
Class participation: 5% (Full)
Class attendance: 9% (Full)
Quiz 1: 20% (16.8/20, mean 14.3/20, median 14.4/20)
Quiz 2: 20% (16/20, mean 14.19/20, median 14.5/20)
Group project presentation: 30% (29/30, mean 26.53/30, median 26/30, low 24/30)
Group project written report: 10% (10/10, mean 9.81/10, median 10/10, low 9.5/10)
Group project evaluation: 6% (Unknown)
Class attendance is mandatory, and unlike some LANG courses that allows some leeway, each absence from lecture deducts 1%, and each absence from guest lectures and group project presentations deducts 2%. Every attempt in answering question in lectures or Canvas discussion board would give you 1% (1% max per each lecture/discussion thread) in class participation. While you only need answer questions for 5 times, answering more questions is certainly interesting in the lecture.
There is no doubt that the quizzes, which effectively act as the course's midterm and final exams, can be demanding to some students:
*Quiz 1 was a closed book MC exam with no cheat sheet allowed. The questions would show some cropped out details of paintings and ask related questions like "which of the following(s) is/are created by [artist name]?". You should prepare for very similar objects being shown on a very microscopic scale. My advice is try to catch every details you can observe: line of sight, position of buildings, and even the background (which may have different level of staining).
*The open-book Quiz 2 was about painting critique. There was a short question that gave you an artwork not shown in lecture created by an unknown artist and 3 other known artwork with known artist. Your task was to find out who is the artist based on the similarity and differences. The long question required you to compare two paintings, with subsections asking about differences and similarities before leading you to the overall evaluation.
Speaking of the project, this year's topic was Tradition and Innovation. A 4-5 member group would select a modern artist and compare his/her works with traditional ones to conclude their similarities and differences, to be reported in a 15-minute group presentation and a written report (to be submitted within 1 week after the presentation). As mentioned by someone before, Professor Fu didn't heavily scrutinize the report, which is reflected in the extremely high mean and median.
I was preparing for a B+ to A- grade, but at the end I get an A for this course, which was certainly satisfying with my (and my groupmates') effort. When compared with Chinese LANG's Schrödinger grading, HUMA2660 is certainly a stabilizer for your GPA.
comment_workload:
As mentioned in the grading section, Quiz preparation constituted a significant portion of your workload. You should seriously familiarize with the artists' names and their paintings, at least for the course's first-half (which included some ~40 artists spanning across 5 dynasties!).
The project requires you to study a modern artist, so you may want to arrange your groupmates to visit an arts museum or a painting gallery for the purpose of taking high-resolution images. Alternatively, you may need to find painting collections in the library if there is no collection in Hong Kong (which was the case for my group). I was lucky to be grouped with some experienced groupmates, and overall, a 5-member group would divide smaller individual workload, which is true for busy year-4 students.

I like the course contents a lot, and I've learnt much from them. I wouldn't enjoy reviewing the contents for some major-required courses, I don't mind doing so for art courses. Yet, I'm pretty aware that I'm not representative, as I'm a liberal art student from Chinese gaokao. Everyone can preserve his/her attitude, while I'm just here to voice mine. After all, it's all about preferences.
comment_teaching:
Prof. Kwong's teaching is fair in terms of contents. She is knowlegeable in art history and her interpretations of art pieces are rigorous. She was willing to answer questions, as I saw students discussing with her after every lecture.
The only thing you need to beware of was her delivery. Her voice was low, and she stuttered a lot. You may need some time to get accustomed to that. Despites, I think this is understandable in the humanities, because the vocabulary could be crazy large and it's hard to always seek for accurate definition of historical or art events.
comment_grading:
Prof. Kwong publishes full statistics of the class every semester, so the grading scheme is transparent. You can argue for the first two quizzes, but not the final exam, since for the final exam, the grade is finalized ahead of the paper-checking session.
The overall grade is determined by these components:
1. Quiz 1 (25%): MC, True/False, Fill-in-the-blanks, short questions
2. Quiz 2 (25%): MC, True/False, Fill-in-the-blanks, short questions
3. Final exam (40%): MC, True/False, Fill-in-the-blanks, short questions, essay writing
4. Attendance (10%): 10 random attendance checks, 1% each
The attendance part was really tricky. People passed the attendance sheets with no order, and Prof. Kwong forgot to remind you about it from time to time. Therefore, you need to check on the attendance in person after every lecture. I didn't, so I lost quite some marks from this.
All details about the scores and grades are as attached. Check it out for more information. Personally, I think the grading is lenient, but I can sense that the course is getting more and more competitive.
comment_workload:
The distribution of workload is clear: it's all preparing for exams. To be honest, I registered for this course partly because it didn't require any group projects, thus manageable subjectivity and no risks from group dynamics.
However, every exam throughout the semester demands your full effort. There were extensive contents to understand and memorize, even though the exams were non-cumulative. Another challenging part was that in my middle school and high school, I learnt history all in Chinese, but the exams were be in full English. In that case, grasping the English terms was the key. On the contrary, for international students, recognizing the reknown painters' names in Chinese pinyin was extremely hard. My suggestion is, pay attention to the highlighted words in her Powerpoints, though the colors might look messy at the first sight.
