title: From an art lover’s perspective
comment_content:
Background info: I’m a science student taking this course to satisfy common core, but I have some background knowledge and interest.
If you are interested in / have background knowledge in art / art history, this course should be quite easy and interesting.
It’s not necessary to memorize everything. Focus on the stylistic characteristics of the PERIODS (less on individual artists or individual works) and the historical reason behind them. The ‘fun facts’ taught in class, size/place/medium of the art and even the names of artists are not important. (WITH THE EXCEPTION OF FINAL - these information might be useful in the essays)
I personally don’t think the quizzes / final are hard. The information needed are pretty straightforward to me. If you truly understand the material, it shouldn’t be hard too.
I never read the reading materials or suggested materials, the ppts are sufficient to understand everything you need to know.
However I recommend to write notes to conclude the characteristics of each artistic period, as the information may be overwhelming.
This might be my favorite course taken in UST thus far! If you are interested, my suggestion is to register to this course (don’t be intimidated by the comments lol)

comment_content: Covers the basics of art history from Ancient Greece to Modern Art (20th century) in chronological order. The module outlines key characteristics of various styles and art periods using concrete examples. It includes the most renowned and representative artists and artworks. For students with an art history background or general familiarity with the topic, the content is manageable. For complete beginners, distinguishing between periods requires more memorisation and effort.
comment_teaching: Lectures are held twice a week, with no tutorials. The professor is clearly passionate about the subject and conveys a deep appreciation for the material. However, if you are not personally interested in art history, the lectures can feel a bit monotonous or heavy.
comment_grading: There are two quizzes, random attendance checks during lectures, one mandatory museum visit, and a final exam. Attendance contributes bonus points, which can be helpful, but success in the course relies heavily on memorisation. The quizzes and final exam are detailed and test your ability to recall and differentiate between styles, artists, and works.
comment_workload: There were two quizzes and a final exam. Since the course is memorisation-based, how well you do depends a lot on your learning style. If you're a visual or structured learner, it can be quite straightforward. Students interested in art will find the material engaging, but those less inclined may find it challenging to stay motivated.

title: 鍾意歐遊必讀
comment_content:
HUMA 2680由ancient Greek and Rome到Gothic and Renaissance再到modern architecture，帶你探索喺時間長河入面，西方建築因應當時文化背景同科技發展嘅轉變。因為architecture嘅特色同結構係同當時嘅cultural/religious context息息相關嘅（例如gothic architecture嘅ideal係同宗教相關，信奉God is light同reach God in heaven，所以gothic architecture會pursuit luminosity同verticality），所以上堂嗰陣唔單止學到唔同時代嘅建築特色，仲可以學到少少唔同時代嘅歷史背景、宗教文化等等。
值得一提嘅係到最後講contemporary architecture嘅時候會包含一啲我哋香港嘅特色建築。記憶最深刻嘅係香港嘅HSBC Headquarter，因為我喺嗰度返過intern，嗰陣只係知佢入面嘅結構好特別，有啲似舊公屋天井式設計，中間係空心嘅，可以望到底。上完堂原來佢咁嘅結構係有講究嘅，真係學到嘢。
如果你鍾意歐遊，我覺得讀下呢個course就幾有用，因為呢個course會包含唔少旅遊勝地，例如羅馬嘅Pantheon，法國嘅Louvre Palace，普通啲嘅basilica, town houses - Palazzi等等。我覺得了解多啲佢哋嘅建築特色同history喺去旅行嗰時都幾有幫助，唔會淨係局限咗喺「嘩，呢個好靚，嘩，嗰個都好靚」咁樣。
comment_teaching:

有上佢堂就知佢識好多嘢，好knowledgeable，地理歷史建築統統都難佢唔到。可能係因為有文化嘅關係，我覺得佢嘅外表同氣質都有一種優雅嘅感覺。同埋你問佢嘢佢會好快覆，亦都會擺lecture recordings上canvas比你重溫。
順帶一提，我覺得佢lecture slides整得好有心機＋整齊，圖文並茂，lecture slide有齊個建築物入面同出面個look嘅相，仲有啲floor plan/ground plan，Anna自己會整埋箭嘴同labels指比你睇個建築嘅唔同elements，就算係beginners都好容易follow。

Course Description 
This course offers an introductory historical survey of the philosophical foundations of select 
Buddhist traditions in South and East Asia and exploration of the history of Buddhism with 
an emphasis on its basic ideas, arguments, and interpretive strategies. We will explore key 
Buddhist concepts such as dependent origination, emptiness, no-self, loving-kindness, and 
compassion as well as philosophical questions concerning knowledge, language, ethics, and 
psychology (meditation and the mind) by closely interpreting texts from Buddhist teachings 
and traditions in relation to their historical contexts, philosophical contents, and their 
potential contemporary significance (such as the environmental and climate crisis). 
Course Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs) 
1. Develop an introductory understanding of classical Buddhist philosophies and their 
motivations and argumentative, interpretive, and rhetorical strategies. 
2. Learn different approaches and perspectives to philosophical issues in the context 
of South and East Asian thought and further develop one’s own philosophical perspective. 
3. Improve abilities in recognizing, evaluating, and discussing ideas, interpretations, and 
arguments. 
4. Cultivate skills in the critical analysis and discussion of textual sources and in scholarly 
communication.

comment_teaching:
Honestly, Cathy is a passionate professor and you can tell from the start of the course. She's just tryna make the class environment supportive and interesting for everyone (that means she'll tell everyone to shut up and listen to her if people keep talking and creating noise, politely). That also means you can always talk to her after class for gaining more understanding on the concepts and assignments and stuff.
She tried her best in every class to be interesting and really, she's just trying to help you at all times. Also she's one of the few professors who actually takes breaks in between, so that's a plus.
Objectively, I think that there are times where the lecture does get boring or vague, because there's just a lot of humanities jargon and sometimes it could also get pretty overwhelming too. However, I don't think it's due to her teaching though, but because of how in Humanities certain people's theories overlap or contradict with each other. Actually if you look at the readings, you'll actually realize how fatally boring the pragmatic theories are when you're simply reading through. This professor has actually made it interesting to learn. I gave up on the readings pretty early on, because the professor makes it much more intuitive and straightforward.
Her English is pretty advanced even for a native speaker myself, so there were times where I struggled to follow her. I realized that it's not that important to know every single concept perfectly though. Anyhow, she is aware when there are tricky concepts and tries to make sure the understanding is clear.
comment_grading:
Attending classes is sorta important in this course, so if you cannot do that, maybe you'll lose out on some marks. Participation marks are handed out throughout the lectures, they are mostly non-graded and simple enough. There are lecture videos though which is a plus.
Sample quizzes are given, which are quite similar, about a week before the Quizzes. Before Quiz 1 and Quiz 2, she spent like 20-30 minutes before the actual quiz time in class to give us hints (rough answers) and also recapped through the material together with us, so that we're clear on what to expect. 
She marks all the quizzes by herself; she said it herself that she tries to give as much marks as she can. She's pretty lenient. Moreover for presentations, she's the type of professor to take into consideration if you're the first group of presenters, so she'll give you extra leniency for extra nervousness or whatever.
comment_workload:
Workload is not that high. Average.
Quizzes: Just study 3 days before the quizzes or even a day before, because the sample question she provides are quite similar, and there are online resources too for past papers.
Presentation: literally 5 minutes, just time it well, not that hard. I could tell some people did it the night before, with just bare minimum effort on slides, reading it out. Presentation is just presenting your progressing on your research proposal, it's not supposed to be a final end-product. 
Research Proposal: It would be in your best interest to find Cathy after class maybe 3 times throughout the semester to check whether you're heading in the right direction with your proposal. She will definitely make time for you and she is extremely friendly.

course_name: Contemporary Architecture: The Pritzker Prize Winners
title: Basically you STALK architects here
comment_content:
My mum, who is an architect, had a look at my lecture slides and said,
"TOTAL BULLSHIT"
...
Lecture schedule in a nutshell
Weeks 1-6: contribution from INSTRUCTOR
Introducing the history of contemporary architecture, architectural styles and notable architects.
Weeks 7-13: contribution from STUDENTS
Group presentations, report composition, final exam.
See attachment A1 for a detailed breakdown.
See workload part to understand how the assessment works.
...
Two main points:
1. You worship architects in this class.
If you have a great architectural sense and dream, go elsewhere. This is a HUMA course, theories only, nothing practical. You would rather treat all architects as heroic figures and appreciate all of their designs, because they are perfect. The instructor does not explicitly label them as idols of course, but she will be mad if anyone in the audience thinks a design is bad.
2. Keywords, keywords, keywords!!!
You will come across with a lot of names that are specially used to describe an architect's style. However, architects often don't define their styles, or limit themselves to certain styles. From one style to another, there is often no clear boundaries to describe it; but if you miss the keywords, the instructor will be mad again and thinks that you begin to make it up instead of using the keywords she taught.
See the grading part for survival tips regarding this issue.
Overall speaking, the course is eye-opening to understand contemporary architects and architecture. But do your due diligence, you do not have to compliment every single design just because they come from the hands of a starchitect.
comment_teaching:
Three key elements for every lecture:
1. Pictures.
2. Instructor yapping.
3. Student yapping.
I.e. the instructor displays the pictures of a certain work of an architect and introduces its background; if her mood swings, she turns to the crowd and asks for the audience's opinions on the works.
The instructor seems to assume we all are professionals and should analyze very well. So I would recommend you making sure your idea is correct or close before raising your hand to answer a question. She will be mad again if the reply is unsatisfactory. Remember, she will remember your name and reflect your performance on the grades. See more in the grading part.
Nevertheless, the instructor can speak English fluently with very minimal accent. And she pronounces names very precisely, e.g. pronouncing Le Corbusier in a French way, so one should not deny her professional teaching attitude.
comment_grading:
Grade allocation:
25% - Project presentation
25% - Project report
10% - Consultation meetings
20% - Classwork
20% - Attendance and comments on presentations
...
Not hard to get a B range if you obey the seven survival tips below. I got a B- by the way, without following #1, #3 and #4.
1. Form your team CAREFULLY.
Triple check if your teammates can all dedicate certain effort into the project because it can be time-consuming. Also if you know the person very well, only let him/her join your team if he/she is a very responsible person. Remember that 10% of the grade comes from the two consultation meetings with the instructor. ALL members must attend both so if even one of your teammates does not show up, everyone in the team will have marks deducted.
2. Choose Norman Foster, or a Japanese architect.
For the group project this semester, every team has to pick one Pritzker Prize winner for their research question and presentation. Among all, I personally prefer Norman Foster as he should be the architect that has the most projects in Hong Kong so far, so it will be easier to conduct research. You can also consider Japanese architects (e.g. Tadao Ando) because they are the instructor's favourite.
3. Impression matters. Sit on the first two rows.
Your attendance is counted by participating in the discussion every lecture. Make sure the instructor can clearly see your face so she remembers you. You will also have to yell your name to let her mark it down on a piece of paper, so it's better to sit nearer to the stage.
4. Pay extra attention to keywords.
Many keywords mentioned in the lecture does not have a lot of information available online (so I boldly believe that the instructor made them all up). Make sure you listen to how the instructor defines each keyword. You can create a keyword list by category:
- Architectural styles (e.g. deconstructivism)
- Building materials (e.g. béton brut)
- Aesthetic principles (e.g. fukinsei) etc.
5. NEVER leave mid lecture.
We have someone leaving the lecture theatre while the instructor is still speaking. When he leaves and closes the door,
Instructor: "What's his name?"
His teammates: "XXXXX XXXXX"
Instructor: "I will deduct his marks!"
6. Worship your chosen architect at all costs.
Be prepared to optimize all means of research to support the evidence you have gathered about the architect your team has chosen. By saying that, you must rely on not only online resources, but also books, magazines, museum collections, or even course materials from friends who are taking architecture in other universities. If research is not seriously conducted (= online resources only), the instructor is going to be mad.
7. DO NOT trust the instructor.
For the group project, there will be a general guidelines that is of the same version for every team. But note! It is a GENERAL one and if your team directly copies the suggested outline, the instructor is going to be mad because your team fails to customize the presentation according to the architect's story. Even worse if your team does not have a specific research question, which is not explicitly mentioned as well.
comment_workload:
The course is chill for the first few weeks.
But it will be hell for the remaining weeks.
Suggest allocating at least 4-5 hours every day to prepare for the group presentation.
After the presentation, you will be given two weeks to finish up the report, also a groupwork. That also requires a lot of research. Allocate 5-6 hours per day.
Meanwhile do not forget to comment on your coursemates' presentations to earn attendance marks (on a comment form that will be distributed by the TA). Be sure to jot down the keywords from their presentations seriously. Unserious comments will result in 0 mark.
See attachment A2 for the detailed marking criteria and guidelines for research.

title: 道家說「得意忘言」，但考試切記不能這樣，乖乖把原文記起來吧。
comment_content:
先寫一下大家關心的吧，期末考試有四題，大概意思是：
1. 老子的人生論與政治論。
2. 老子說「道沖而用之或不盈。淵兮似萬物之宗。挫其銳 解其紛 和其光 同其塵。湛兮似或存。吾不知誰之子 象帝之先。」。翻譯並論述這段話在老子思想體系中的含意。
3. 逍遙遊主要用哪些寓言故事說明「至人無己，神人無功，聖人無名」的意思，並論述這一主張的含義
4. 養生主論述了莊子什麼養生思想。
評分準則是每題25+8分。25分是內容，8分是表達分，四選三作答。所以滿分是99分。內容分是一個重點一分，有嚴格的marking scheme，不是impression marking，所以不要浪費時間寫自己的見解，而是回答課堂上講過的重點。（課堂上沒講過考試模式是這樣的，相信不少人包括我也寫了很多個人見解）
從marking scheme去看不一定要一字不漏背誦原文，但有些部分幾乎是逐句給分，漏一句都會失分，所以拿高分還是要背誦的。例如第一題政治論有6分就是要解釋「不尚賢，使民不爭」，「不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜」，「不見可欲，使心不亂」，各兩分，不必背原文，但不能籠統的講，必須分述。
雖然第一題人生論通常是指老子的第二章，政治論是第三章，但要是你舉了其他章節有相關人生和政治的也能有分，例如「上善若水」這些，應該算是bonus分數，可以彌補你在第二三章漏掉的分數，我考試時沒有這樣做所以只拿了18/25左右的內容分數。
內容方面，其實上頭幾節課已經把思想說透徹了，後面全部都是重複前面的東西但以不同角度說明，不會讓你有什麼大徹大悟的感覺。可是考試上還是需要你把這些不同角度都記起來才能拿到好分數。道家說「得意忘言」，但考試切記不能這樣。
要拿滿分是很難的，首先你要背得到所有相關原文（至少每一句意思都要記得），然後按照老師課上詮釋的方向解釋而且不能有所缺漏（例如天下皆知美之為美，斯不美矣要用縱橫角度說明，然後再從相對角度說明，共3分），在原文上正確的elaboration也是有分數的。前面四題評分準則我都記下來了，有興趣可以向我購買，雖然這個course不一定會再開了。

教學是很好的，有老師自己的理解，有例子輔以說明，有些堂上例子在考試時複述可能有分（例如小金與蛇的例子說明和光同塵）。只是道德經本來重複性太高，背後思想比較單一，所以到後面沒有說非常有趣。
一個很大的問題是這節課改Essay和Final Exam非常的慢，這是TA辦事效率不高的問題，可能是因為這節課這個學期多了很多人上（？），但我仍然不認為需要將近一個月來完成批改。而且改這種模式的Final Exam非常費時。

comment_content:

思想上其实很简单，也很富有哲理：老子围绕着无为，庄子围绕着无待。黄教授也谈论了一些辩证法，以及道处于绝对而非相对，举了很多有意思的例子。其中一个我最受启发的就是和光同尘，水如何去适应不同的身形，以阴柔但是不执着于自我的，无待于我的姿态穿过各种苦难而身体不受伤害。大家如果平常多用心在这样的举例上，最后对final还是会很有裨益的。

comment_content:

title: Amazing introductory course - definitely something new even if you're already self taught in philosophy
comment_content: Content is a brief history of modern western philosophy, from Descartes to a few modern philosophers. The course is split into scientific revolution era philosophers (Descartes, Spinoza, Cavendish, Conway, Leibniz) with a focus on epistemology and metaphysics, enlightenment era philosophers (Hume, Kant, Mill, Dilthey) with a focus on more epistemology, and some modern and contemporary philosophers (Heidegger, Beauvoir, Moore, Wittgenstein, Arendt, Quine, Jaeggi) on truth and identity. Due to the short period of this course, most philosophers only get a couple of lessons dedicated to them, so don't expect a lot of depth and detail on any particular worldview. You should see this as an eye-opener that exposes you to many different flavors of modern philosophy that you can then look deeper into.
comment_teaching: Eric S. Nelson is an excellent philosopher who is great at explaining deep and difficult philosophical concepts. He freely welcomes and encourages students to raise their hands and ask questions in the middle of his lectures, making the class feel more like a discussion group - essential for philosophy. He also spends a lot of time after class explaining to anyone who has questions to ask him - if you take his class, don't be shy to chat with him about anything at all, his passion for philosophy is infectious.
comment_grading: Grading is rather lenient, the professor and the TA don't expect you to be a genius philosopher at this stage. What they do expect is an understanding of the concepts taught in the class, what the abstract words actually mean - if you can do that, you'll get very high marks, and you don't need super high marks to get an A.
comment_workload: There are 3 quizzes that should only take a short amount of study - though this depends on how quickly you can grasp the concepts - and a 2 minute poster presentation at the end that should only take a couple days of work. No final exam with all the concepts, just a quiz after each chapter. By UST standards, this course is a welcome break from literally everything else.

As I mentioned in my title, this is a risky course with an unclear grading. Let’s break everything down and talk about the details. 
Homework: Homework is manageable if you refer to lecture notes and collaborate with classmates. They tend to use the same homework questions every semester so asking students who took this course previously is helpful. However, some homework questions are not clear enough for students to understand its meaning. The grading is weird, in a way that even if TAs pointed out your mistakes, deduction in marks may not be necessary. 
Group project: The group project is one of the drawbacks in this course as it brings about some uncertainties. In the group project, a group of 5 or 6 is required to solve a real-world problem with methods regarding IEDA (not necessary to be the materials provided in this semester). Normally, students have to start working on that 1 month before the presentation, which is on the last 2 lectures of this course. The first thing is the choice of the topic. More than half of the group chose issues related to UST. After that, survey is required for some group as data base for research. In our group, some data are made-up since it’s not reasonable compared to the fact. After calculation base on data, conclusion can be drawn. Then, the preparation of presentation is available. The grading is based on the presentation with some requirements. Some important requirements are that everyone in the group has to present and the time for the presentation should be less than12 minutes.  
Exams: Exam paper consists of 10 MCs and 4 or 5 LQs with midterm covering L1-L6 and final covering L5-L9. A page of double-sided A4 cheat sheet is allowed in the exams. A sample paper is provided before the exams. A try of sample paper is worthwhile since some of the MCs in the exams are the same as that in the sample paper. The midterm questions are a little weird compared to the exercise and homework but still manageable with a high mean. The final is more difficult than the midterm becuase the process of LQs are more complicated with abundant calculations. 
Remark: Same as previous semesters, grade of group project and final weren't released officially. In my opinion, this behaviour is irresponsible for students who have the right to get notified of their academic performance. What’s more, my friend and I both got a grade that is a subgrade lower than our anticipation and as you may notice from other reviews that the grading is harsh in recent 2 semesters. So, if you really mind your grade, don’t enrol in this course. Take it easy and accept your B/C range grade if you are confident enough to get an A/B range.

It then examines types (product vs. process, radical vs. incremental), patterns (S-curves, technology cycles), and disruptive innovation dynamics (Part 2).

Organizational structures that foster innovation, including the impact of firm size, formalization, centralization, and balancing creativity with efficiency (Part 6)
The shift from closed to open innovation paradigms, emphasizing external collaboration and crowdsourcing (Part 7).

comment_content:
1. Lecture Slides:
There are 12 lecture slides from 11 topics with 4.0 Product and Process Design being the longest at 56 pages and 11.0 Social Enterprise in Hong Kong being the shortest at 18 pages.
2. iPRS
You get 1 minute for each question with there being 5 each day. They require you to watch videos and read case studies after lectures. However, there was one question where the answer can only be found if you had stayed for the lecture. or you can tell AI to summarize the videos and case studies. Then screenshot the question. Well I do think the iPRS questions are a pretty good way to check if you actually understand the material. Only ask AI if you really don't know the answer. Worked for me.
3. Exams
The exam is close book and is made up of 60 MCQs with a 2 hour time limit (Quite a lot of people left early). None of them are quantitative. The whole syllabus is just those 12 lecture slides plus the final case study. The number of MCQs from each topic will be provided so you can plan out which topics to spend more time on.
comment_teaching:

As others have mentioned, the professor sometimes will start talking about his personal life during the lectures. These stories may seem to be off topic. SOME do relate to the teaching material. For example: 
Teaching topic at the time:
Just-In-Time Inventory, where we should keep inventory as low as possible to reduce waste and force process improvement.
Life Stories: 
Many years ago, he gave his sons 1000 dollar allowance. Then he cut it by 10% each week. If his son can live without the 10% he continues, until his son starts complaining.
How they link:
When the son complains, the minimum allowance amount is found just like lowering inventory reveals hidden inefficiencies in operations.
There are some life stories that is not related at all like how he saw combs of bananas being on discount at 3 HKD in Fusion so he bought a lot and now eats 2 bananas a day. Did you know you can preserve bananas by covering them in plastic wrap?
Overall, the life stories and jokes, made the long lectures less boring and tiring. I personally prefer this type of teaching. Its way better than him just throwing knowledge at us without making it relatable.
2. Lecture Structure:
9:30 - 11:00 Talks about the main slides
11:00 - 11:10 Break
11:10 - 12:50 Case study
iPRS can either be just before or just after the break. It can be at the start or at the end I guess. That didn't happen this semester though.

6.0 Sourcing and Supply Management PPT -> Break -> iPRS -> 6.5 Case Study: 759 Store PPT

title: the easiest course i have studied in ust
comment_content: The course content is exceptionally structured, straightforward, and very easy to understand. The entire syllabus relies solely on 12 lecture slides and a final case study, meaning everything you need is clearly laid out from the start. Furthermore, the number of multiple-choice questions from each topic is provided in advance, allowing you to plan your revision efficiently. Best of all, the 60-question closed-book exam is entirely qualitative, so you do not have to stress over complex mathematical calculations or heavy quantitative problems.
comment_teaching: Prof. Lau’s teaching style is brilliant, making the lectures very easy to catch up with and follow along. He brings a wonderful touch of humor to the classroom and often shares quirky, entertaining personal stories. While some stories sound like random anecdotes, others brilliantly bridge abstract business concepts with real-life logic—making long lecture hours much less tiring and surprisingly engaging rather than dry. The lecture structure, complete with a well-timed break, also helps keep your energy up.
comment_grading: The grading scheme is fair, transparent, and has turned out very favorably for me. The grade distribution is quite reasonable, and because only 8 out of 10 iPRS quizzes actually count toward your final score, there is a built-in safety net. Securing a strong grade is very achievable as long as you stay reasonably consistent with your daily coursework and quiz submissions.
comment_workload: The overall workload is wonderfully light and easy to manage around a busy student schedule. The two main writing assignments are just case studies where you read a firm's background document and answer three targeted questions. I only had to spend about three to four days in total to complete both of them. Additionally, the daily iPRS quizzes are quite straightforward to get high marks on—especially if you utilize quick summaries or stay caught up with the materials.

The questions are quite straightforward, but some questions only rely on 1 particular slide or video, or even what the professor said in class that was not shown in the files. So I just used AI to help me answer the questions, may also need to rely on the help of other classmates, so an average student loses 1-4 questions.
The average for the 2 assignments is about 7-9/10, I guess, so not that difficult.

title: Very short, very intense and very competitive common core course
comment_content:
Topics:
1. Introduction to the Information Infrastructure (Jan 2)
2. Digital Convergence; Wireless Communications and Spectrum Regulation (Jan 3)
3. The Next Generation Information Infrastructure (Jan 4)
4. Business and Socioeconomic Implications of Information Infrastructure (Jan 6)
5. Web 2.0 and Innovation (Jan 7)
--- midterm assignment (Jan 4-8) ---
6. Diffusion of Telecommunications Services; Case Study: SMS Adoption in Hong Kong and China (Jan 8)
7. Theoretical Framework of Information Infrastructure Deregulation (Jan 9)
8. Organizational Restructuring of Information Infrastructure (Jan 10)
9. Network Interconnection; Local Network Competition in Hong Kong (Jan 11 am)
10. Foreign Direct Investment in Telecommunications and WTO’s Basic Telecommunications Agreement (Jan 11 pm)
--- final exam (Jan 15) ---
As you can see, this 2-week course is divided into 2 parts, the first half about technology and the second half about policies. Whoever designed this course for some reason thought that cramming 18923791283 things into 2 weeks is a good idea, which leads to this super intense schedule.
The first half started off by briefly going through the whole ELEC1200 and DSE ICT networking unit (not joking) in the first 2 lectures, then moved onto introducing many, MANY new telecommunication technologies to you, talking about their working principles very briefly and mainly focusing on their societal and business impacts. This half is honestly pretty fun for technology enjoyers, and is really easy if you have studied related courses before.
I only went to like 2 lectures after the midterm due to being busy organizing Firebird CTF (please join COMP2633), so I could not really say much about the second half of the course. The second half is all about business theories, with a ton of easy concepts and terms that you can understand effortlessly but would take you a lot of time to remember that they exist. The economics theories are pretty tough for me to handle since I have never studied DSE economics back in secondary school, but there were not many of them and they did not appear in the final exam anyways. Overall speaking, the second half is really easy if you have studied some economics before, and the rest is basically just a bunch of terms and concepts added onto common sense. It is quite boring for me, but I think it would be more fun had I actually watched the lecture videos.
comment_teaching:
Professor Xu is a pretty chill guy. He clearly knows a lot about telecommunications and has a lot of personal experiences to share with us and enrich the main teaching content. I would go as far as to say that his teaching really carried the relatively boring second half. He explains concepts well, tries to arouse students' interests in the lectures (by going around the classroom at times and asking questions), and is very willing to answer questions. He has a bit of mainland accent which does not affect the clarity at all. Overall, a solid professor.
However, the main issue that I have to pick on is the quality of the powerpoint slides. Yes, they look pretty and is fairly rich in content, but it occasionally gets quite abstract by replacing words with pictures, and a number of the slides are duplicated in content. The same graph, same slide appears in 3-4 different powerpoints across different lectures, which is not the worst thing in the world, but it looks quite disorganized to me and is pretty annoying to scroll through them. Sometimes Professor Xu will talk about things that are NOT on the powerpoint but WILL BE examed, so you need to actually watch lecture videos (which I didn't and is a big mistake) and jot those down by yourself.
comment_grading:
Grading scheme:
Midterm assignment (Jan 4-8, take home, online, 1 attempt unlimited time) - 50%
Final exam (Jan 15, 3-hour face-to-face paper exam) - 50%
The midterm assignment contains content from lectures 1-5 only, and is completely open book, open Internet. The final exam contains content from lectures 6-10 only (non-cumulative), and you are allowed to bring a double-sided A4 cheatsheet (printed or handwritten both ok) to the exam.
The midterm assignment and final exam are in similar format. Both consists of a LARGE number of T/F questions, MCs, fill-in-the-blanks and a few short questions (which are essentially just point-form essays). The midterm assignment had a 10-mark short question about the benefits of cellular communication system on mass communication in the technological aspect, followed by a 20-mark "long" essay which told you to do a "case study" (i.e. copying information) from a company that went through the process of "from atoms to bits to intelligent bits", while the final exam has 3 10-15 mark short questions.
Statistics of midterm assignment:
Mean: 90.52/100, SD: 6.16
My score: 91.5/100
Statistics of final exam:
Mean: 84.29/100, SD: 7.16
My score: 91/100
Final grade: A
--- huge rant below, you can safely ignore ---
Disclaimer: I am in no way trying to boast about my scores or what I have done in this course (as there is genuinely nothing to boast about, I should be ashamed about them instead), and these are all just my *extremely biased* personal opinions.
This looks like a fairly positive review so far, right? Well, I have to say, I ABSOLUTELY HATED THIS COURSE. I was NEVER a single day happy with this course, and only realized I fell into a REALLY DEEP rabbit hole when the midterm comes. This leads us to the worst part of this course: grading.
This part is the ONE part that I ABSOLUTELY DESPISED during my 2 weeks struggling in this course. The assessments were unable to let students show their true capabilities and differentiate the abilities of them AT ALL.
If you have seen previous reviews, you will notice that the mean for midterm assignment is always very high. This year, for absolutely no reason, they pushed the mean even higher.
Statistics of midterm assignment:
Mean: 90.52/100, SD: 6.16
My score: 91.5/100
I was speechless when I first saw the mean. I knew the mean would be high as the midterm assignment is fairly easy, but this is likely the highest mean in all these years that only allow 1 attempt submission. When I went to the paper checking session to check what mistakes I made, I realized how bad the 113-question assignment is. The wordings were VERY vague and you could only do a 50/50 guess on some questions because of that. Fill-in-the-blanks questions sometimes went completely out of context to the point that you have to pray to God and ask for directions. The short question was literally disguised to be an essay, which at first gave you an impression that you could write whatever you want and you will get full mark as long as your points all make sense. However, the marking scheme said you only need to LIST OUT 2 exact points that the professor wanted and you get a HUGE mark deduction if you did not. Last time I saw such a similar exam was ~2 years ago when I was doing my DSE ICT paper 1, which shows how terrible the paper was. Half of the marks that I lost were from MCs, while the other half was from the short question. I know this is much of a skill issue, but it does little to affect my opinion on the paper.
The final exam is more business-oriented, so the portion of short questions become larger. The short questions are usually the part which lowers the mean by a lot, but this year they decided to put the EASIEST short questions that I have ever seen, which raised the bar a lot higher than previous years.
Statistics of final exam: (they decided to release it this year)
Mean: 84.29/100, SD: 7.16
My score: 91/100
Remember when 66.5 marks was the mean of the final exam? NOT ANYMORE! The paper was the same difficulty as the midterm assignment, and the only reason why the mean is slightly lower is that not all people could not put 500 slides of content onto a single A4 paper (most of the people managed to do this by setting the font size to like 0.0000000001, I have no idea how they could read that). The short questions were SO EASY to the point that you just have to copy points from the lecture notes and use a little bit of your common sense to score you high marks. The MC wordings are still vague and the fill-in-the-blanks are EVEN MORE GUESSY than the ones in midterm assignment, which really makes me question my life and regret not dropping the course 1238971239123 times during the 3 hours i was in front of the paper.
To illustrate how bad the exam format of this course actually is, I should probably talk about my personal experiences first. The night before the final exam, I was rushing my cheatsheet and did not sleep at all, so I was super tired and my brain completely turned off. The worst thing of all is I literally fell asleep while doing the paper. I had no idea how long I slept, but even with such a terrible body condition into the exam, I still managed to finish the exam with AROUND 1.5 HOURS TO SPARE. The majority of the students finished their paper in around an hour or so and decided to leave early, so the classroom went from fully seated at the start of the exam to more than half empty towards the end. I did not want to leave early, so I literally wrote explanations on the question paper next to every MC question. To lengthen my short questions to make myself look like I was thinking, I kept repeating my points and paraphrasing them until all the answers went out of the answer boxes. Even after all these meaningless actions, I still had enough time to thoroughly check my entire paper a few more times.
The exam format, as you can see, is extremely frustrating. The course gives you an 3-hour exam paper which you can finish in 1.5 hours to waste your precious time, and just completely destroys your confidence and hard work by grading the short questions according to a not-so-reasonable marking scheme. I guess this might be more of a personal issue and massive skill issue (again), but I really believe the assessment part is what singlehandedly pulls the quality of the course down.
The ideas of open Internet unlimited time midterm assignment and printed cheatsheet without regulation in the final exam are pretty bad for distinguishing the students as well. In the midterm assignment, all you need to do is to copy the question and paste it onto the browser, and you will get so many useful answers that you can immediately copy and paste into your assignment. You can even directly ask questions on Chegg and websites like that so you can get full mark as long as you pay for it! In the final exam, everyone just decided to copy every single slide onto 1 A4 paper so they can copy whatever and whenever they want! Does this really show that they have learnt stuff from the course? NO! These 2 things along with easy assessments are the main culprits as to why this course's mean is always so high. The exams are not about understanding, but are about copying and copying only. Whoever copies the fastest gets A+ despite not learning a single thing from this course! Meanwhile, the ones who worked hard and understands everything get C instead. Why not actually design fairly fun and challenging exam papers that requires thinking instead?
The only thing that keeps the rating from being a solid E is the fact that the final grade has not been assigned yet. There are reviews that say +1 SD is still B+, which means the grading is rather harsh; On the other hand, there are also reviews that say the professor gives maximum A range, which means the grading is fairly good. I know my score is completely out of A range already, which is something that I expected coming into this course, so it is really just a test of whether I will get B+, B or B-. Will come back to update this review after the letter grade is out.
Update: My final grade is A, which is extremely surprising as the grading is really lenient this year. However, please check the comments before thinking that this is a good grade course. This course's grading is VERY inconsistent and unpredictable, so please think twice before enrolling in this course.
In conclusion, I strongly DO NOT suggest anyone who cares about their CGA to study this course, as this course is straight up brutal in terms of competition, and A range will be difficult to get no matter how good you are. However, if you just want to take an SA common core out of your way without caring how bad your TGA in winter will be, this course is a very good choice. The shorter the pain, the better.
comment_workload: The workload is not very heavy for a 3 credit course. All you have to do throughout the winter semester is to finish the midterm assignment in time and prepare a double-sided A4 cheatsheet for the final exam. I would say the 3 credits mainly comes from the fact that you have to watch the lecture videos to fully know what will be tested in the 2 assessments, and that you have to read through and summarize probably around 1000 powerpoint slides into 1 piece of A4 paper. As a super lazy person, I only finished my midterm assignment 1 minute before its deadline, and started making a mediocre cheatsheet at around 1am the night before the exam, which made this course pretty tough for me. However, if you are an average dilligent UST student unlike me, you should be hardworking enough to handle this course well while (not so) enjoying your (not so) long winter holiday.

comment_teaching:
After reading all the horrible reviews previously about her and how she "ruined the course" for them, I was wondering if her teaching was really THAT bad. 
To summarize, some people may think she is a good professor, but I'd say her teaching still leaves a lot to be desired. DO NOT choose this course as CC if you're quiet/introverted!
Her accent, especially if your first language isn't English, is pretty thick. I didn't really have a ton of problem understanding her given how I'm non-local but many others had difficulty understanding her. 
She is late for lesson frequently; I'd say around 50-60% of the time she is late for 5 minutes or over, the TA always says it's because of "traffic" but sometimes she'd admit herself she was late because she was at Pacific Coffee too long. 
She consistently says to follow the course syllabus to prepare for lectures, but unfortunately after her having to miss multiple weeks of of classes due to illness (which is obviously out of her control, so not blaming her for this) a lot of things in the schedule changed making the the syllabus mostly useless. However, she constantly said the syllabus is being updated regularly, but most of the things like the class schedule never aligned with what she actually taught in-class. 
Unfortunately, the rumors that she is not organized is kinda true. There was one time where because she was sick for multiple days in a row, she was unable to give us enough information initially to work on the group project. Then one day randomly she asks the class why we haven't turned in our survey for the project yet, which we had NO indication on Canvas or the syllabus it was due that day (also why are you talking so much about paying attention to the syllabus when you don't even follow the syllabus yourself while also assuming deadlines not in the syllabus?). Given how no one has even started working on it, her and the TA then said they were "pushing back" the survey submission deadline to Friday (the class was a Wednesday that same week. During midterms. 48 hours to simultaneously do research about multiple brands, select one, and write a survey about the product that they were going to market at the school.). I may be judging her too harshly on this, but it honestly seems kinda irresponsible on her part or the TA's part. 
I honestly cannot say if her grading is biased or not (because obviously I can't see other people's grades), but I think she does have some favoritism towards certain students. She seems to like international students and especially exchange students a lot, and gets really enthusiastic when they answer her questions or open for discussion (she also likes students who took her other courses on marketing). She still allows everyone to express their ideas during discussion though and can criticize other students for their answers, it's just her demeanor towards certain students may give off the perception to many that she is "biased". 
If you even get the chance to discuss and talk in her class at all; most of the class time is her just talking on and on about the course material, then 5 minutes later she goes off topic on a tangent without context to the course material, repeat the process again and again and that. Sometimes she would ramble about her ideas during discussion time for so long that the class ends. So, if you want to get participation marks, find every chance that you can to participate and don't be afraid to say something, no matter if it's good or not (because she'll interject you anyways, at least you get the participation points).
EDIT: I noticed there were quite a few reviews praising her teaching and the course in general, even blaming the people who wrote negative reviews on this course for not being very dedicated to the course. I would like to say that I am being 100% honest with this review, based on what I had seen and what my groupmates (who were MARK students) had experienced. I am also from SSCI and took this course to fulfill a CC, so I have zero knowledge on anything that occurs within the teaching environment in SBM I am not trying to make a bad name out of her, I just believe that despite some positives, there are still inherent flaws to her teaching. comment_workload:
Why are people saying the workload is light for this course, I'd say it's heavier than other CC's at least if you want to score higher/be on her good side.
Before every lecture you are "expected" to pre-read the lecture notes, watch the pre-lecture videos and read the pre-lecture articles. In class, as discussed in the teaching portion, students are expected to engage in discussion for participation marks by answering questions or showing their perspectives on an open-ended task. Attendance is not mandatory, but as usual they highly "recommend" people attend all lectures. 
The two essays are just 250 words each, and if you write any topic related to marketing or its effects you could probably get full marks for both essays.
In terms of the presentation, the workload really depends on your groupmates. Those who do not know any people in the class are assigned random teammates (otherwise you could work with your friends), so if there are any freeriders in your group your workload may be higher. Generally, my group was pretty good as two of my groupmates were Marketing students and were willing to contribute a lot, so my workload throughout the presentation and project was quite manageable.
The final quiz, held during the last teaching week of the semester, is comprised of 24 MCQ's and one open-ended question regarding the evaluation of an ad campaign. In my opinion, the quiz really only benefits those who attend the lecture and pays attention to the supporting material. The quiz included some very specific memorization-based questions (like how many SDG's are there or what is the triple bottom line in a social business), but also a lot of conceptual questions (like what is this ad trying to say about this concept), which has answers that could only be understood if you not only were in-class, but participating in-class. No matter how obscure some of the lecture information is, there is always a chance she WILL test that (like asking what marketing campaign did the Chinese history museum did to raise more funds, which I hardly remember if we ever went over in-class). NOTE: DO remember to watch the videos that were given as pre-reading or shown in-class! They accounted for around 60% of the MCQ's (they literally ask "In the TED Talk about this topic by this person" frequently). The open-ended question was a bit easier, as they'd show an ad related to a major topic of the course, and ask whether the ad could attract new customers/raise brand and market value/make a difference etc. You have 220 words to list your answer and give reasons supporting your answer and you are evaluated based on whether your ideas were logical and relavent (no right or wrong answer); it's like writing an English examination but with Marketing concepts. 
In general, if you want to score high on the quiz, the amount of active engagement you need to do in-class and studying out-of class is equally as high. So I would definitely NOT say this course has a "low" workload, especially towards the end.

comment_content:
3 parts:
Basic Financial Mathematics (very easy)
Linear Algebra
Calculus
For the midterm:
It covers Financial Mathematics and Linear Algebra. Calculators are allowed. The midterm is not very difficult—if you study the lecturer’s handwritten notes thoroughly, you should easily secure at least 80% (at least based on this year’s paper).
The sample paper has a similar difficulty level to the actual midterm. Some questions follow exactly the same format as those in the sample paper or the examples shown in lectures, with only the numbers changed. So make sure you understand and remember the steps for every type of question.
For those who have never studied linear algebra before: don’t worry, it’s perfectly manageable. It’s just basic mathematics that requires a bit more time to get used to. Personally, I didn’t take M1/M2 in HKDSE and only got Level 4 in Maths, yet I found the midterm very easy.
For the final:
Calculus only. No calculator is allowed, but you may bring one double-sided A4 cheat sheet.
This is where things get really challenging. Calculus is taught starting around Week 7, leaving only about 5-6 weeks to prepare for a final exam that is worth 65% of the total grade. Unlike the earlier topics, calculus involves a lot of symbolic manipulation—lots of variables, exponents, subscripts, integrals, derivatives, and complicated equations—rather than straightforward numerical calculations. Many new concepts are introduced, and they can be quite difficult for beginners to grasp.
This year, the final paper was WAY MORE HARDER than the sample paper, so don’t be misled into thinking that memorising the solutions from the sample will be enough. It absolutely won’t.
The exam was genuinely tough—you’ll see what I mean when you look at the grade statistics below. To do well, you need to practise more difficult exercises from the textbook. The TA exercises, lecture examples, and sample paper are far too easy to prepare you adequately. Make sure you’re thoroughly prepared!

title: pretty good
comment_content:
The course content is a well-structured survey of essential mathematical tools for business and social sciences. It is highly practical and application-oriented.
Part 1: Finance & Algebra (Ch. 3 & 4): The course starts with the mathematics of finance (simple/compound interest, annuities, amortization), which is immediately relevant for any business student. This is followed by an extensive unit on matrices and systems of linear equations. This section is fundamental for understanding data organization, solving multi-variable problems, and is a building block for more advanced topics like operations research.
Part 2: Differential Calculus (Ch. 10, 11, 12): This is the core of the course. It covers limits, the derivative, and all its applications. Key topics include various rules of differentiation (product, quotient, chain), implicit differentiation, and concepts like elasticity of demand. The most valuable part is applying derivatives to curve sketching and optimization (finding max profit, min cost), which are crucial for economic modeling and decision-making.
Part 3: Integral Calculus (Ch. 13 & 14): The course concludes with integration, covering antiderivatives, the fundamental theorem of calculus, and techniques like substitution. The applications to area between curves and analyzing probability density functions provide a strong foundation for economic analysis and statistics.
Overall: The content is demanding but incredibly useful. It doesn't delve into the deep theoretical proofs of higher-level calculus but focuses intensely on how to use these tools, which is exactly what a business student needs.

comment_content:
Wow, they actually did it, they have somehow managed to put every calculus thing in M2 in a 3-month course. Is it fun? I'll let you decide.
There are mainly 2 big topics: Preface, and Actual Calculus.
The first topic is Preface, which has a huge range of tiny stuff in it. From intervals, to composite functions, to some trigonometry stuff, and finally limits, stuff you have to understand before moving onto the actual "good" stuff. It can be overwhelming for some, but you really need to fully understand them (except trigo) before moving on, and there are couple ways to help with that, which I would talking more in the Workload section. Almost forgot, Squeeze Theorem and Intermediate Value Theorem, REMEMEBER THESE NAMES.
Here comes the big daddy: Actual Calculus. This course mostly discuss about Differentiation, from first principle, to all the rules, to implict differentiation, and finally related rates and optimization. It's honestly kinda fun to work around the problem, but unless you're a psychopath like me, you might not like it as much.
One more topic: Integration. There's honestly not a lot to talk about, only two main things to worry about: U-Substitution and fundemental theorem of calculus, and that's about it.

comment_workload:
Here's the thing, you're probably a science/engineering student, so you know you have other math courses to study. VERY IMPORTANT: START LEARNING ABOUT CALCULUS BEFORE LECTURES. Treat the lectures as review sessions. If you are able to do that, you will have a much better time understand what the professors are talking about. It might sounds difficult, but trust me, just use an hour or two at the end of the day to understand the basic concepts, when the lectures starts talking things that are more in-depth, you will have a good time.
For homeworks, apparently the questions are not so easy. You do need to spend some time on them, but you will learn a lot from them after trial and error.
For preparing midterm and final, here's a very dirty trick, instead of doing 1012 past papers, do 1013 past papers. They're basically the same course, but one of them is harder, and if you study harder past papers, you will be prepared a lot. No joke, the SAME questions were copied from 1013 to 1012, doing this helps a lot.
Overall, you do need to spend some time on this, or else you might easily fall behind. If you hate math, I would say C or D, but if you like math, I would say B, I honestly learned a lot.

title: math 1012
comment_content:
This is an introductory course in one-variable calculus, the first in the Calculus I and II sequence, designed for students that have not taken HKDSE Mathematics Extended Module M1 or M2. Topics include functions and their limits, continuity, derivatives and rules of differentiation, applications of derivatives, and basic integral calculus.
Yes, correct, but it is not just basic in my opinion. As a student that never have been tapped in calculus, it is already very hard and advanced. (Moreover, I am weak at maths. :( )
It is fairly acceptable before midterm, which only included some basic differentiation and trigonometric identities, (but double angle formulas are as hard as hell for me.) But once you reach the final exam, it is another stuff. The preparation for the final exam took me at least 2 whole weeks to handle well with integration by doing the exercises given by tutorial. And when I tried to do the final exam past paper, I have no idea on how to do the first long question at all! The final exam past paper given is just ridiculously hard and not able to do the long question section. Although the final exam is an open-notes, full multiple-choice question paper due to the epidemic and the difficulty is decreased, it is still challenging for a newcomer to calculus.
The lectures teach you basic theory on calculus with simple examples. While the tutorials give you more moderate exercises. So that you can earn some confidences from them. When the exams arrive, they give you questions with 100% different from what you have done before, so that you have no idea on how to solve them, crash your confidences that you have built before, and your grade is broken.
comment_teaching:
Mr Jiaxi Ying is good at teaching and I am fortunate to be taught by him. It is easy to understand the theory with his explanations. He will solve some webwork questions in class and it is nice. The only problem is the questions taught in class are too easy compared to exam level. And you will find a hard time if you are studying for final exam with just his notes.
It is good to point out that I only attended for the first 3 tutorials, then I had skipped all of them, as I feel like the difference is not big if you have finished all the exercises in notes. While I attended the first 7 lectures because I feel okay and not waste my time. But for the remaining 13 lectures(not included with 7 video lectures after November), I think I have things more meaningful(like playing and studying mahjong) rather than attending them.
comment_grading:
if you are good at maths, the course is fine for you. I believe getting A is not that hard for geniuses. Even so, paying more efforts to ensure you to get high enough marks.
If you are bad at maths like me(DSE math level 3~4), you better to be prepared to get C or B- even you did tons of exercises included sources from the internet, you just don't have enough talent to overcome the problem sometimes.
Find some pals that you can work with and good at maths would help you a lot, start studying at least before 2 weeks the exam, and struggle with those who are not good at so you feel less painful when you don't know how to do the maths.  I get a D grade.

title: The worst part of this course is not the content but rather Samuel Ma
comment_content:
Overall:
This course (or 1013) is mandatory for all science students for good reason, as introductory calculus is important for many fields in STEM. The content in this course is pretty much identical to that of IB Math AASL. If you have no calculus background, be prepared to grind out practice problems for a good grade.
Even for people with a strong background in calculus, the final exam can be quite challenging, so make sure to attempt at least a few before going into the exam.
Some tips for doing well: 
- Having a strong precalculus (algebraic manipulations, trigonometry, etc.) foundation is important, so if you aren't confident, spend some time practicing the fundamentals before starting the course
- Getting a conceptual understanding of key calculus concepts is crucial for doing well. As such, I recommend watching the following playlist by 3b1b: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDMsr9K-rj53DwVRMYO3t5Yr
- Do as many past papers as you can, including the past papers for MATH1013. This is because the content covered in 1013 is practically identical to that in 1012, and there is a wider selection of 1013 papers to attempt.
Pre-midterm content:
- Elementary functions, intervals, continuity, limits, basic derivatives
Post-midterm content:
- Implicit differentiation, derivatives of inverse functions (trigonometric, logarithmic, etc.), related rates, optimization, mean value theorem, curve sketching, L'Hopital's rule, antiderivatives, definite integrals, FTC, integration by substitution

comment_grading:
Weighting:
10% WebWork
35% Midterm (1 hr 30 mins)
55% Final (3 hrs)
Both exams had around 30% MCQ and 70% LQ. Make sure to double check your answers, especially for MCQs, as a single error could drop you down a subgrade. The time given is plenty for both exams.
In my opinion, the midterm was far easier than the final. 
Absolute grading (though I heard the boundaries were relaxed a bit, possibly due to unexpectedly low exam scores):
A+/A/A- > 85% > B+/B/B- > 70% > C+/C/C- > 50% > D > 40% > F
Approximately 5% per sub grade, so 95% is required for A+, which is not easy.

As you can see, the average grade is ~C, with around 40% of people getting a D. However, B range is easily attainable with enough practice (A+ is challenging due to the little margin of error).

In terms of revision, you will need to do past papers in order to do well. If you do not have a strong mathematics foundation, you'll need to try extra hard to get a good grade.
If you just want to pass, the workload is not bad at all.

The content itself is not too difficult, as it covers functions, derivatives and integration, focusing on mostly the theory behind how these work. However, as this is supposed to be a Maths Course for students who have no intention to take Maths, it feels quite boring, as the maths learned is useless.

Midterm: 35% 
Finals: 55%
Webwork: 10%

For our Midterm, the mean was under 60% which seems better than previous years at least.

comment_teaching:
C- for 水山哥(Tu), A- for Phyllis, Overall C+.
水山哥's spoken English has a thick mainland accent and unclear pronunciation, which can be challenging to understand. Interestingly, he pronounces 'exam' as 'example',so when putting it into a sentence, the sentence will be like ' There will be a final example next week'. During his lectures, he primarily focuses on fundamental theories that may not be directly applicable to homework and exams. However, you can find some useful things in his lecture notes and he is available to answer questions after class. Overall, I don't know why I was able to attend all his lectures.
Phyllis is often late to class, but provides helpful notes and clear explanations. Students should be prepared to preview the content before her lecture or tutorial, as she moves quickly. Some of the examples she provides may be difficult for beginners in the relevant content, and even more challenging than exams. Despite this, attending her lectures and tutorials is strongly recommended. It is sufficient to review Phyllis's notes before exams, as they are helpful and comprehensive.
There is some overlap in content between Phyllis' lectures /tutorials and 水山哥's lectures, which might be a waste of time for students.

To review Phyllis's notes, it's recommended to start by reviewing the concepts and theorems. If you find anything difficult to understand, you can refer to 水山哥's notes, which provide a more fundamental explanation. Once you have a good understanding of the concepts, you can try to answer the questions and examples in Phyllis's notes on your own. title: DSE m2學子最輕鬆的一集
comment_content:
課程內容：
syllabus基本上有一半和m2重疊（first principle, differentiation, integration），會更深入地教DSE m2和math core沒學到的部分，例如limit、set theory、inequality、absolute value等等
1.set theory, inequality, absolute value
一開始會先教一些set theory的基本符號和不等式inequality，主要是為了在之後的課題讓學生們去知道或者表達一個函數function的domain、co-domain、range。而absolute value就是教學生怎麼去處理涉及到absolute value的不等式問題也是為了以後的課題做鋪墊。這一課的東西不用特別去溫習，考試的時候極少單獨出一條這一課的問題，建議把精力放在後面幾課。
2, function
這一科function比較基礎的一課。首先會教domain, co-domain, range的定義，挺容易懂的。然後會教一下function符號間的加減乘除和composition實際上是代表什麼意思，因為在DSE我們接觸的function都是f(x)-g(x)之類的，到了大學就會簡化成（f-g）(x)，簡單認識一下這些function之間的operation還是有必要的。接著就是，讓你認識各種各樣的function圖像，odd function是什麼樣的？even function是什麼樣的？periodic function是怎麼樣的等等等等，還會教DSE core學過的圖形變換。
3.limits and continuity
終於到重頭戲了（在midterm確實佔大頭），首先會說一下limit的定義，然後會教你幾個limit問題的處理方式，如：有理化、換元（substitution）和夾逼定理（squeeze theorem）。第二個部分是教你怎麼分辨一個function是否具有連續性（continuity），把前面學到的裡面知識拿來用就行了。最後會教你一個比較重要的定理是Intermediate Value Theorem。
4.Derivatives
終於到m2學生狂喜的一課了，啥都不用學，可以隨便走堂咯~
如果你是這麼想那你炸了一半。雖然他在這一課教的是first principle，怎麼d 多項式、三角函數、e^x、chain rule之類的。但他會在其中摻雜一些m2沒學到的部分，例如可導性（differentiability），怎麼d inverse function，怎麼d arcsin arccos這些，千萬不要掉以輕心。
5.Applications of derivatives
我去，這不是我們DSE m2的rate of change和graph sketching嗎？下次記得標明出處！
你以為這終於是一課可以走堂的課，那我拿出Linear approximation、error analysis、Newton’s method、ľHôpital’s rule、Rolle’s Theorem和 Mean Value Theorem 你不炸了嗎？這其中會有很多定理需要背公式，記得認真聽。還有，記得溫Mean Value Theorem，重中之重。
6.Integrals: an informal introduction
恭喜你，親愛的DSE M2學生，這一課，你是真的可以走堂了。大學和珍珠奶茶一樣，走糖對身體更好。
基本就是m2的integration範圍，學到by part分部積分法，不會考用integration算體積的問題，因為根本沒教。需要注意的這節課對integration的引入是用計算坐標系上的面積作為引入的，所以考試的時候記得看一下，如果可以直接用幾何的方式算面積，何必直接開in呢？

title: L1 or not, please reg Henry, or at least sit his class and use his resources
comment_content:
Many other reviews have talked about the syllabus and I’m not gonna regurgitate it, I wanna share with you my journey to getting an A+ (non-L1) , which is a result of both hard work and luck.
I got 5** in both DSE Math Core and M2, which made me think it would be an easy task to get an A+. In fact, there is not much new content, so I didn’t spend too much time revising. 
The mid term was easy and I scored 96/100, many people got 100 marks. I thought 1013 was much easier than DSE M2.
It was not until I started doing pastpapers that I realised that Math 1013 wasn’t that easy. My first pp was 2018 finals, and I only got 61 marks. Yes, 61 marks, barely a C+? And then, I finally realised that Math 1013 was much more conceptual than DSE M2, each step has to be supported by theorems, and we have to observe whether the prerequisites are satisfied (eg. Before applying IVT, we need to make sure f is continuous) Thus, much more thinking is required but not just calculations. 
Realising this, I did a few more papers and did the problem sets by Henry (I actually looped the problem sets for 3 times and it ended up that some questions are similar to those in problem sets)
Eventually, I got 83.5 marks in the finals. Only 7 out 1200 ppl got 90+ so my score actually isn’t that bad. A fun fact is that scoring 83 in the finals yields a higher standard score than scoring 100 in the mid terms as the mean is reduced by 17 and the sd is lowered by a bit. 
My score was 89.52% (Webwork full marks of course) and because of the difficulty of the paper, the cut offs are adjusted and conservatively 89%, rather than 95%, was the cut off of A+ (a friend got 100 in mid terms and 80 in finals and got A+) so yeah, a bit of luck involved after shedding blood and tears (not blood and tears actually, I do enjoy Maths) 
The moral of the story is twofold 
1) don’t take it lightly even if you get good grades in DSE Maths and M2 
2) Understanding the content is as important as practicing, cuz the finals are not that repetitive like DSE, but doing some practice does help.

What really sets it apart from L2.... is that it's more about understanding *why* things work rather than just crunching numbers. You actually learn how to think and reason mathematically, which I found super valuable.

comment_content:
Course Content
This course offers an in-depth study of differentiation and integration. For students with a background in DSE M2, a significant portion of the material will be familiar, making the overall difficulty manageable. However, the course also introduces many new, advanced topics.
The main chapters covered are: Functions, Limits, Derivatives, Applications of Derivatives, and Integrals. A non-exhaustive list of topics that go beyond the DSE M2 syllabus includes:
Continuity and Differentiability
Intermediate Value Theorem
Mean Value Theorem and Rolle's Theorem
One-to-one functions
Solving problems with absolute value functions
Sandwich (Squeeze) Theorem
Linear Approximation
Newton's Method
Critical Points
L'Hôpital's Rule
Riemann Sums
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (covered in more depth than in M2)
comment_teaching: attending tutorials is more beneficial than attending lectures, especially for those already familiar with the M2 content. Many students choose to skip lectures that cover revision material.
comment_grading:
The grading is semi-absolute, which is considered much fairer than a strict curve.
15% - WebWork (Online Homework)
35% - Mid-term Exam
50% - Final Exam (comprehensive, covering all content)
The typical grading scale is:
A range: ~85% and above
B range: ~70% to 85%
C range: ~50% to 70%
D: ~40% to 50%
Fail: Below ~40%
The mean score is typically around a C+ to B- (e.g., 67/100). WebWork is critical as it allows unlimited attempts, making a full score (15%) highly achievable. Exams do not allow the use of a calculator, so manual calculation skills are essential. There is reportedly little tolerance for clerical or calculation errors; answers must be correct to receive most of the points.
comment_workload:
The workload is moderate to high but manageable and reflects a "more work, more reward" approach.
Homework: One WebWork assignment per week, each with 10-18 questions. After the first assignment, each takes approximately 2-4 hours to complete.
Exams: It is highly advised to score highly on the mid-term to secure a good grade early. Since the final is cumulative, do not neglect earlier topics like limits while revising later ones like integration.
To achieve an A/A+: Secure full marks on WebWork, avoid careless mistakes on exams, and ensure you are not only proficient in solving problems but also understand the underlying proofs and concepts.

title: MATH 1013 is not a hard course if you are willing to put in steady effort. The content is basically standard Calculus I: limits, continuity, differentiation, applications of derivatives, and basic integration. Some parts may feel more conceptual than high-school calculus, but overall it is very manageable. My honest advice is: use Stewart’s Calculus textbook properly. The textbook explains the ideas clearly and has more than enough examples and exercises. If you really go through the relevant Stewart sections and do enough problems, I think an A-range grade is very achievable.
comment_content: MATH 1013 covers standard Calculus I topics, including functions, limits, continuity, derivatives, applications of derivatives, and basic integration. Most of the course is computational and problem-solving based, but some concepts require a bit more understanding, such as continuity, differentiability, Mean Value Theorem, L’Hôpital’s Rule, Riemann sums, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Overall, the content is quite manageable if you keep practicing. Stewart’s Calculus is more than enough for this course, and doing the relevant examples and exercises properly should prepare you very well for exams. The course is not conceptually too difficult, but careless mistakes can cost a lot, so accuracy matters.
comment_teaching: I did not attend any lectures, so I cannot comment too much on the live teaching quality. From what I heard and from the materials, the teaching pace seemed quite slow, especially for students who already had some calculus background. For me, self-studying from Stewart and practicing problems was more efficient.
comment_grading:
The grading is fair. The exams are not impossible or designed to trick students unfairly. If you do the homework seriously and, most importantly, finish all available past papers carefully, you should be well prepared.
The key is not only knowing the formulas, but also avoiding careless mistakes. Since the course is relatively standard, exam preparation is quite straightforward: understand the concepts, do past papers, check your mistakes, and repeat
comment_workload:
The workload is very light. Apart from online homework and exam preparation, there is not much regular pressure. The homework is manageable, and if you keep up with it, the course will not take much time weekly.
Overall, I would say this is a pretty easy course if you are disciplined. If you slack off until the last minute, it can still punish you, but if you consistently do Stewart + homework + past papers, getting into the A range is very realistic.

As the course progresses into later weeks, each assignment will contain around 13 questions and typically take about two hours to finish. Some problems are relatively lengthy, while others demand strong graph-reading and interpretation skills. Therefore, consistent independent practice and focused attention during lectures are essential to master the solution approaches.

comment_content: The content of L01 is rigorous and theory‑driven, clearly designed for students intending to major in mathematics. Instead of focusing mainly on computational techniques, the course emphasizes logical reasoning, foundational concepts, and proof writing. Topics such as logic, set theory, injectivity/surjectivity, limits, continuity, differentiability, and the mean value theorem are treated with a level of depth that goes beyond standard introductory calculus. This approach builds strong mathematical maturity and prepares students well for higher‑level pure math courses. However, students expecting a more application‑oriented or formula‑driven calculus course may find the abstract style challenging.
comment_teaching: Dr. Cheng adopts a clear, structured, and concept‑focused teaching style. His lectures prioritize understanding over memorization, often explaining the motivation behind definitions and the logic behind proofs. The course environment encourages students to think critically and engage with the material at a deeper level. Office hours are generous and flexible, and the instructor seems approachable and supportive. The TAs also play an important role, especially in tutorials where students practice writing proofs and clarifying conceptual difficulties.
comment_grading: The grading scheme is heavily weighted toward the midterm and final exam (42% each), with written assignments making up the remaining 16%. The assignments emphasize clarity of reasoning and proof writing rather than routine calculations, which aligns with the course philosophy. The lowest homework score is dropped, which helps reduce pressure. Because the exams are long, closed‑book, and conceptually demanding, students need a solid grasp of the material rather than surface‑level familiarity. Overall, the grading is fair but challenging, rewarding students who genuinely understand the concepts.
comment_workload: The workload is moderate to heavy depending on your background. Students with strong mathematical foundations (e.g., HKDSE M1/M2 or prior exposure to proofs) will find the pace manageable, though still intellectually demanding. Those new to abstract reasoning may need to invest significant time outside class to digest the material. Homework assignments require careful writing and cannot be rushed. While there is no WeBWork component for L01, the depth of the written assignments and the conceptual nature of the exams mean consistent weekly effort is essential.

comment_content:
This course covers basic single-variable calculus: limits and continuity, derivatives and differentiation rules, applications of derivatives (like max/min problems, related rates, optimization, Newton's method), and a basic intro to integration, like substitution rule and integration by parts. Around 60-70% of the material overlaps with DSE M2, but the exam questions go deeper than hw rather than just calculations. Some new topics include the Squeeze Theorem, L'Hôpital's Rule, Mean Value Theorem, Linear Approximation, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
You really need to understand the concepts clearly, not just memorize steps. If your understanding is only surface-level, the exam can easily screw you up because they change the question style and test whether you actually get the theory. Don't just rely on homework. The exam is way harder.
comment_teaching:

​
Don't rely too much on going to lectures, especially if your professor has a strong Chinglish accent that's hard to understand. It's better to self-study following the course schedule or watch Henry Cheng's lecture videos. Many students from other sections sit in on his classes or watch his recordings because he explains things way more clearly. His notes and problem sets really help your exam.

comment_content: Calculus I serves as the gateway to understanding change and motion, bridging abstract mathematics with real-world phenomena. The core concepts—limits, derivatives, and integrals—form the foundation for analyzing functions, rates of change, and accumulation. Derivatives model instantaneous behavior, such as velocity or growth rates, while integrals quantify total change, like area under a curve or accumulated distance. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus elegantly unites these ideas, revealing the inverse relationship between differentiation and integration. Though initially challenging, mastering these tools empowers problem-solving in physics, engineering, and economics. Calculus I isn’t just about equations; it’s a language to decode the dynamic patterns shaping our world. Embrace the rigor—it’s worth the “limit”

comment_teaching:
Henry Cheng: A
A very effective instructor.
WARNING: yapping
Let's admit it, maths is a relatively boring subject: one can watch interesting demos/illustrations in phy/chem/bi(o), one can read/watch comedies in humanities/language. However, there is not much entertainments or interactions when it comes to maths, besides problems and exercises.
This is where Henry shines. When introducing topics, he often includes details related to them: from memes (funny or not) attached to the slides, to stories like how l'Ho(s)pital "stole" Bernoulli's works. He clearly explains topics by not only going through what the topic is, but also common misconceptions surrounding it. E.g. invalidity of |tanb-tana|≤|b-a| due to tan being discontinuous, flaw of using l'Ho(s)pital rule for equations like lim(x->+inf) (e^x+sinx)/(e^x+cosx) (unfortunately, I still got those questions wrong in the final). On top of that, he does examples of topics by writing on a piece of paper, clearly projected on a screen. This makes it easy to follow through the steps.

    This chapter is just a revision of high school knowledge. No matter what background you have (International student, HKDSE or Mainland JEE), you should be very familiar with these stuff.
a) Basic set theory (sets, elements, relationship between two sets; intervals: open and close)
b) Inequalities in one unknown (solving basic inequalities)
c) Absolute values (solve inequalities with absolute values)
d) Sigma notation (here introduces some summing formulae that will be useful in later chapters -> the calculation of Riemann Sum when sub-interval tends to 0)
2. Chapter 1 Functions
    Different from MATH 1023 (the honor version), this course will start from talking about functions (not sequences). 
a) Basic notions about functions: Domain, codomain, range
b) The graph of a function, “vertical line test”
c) Arithmetic operations on functions (the harder part is composition)
d) Piecewise defined functions (absolute function and general piecewise defined functions)
e) Transformations of graphs of functions (more focuses on graphs)
f) Properties of functions (Odd functions / Even functions / Periodic functions / (Strictly) increasing functions / (Strictly) decreasing functions / Bounded functions / One-to-one functions, “horizontal line test”)
g) The inverse of a one-to-one function and its graph (the inverse function will become harder when differentiation is introduced)\
h) Drawing graphs of functions
3. Chapter 2 Limits and continuity
    From this chapter you will finally 'realize' you are learning calculus. Many concepts will be introduced and the hardest part in this chapter is the calculation of limits (when I say 'hard' it does not mean its super complicated, instead, its the thing that you should pay attention. -> in exams)
a) The informal definition of limits of functions at a real number / One sided limits
b) Basic arithmetic operations on limits / Limits of elementary functions / Evaluating limits of functions using factorization or rationalization
c) Evaluating limits of functions using a change of variables
d) Squeeze Theorem
e) Basic limits
f) Limits related to functions (Limits at infinity / Asymptotes)
4. Chapter 3 Derivatives
    This chapter will teach you how to calculate derivatives using limits (not the rules and formulae) -> based on what you have learnt in previous chapter.
    The most important thing you should practice is Implicit differentiation. You will see them everywhere in Midterm and Final.
5. Chapter 4 Applications of derivatives
    In this chapter, you will learn L'Hôpital’s rule (so you are not expected to use it in the Mid-term.)
    You will use everything you learn to solve problems (optimization / physics / graph sketching etc.)
6. Chapter 5 Integrals
    In the last chapter of this course, you will learn integration (staring from the calculation of Riemann Sum).
a) To estimate areas bounded by curves using rectangular strips (Riemann sums / Error approximation)
b) To evaluate integrals from definition or using known results from geometry
c) Properties of integrals
d) Area function
e) Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in two versions (here you can use the formulae to calculate anti-derivatives)
f) To evaluate antiderivatives and integrals by substitution
