title: [L1 MATH Major Section Review]
comment_content:
**This review is for L1 math major section**
This course consists of 5 chapters:
[Chapter 0: Preliminaries] Difficulty 5/10
-focuses on mathematical logic.
-logical operations, converse, contrapositive
-proof by contradiction etc. 
It's not difficult at all. However, please pay attention to statements involving 'for all' and 'for some'. In exams, they may ask you to write the negation of those statements. Also, remember the format of the second principle of MI (proof for n=1 and n=2 case, assume n=k and n=k+1, then proof n=k+2 case), as it may be useful for future chapters.
[Chapter 1: Functions] Difficulty 5/10
- Domain, codomain, range 
- transformation of graphs of function
- odd, even, periodic functions
- injective, surjective, and bijective functions (VERY IMPORTANT)
- Monotone squeeze thm (IMPORTANT)
- other elementary functions
The only difficult thing in this chapter is proving why the function is injective, surjective, and bijective. Also, injective functions will be cross-linked with other chapters, so pay more attention. 
[Chapter 2: Limits] Difficulty 8/10
-Convergence
-Squeeze Thm (IMPORTANT)
-Monotone Squeeze Thm (IMPORTANT)
-Rigorous definition of limits (DIFFICULT)
-Continuity
-Intermediate Value Thm. (IMPORTANT), Extreme value theorem.
Proofing limits using a rigorous definition of limits is required. If you do not get the idea in the beginning, please watch youtube videos (e.g. blackpenredpen) to help you learn. 
[Chapter 3: Dervatives] Difficulty 3/10
You can take a rest while learning this chapter :) Since 60-70% of stuffs are already covered in DSE M2. 
Some new things but not difficult:
- differentability of piecewise defined function
- derivative of inverse
- Leibniz Rule
- linear approx. and Newton's method
[Chapter 4: Mean Value Therom (MVT)] Difficulty 7/10
This chapter covers MVT and the consequences of MVT.
First 50% of Ch4: Rolle's Theorem and Mean Value Theorem
It is challenging to write proofs using MVT. You can use graphs to help you think but your proofing should not rely on graphs.
Last 50% of Ch4: Curve Sketching and Basic Integration.
Easy, mostly DSE stuff. You are required to draw curves involving trigonometric functions, piecewise-defined functions, functions involving absolute signs etc. So pay attention to differentiability and asymptotes.

Final review and/or overview of MATH1014
This is an introductory course in one-variable calculus, the first in the Calculus I and II
sequence, designed for students who have taken HKDSE Mathematics Extended Module
M1/M2 and aim at majoring in mathematics. Major topics include: logic and basic set
theory, functions, injectivity and surjectivity, limits of a function, continuity, differentiability,
derivatives and rules of differentiation, mean value theorem and its consequences.
Important Note: This section L01 is specially designed for first-year students who aim at
majoring in mathematics. A more pure-mathematical approach will be
adopted. At the end of the course, students are expected to be able to
write simple proofs apart from doing mere computations. Lighter
emphasis will be put on real-life applications and mathematical modellings.
Credit points: 3
Prerequisite: Level 3 or above in HKDSE Mathematics Extended Module M1/M2
Exclusions: AL Pure Mathematics or Applied Mathematics, MATH1003/1012/1014/
1018/1020/1023/1024, any MATH course at or above 100-/2000- level

comment_grading:

For reference, the midterm mean was 42.74 with a standard deviation of 17.90, while the final exam mean was 43.49 with a standard deviation of 18.40. title: 选择鄭錦恒作为您的教授
comment_content:
本人读的1013的L1。
要注意如果要读Math Major的要去选L1。
L1侧重证明，其他Lecture侧重计算。
课程概况
MATH1013 是港科大主流单变量微积分入门课，属于微积分 I+II 序列的第一门，面向有 DSE M1/M2 或同等数理基础的学生，以直观教学、重计算与应用为核心，为理工、商院等专业打数理基础。
核心内容
函数、反函数、三角函数与指数对数函数
极限、连续性、导数定义与求导法则
导数应用（极值、优化、洛必达、中值定理）
定积分、微积分基本定理、换元积分
课程优点
定位清晰，适配多数专业
不搞抽象证明，侧重计算与应用，完美匹配工院、商院、理院非纯数专业的后续课程需求。
教学体系成熟
课件、习题、辅导课（tutorial）配套完整，WeBWork 在线作业自动批改，学习路径清晰。
师资与答疑友好
多数讲师逻辑清晰、录课上传，论坛与邮件答疑及时，课后可一对一沟通问题。
难度适中，节奏可控
比 MATH1023（偏分析证明）简单，比 MATH1012 更扎实，适合想稳拿学分的学生。
课程不足
进度偏快
每周 3 小时 Lecture，知识点密度大，零基础容易跟不上。
考核偏应试
期末占比超 50%，题型灵活，临时抱佛脚很难拿高分。
习题量较大
WeBWork 作业 + 辅导课习题，需要持续投入，容易堆积任务。
评分与考核（常规版）
在线作业（WeBWork）：10%–15%
期中考试：35%
期末考试：50%–55%
无课堂参与分，考试决定最终成绩
学习建议
每周跟紧 Lecture，及时补录播，不堆积知识点。
认真完成 WeBWork，它是期中 / 期末的原题题库。
多刷往年真题，熟悉题型与计算套路。
辅导课积极提问，解决计算与概念漏洞。
适合人群
有 DSE M1/M2、A-Level Further Math、IB HL (AA) 基础的学生
工院、商院、理院非纯数专业，需要扎实微积分基础的同学
不想啃抽象证明、偏好计算 + 应用的学生
总结
MATH1013 是港科大性价比很高的主流微积分课，内容实用、难度友好、体系完善，只要保持每周投入，稳过甚至拿 A 不难，是大一数理必修课的优选。

The content is way harder than math 1013, as this course puts high emphasis on mathematical rigour and for sure there are proofs in almost every piece of homework. As joked by Prof. Ivan this course is “introductory mathematical analysis” disguised as calculus/differentiation, but the difficulty is actually harder than mathematical analysis. 
As of now we’ve went through 
Limit of sequences
Rigorous definition of limits (sequence) 
Criterion of convergence (Cauchy criterion, monotone convergence thm, bolzano-weierstrass thm, and some closely related concepts like axiom of completeness, nested interval property)
Limit of functions 
…

comment_grading:
Homework 20%
Midterm 10%-40%
Final 40%-70%
The weight of midterm and final are taken such that your own score would be at maximum. Eg if u scored horribly in midterm but got a rlly high score in final then midterm weight will be at 10% and final would count for 70%. 
Usually ppl would use homework to “pull” the total score upwards. 
As Prof. Ivan’s papers may be more challenging, the grading is more lenient (ie lower cutoff). As explicitly stated in the syllabus, top 10% or over 90% total score will be guaranteed an A+, while 70+% total score will be guaranteed an A-range. As of 2526 fall, Prof. Ivan decided to try something experimental, that is beating Deepseek V3.1 in midterm and final would be guaranteed an A.
From the previous cohort (22-23?) he taught, around 80% total score is an A+, and A-range is around 60%. 
Finally, generative AI is permitted in homework, but don’t expect it to be very useful, as the current AI technology has not been developed well enough to carry out consistent and accurate mathematical proofs. If you decided to find AI for assistance, make sure to check the response meticulously so as to ensure there are no logical errors. Although the AI may sometimes give correct answers, it may not be the “best” answer (eg correct approach but too many steps). Personally I found Deepseek and Grok give the most consistent answers. Make sure to enable the advanced thinking modes for the gen AI, or it’ll give logically incorrect responses for sure.

I can say by far MATH1023 has the most intense workload among the all courses I’ve taken. To be frank, if you’re not passionate enough about Math, this course will be a hellhole; if you love math, this course opens up a new world for you, and it’ll be fun and challenging

comment_content:
1 limit of sequences - rigorous definition

4 infinity, limit of functions

7 continuity
8 derivatives, differentiability
9 chain rule, implicit differentiations

11 mean value theorem, l’Hospital’s rule

Challenging content, with some from analysis. The concept of supremum and infimum is tested in both exams, luckily the techniques are taught by FF thoroughly in class. I think I learnt a lot of bonus things from this course too, such as the way to reindex  and reorder a double sum--I was always scared to deal with those. I'm sure there are other extra things I learnt along the way, but it's hard to come up with it on the spot. Anyway, this course is a good place to develop your mathematical rigor. The grading is very nice. Above 74 will be A-, above 80 will be A, and above 93 will be A+. A friend of mine scored like 20-30 in both exams and somehow he still passed as C+, quite nice indeed.
There is also a bonus marks scheme where you post solution to the lecture notes exercise, but the marks are trivially little. By that I mean you need to post like 30 solutions first and correctly in order to earn 1 extra mark. So just work hard in exams and don't even trust this bullshit system--it was designed for you to help your peers only.
Finally, the grade is calculated as follows. grade = max{λ homework + μ midterm + ν final : λ ∈ [0, 0.2], μ ∈ [0, 0.4], ν ∈ [0.4, 0.7], λ + μ + ν = 1} It appears this system allows you to all in final, but I do not dare to do it.

title: A range? u are wrong!
comment_content: The course content delivered by the professor is profoundly rigorous and intellectually stimulating, rooted in the fundamental logic of mathematics. He starts from the perspective of real number completeness, systematically deriving the entire framework of mathematical reasoning from its most basic principles. For students genuinely passionate about mathematics and pursuing in-depth academic exploration, this content is exceptionally high-quality—it builds a solid theoretical foundation that is invaluable for advanced studies or theoretical research. However, it is utterly unsuitable for students outside pure mathematics, such as those in physics, engineering, or business. The material is overly theoretical, offering little practical utility for applied fields; its value lies solely in deepening one’s understanding of mathematical fundamentals, making it irrelevant for anyone not aiming for a career in theoretical math.
comment_teaching: The professor’s teaching style is incredibly engaging and humorous, enhanced by his identity as an avid anime and manga enthusiast. His instructional methods are creative and memorable: for instance, one exam question playfully asked students to write the full names of Cauchy and Weierstrass, adding a lighthearted twist to rigorous mathematical learning. Additionally, his PPTs are designed with charming anime-style visuals, which make even abstract mathematical concepts more approachable and enjoyable. His lectures never feel tedious—he skillfully weaves humor and pop culture references into complex theories, keeping the class dynamic and maintaining students’ interest throughout. This unique blend of academic rigor and playful presentation makes his classes stand out as both informative and entertaining.
comment_grading: My experience with the course’s grading policy was extremely disappointing and unreasonable. Prior to enrolling, I heard rumors that the honors course had a generous A-range, supposedly up to 50%, which motivated me to sign up eagerly. However, after the midterm exam, the reality proved drastically different: out of 200 students, only 23 received an A+. For everyone else, grades started directly from B and declined downward, with no A- or A grades awarded between B and A+. This policy is absurdly rigid and unfair. I ranked 29th in the class, just a few points shy of the 23rd place cutoff, yet I was only given a B. Such a harsh and inflexible grading scale fails to recognize the nuanced differences in performance among students, making the initial claim of a "large A-range" misleading and frustrating.
comment_workload: The workload for this course is overwhelmingly heavy—far exceeding the combined workload of my other four courses, even by several times. The problem sets are extremely intellectually demanding, requiring hours of intense critical thinking and problem-solving that often feel mentally exhausting. Exams are equally challenging, designed to test not just basic understanding but also the ability to apply deep theoretical knowledge to highly complex scenarios. I frequently found myself spending entire weekends and late nights working on assignments and preparing for exams, sacrificing time that could have been allocated to other courses or personal pursuits. For students already balancing multiple demanding classes, this excessive workload becomes unsustainable, making the course a significant source of stress rather than a fulfilling learning experience.

title: Extraordinary Course for Students with High School Physics Background
comment_content:
Should you take the course?
If you have taken HKDSE Physics (esp. E3 -- Energy and Use of Energy), you must take this course! This course is just an extension of HKDSE Physics E3, covering everything in buildings. 
If you are not a science student/ have not taken HKDSE physics, you may still enrol in this course and just give it a try.
Details
A. Course Schedules
For course details, you may refer to other reviews about Prof. Ng on this course. He just grouped 2 lectures in the regular semester into 1 lecture in the summer semester, with 2 hours 50 mins long (including 10-15 mins break). 
In the final week, one lecture would be a course review covering all calculation problems, homework solutions and a case study on green buildings. While the last lecture would be the final exam.
B. Assignment
There will be a total of 5 assignments on calculation ONLY.
Assignment 1: Calculate the electricity bill for both commercial and residential consumers in Hong Kong (CLP users only).
Assignment 2: Calculate the amount of CO2 released by different public transports.
Assignment 3: Calculate the capacity factor (actual energy output/designed energy output*100%) of wind turbines.
Assignment 4: Calculate battery capacity and air fuel ratio
Assignment 5: Calculate the rate of heat flow by conduction and lighting quantities
C. Quiz
There is no mid-term exam in the summer semester. To replace it, 4 closed-book and **pop-up** quizzes were held in the last 30 mins of the lecture without prior announcement! So make sure you attend the lectures :) All quizzes are long questions with a full mark of 10.
Quiz 1: How can buildings benefit occupants?
Quiz 2: Name 5 aspects of green buildings and briefly explain.
Quiz 3: What are the differences between LPG and LNG?
Quiz 4: Draw a diagram of the system of an air conditioner and explain how an air conditioner works.
Tips: If Prof. Ng suddenly repeat the contents in the previous lectures, they will likely appear on quiz.
D. Final Exam
Full Mark: 100 marks     No. of Qs: 6
You are allowed to bring 2 A4 cheat sheets with handwriting ONLY.
2 Long Questions (20%@10%) Format similiar to quiz
Q1: Explain some methods that can control the noise produced by HVAC systems in buildings.
Q2: Describe the green features of green building materials in manufacturing, building, and their waste management stage.
4 Calculation Questions (80%@20%) Format similiar to homework
Q1: Calculate the electricity bill
Q2: Calculate the capacity factor of hydroelectric power
Q3: Calculate the power loss in the transmission line
Q4: Calculate the lighting quantities of table lights

title: A Monument to Educational Failure: Why This Course and Its Professor Represent Everything Wrong IN THIS COURSE
comment_content:
The broader context makes the failure worse. Higher education faces legitimate criticism about cost, relevance, and declining standards. Courses like this supply the critics with evidence. When a professor treats class time as a personal platform and reduces the curriculum to unreadable slides, he is not merely disappointing a room full of students. He is contributing to the erosion of trust in the institution itself. Students leave such courses cynical. They learn that the formal structure of education can be hollow, that credentials can be awarded without corresponding instruction, and that some faculty view teaching as secondary to whatever private interests currently hold their attention. That lesson is more lasting, and more damaging, than any of the actual course content.
It is possible to imagine a version of this course that works. The same material, delivered by an instructor who prioritizes explanation over self-reference, who designs slides that illuminate rather than overwhelm, who treats class time as a scarce resource to be used for the students’ benefit rather than his own amusement, would be unremarkable in the best sense: solid, useful, respectful of the students’ time and money. The gap between that hypothetical course and the one actually offered is the measure of the failure. The professor does not teach the course content. He yaps about his AI chatbot and other bullshit. The slides are long paragraphs. The semester is a lost opportunity. Students deserve better. The subject deserves better. And any institution that tolerates this level of instructional neglect should be embarrassed.
comment_teaching:
There are courses that challenge you. There are courses that frustrate you in productive ways. And then there are courses that make you question the entire premise of higher education, the value of your tuition dollars, and the basic competence of the person standing at the front of the room. This course belongs firmly in the last category. It is not merely mediocre. It is actively corrosive to the learning process. The professor does not teach. He does not facilitate understanding. He does not even attempt to make the material accessible. Instead, he treats the classroom as a personal stage for monologues about his AI chatbot and a parade of other irrelevant tangents, while the actual course content is reduced to dense, unbroken walls of text dumped onto PowerPoint slides. What follows is not a polite student evaluation. It is an indictment.
Let us begin with the most glaring failure: the professor does not teach the course content. Teaching, in any meaningful sense, requires structure, explanation, scaffolding, and engagement with the material students are expected to master. None of that happens here. Class sessions are not lectures on the syllabus topics. They are free-associative performances in which the professor drifts, at length and with evident self-satisfaction, into extended commentary about his AI chatbot. He will spend twenty minutes describing how the bot responds to certain prompts, how he has fine-tuned it, how it generates surprising outputs, how it might one day replace certain professional tasks. Students sit there, notebooks open or laptops ready, waiting for any connection to the week’s readings, the assigned theories, the concepts listed in the course outline. The connection never arrives. The chatbot is not an illustration of a course concept. It is not a case study. It is simply the thing the professor finds interesting that day, and the classroom exists to host his interest.
This is not occasional digression. It is the dominant mode. On days when the chatbot is not the star, the professor substitutes other forms of bullshit. Personal anecdotes that go nowhere. Opinions about unrelated campus politics. Long asides about technology trends that have nothing to do with the stated learning objectives. Rhetorical questions that he answers himself at length. The pattern is consistent: the actual subject of the course is treated as an inconvenience that must be briefly acknowledged before the real business of talking about whatever occupies the professor’s mind can resume. Students who try to steer the conversation back to the material are met with polite deflection or, more often, simply ignored as the monologue continues. The result is a semester in which large stretches of class time are consumed by content that will never appear on any assessment and that contributes nothing to understanding the field.
When the professor does deign to address the course material, the method of delivery is almost comically inadequate. The PowerPoint slides are not teaching tools. They are dumping grounds. Long, unbroken paragraphs of dense prose are copied or lightly paraphrased onto slides, often in small font, with minimal visual hierarchy, no diagrams that actually clarify relationships, no progressive disclosure of ideas, and no attempt to highlight key claims or distinguish primary arguments from supporting detail. A single slide may contain an entire page of textbook-style text. Students are expected to read this while the professor either reads it aloud in a monotone or, more commonly, ignores it entirely while returning to his preferred topics. The slides do not support learning; they actively obstruct it. Cognitive science has established for decades that people cannot effectively process dense text while simultaneously listening to a speaker. The design of these materials violates every basic principle of instructional design. They are not slides. They are poorly formatted handouts projected onto a wall.
The cumulative effect on students is predictable and damaging. Motivation collapses. Why prepare for class when class will not engage the preparation? Why struggle with difficult concepts when the person responsible for guiding that struggle is instead describing chatbot outputs? Attendance becomes a performative exercise rather than a learning opportunity. Students who care about the subject are forced into a double workload: they must teach themselves the material outside of class while also enduring the opportunity cost of sitting through sessions that add nothing. Those who are less intrinsically motivated simply disengage, collect whatever grade the assessments allow, and leave with the accurate impression that the course was a waste of time. The assessments themselves often feel disconnected from what happened in the room, because what happened in the room had so little to do with the content. Students are graded on material the professor never meaningfully taught.
This is not a matter of teaching style. Different styles can be effective. Some professors lecture tightly. Some facilitate discussion. Some use cases, problems, or demonstrations. What is not a legitimate style is the systematic refusal to engage the subject matter in favor of personal preoccupations, paired with presentation materials that treat students as readers of projected walls of text rather than learners who need guidance. The AI chatbot fixation is particularly revealing. It suggests a professor more interested in signaling proximity to a trendy technology than in developing competence in the domain he is paid to teach. The chatbot becomes a form of academic performance art: look at me, engaging with the future, while the present responsibility of instruction goes unmet.
One might object that students should simply read the slides and the assigned materials and succeed independently. That objection concedes the point. If the classroom adds so little value that independent reading is the only reliable path to learning, then the course has already failed as a taught experience. Universities do not charge tuition for the privilege of reading dense text alone. They charge for expertise, structured guidance, intellectual modeling, and the creation of an environment in which difficult ideas become clearer through interaction with a knowledgeable instructor. None of those goods are delivered here.

title: Review from a year-1 engineering student
comment_content:
Topic of the 9 lectures:
Foundations and History of Management, Motivation, Decision Making, Personality &Emotion, Leadership, Diversity, Human Resource Management, External Analysis, Internal Analysis.
As an engineering student, the content of this course differs from my typical coursework. During each lecture, I've learned about theories, models, and concepts developed by scholars throughout history. Although I'm not particularly interested in this material, the course has equipped me with valuable knowledge, such as 'how to stay motivated' and 'how to establish leadership' - skills I believe will serve me well in the future.
comment_teaching:
This semester, the two instructors are Amanda and Mingyu, who are both pursuing their PhDs. I really appreciate how they deliver the course materials - it's better than many of the instructors I've had in the SENG and SSCI courses. Their teaching style keeps students engaged to the greatest extent possible. The way they speak and write, as well as their prompt email response times, exemplify the professionalism I expect from excellent instructors.
Mingyu has a more gentle demeanour, but she tends to include an excessive amount of information on her slides. In contrast, Amanda maintains a serious presence, but her explanations are concise and clear. While I may be slightly particular in my preferences, during some lectures, my friend and I have found it challenging to keep up with the sheer volume of material they cover. I believe it would be more effective if they provided students with materials to preview and prepare before the discussions in class.
comment_grading:
10% Attendance&Participation
The attendance policy for this course stipulates that students cannot miss more than 2 lectures to receive the full attendance mark. To earn the participation component of the grade, students must actively engage in class discussions. However, the calculation of the participation mark is ambiguous.
40% Group project
The grading is based on slides and presentations, with the assessment comprising identification and description of management issues (20%), analysis of cause (20%), generation and evaluation of alternative actions (40%), description of recommendation/implementation (10%), and presentation skills (10%).
50% Final exam
The final exam consists of 20 multiple-choice questions, 3 short answer questions, and 2 scenario analysis questions. Students are permitted to bring a double-sided A4 cheat sheet for the exam, but it is not sufficient to cover all the necessary details. With only 1 sample scenario analysis question provided beforehand, it was difficult for us to anticipate the exact content that would be covered in this portion of the exam. As a result, many students ended up including unnecessary information on their cheat sheets.
The MCs primarily test conceptual knowledge, so they are relatively manageable. However, the LQs are more challenging, as they often require providing multiple examples or applying theories to real-world problems, rather than just recalling information. This combination of question types and formats made it quite demanding to prepare thoroughly for the final exam.
Remark:
After the grades were released, I was pleasantly surprised by the final result. In my opinion, the grading was quite good, even though there were a few areas where I struggled. It's certain that I attended all the lectures, but I only participated in discussions around three times throughout the semester. 
Our group also encountered challenges with the group project, as we ended up including an excessive amount of content, which seemed to leave everyone in the class a bit confused. 
In the final exam, I didn't perform as well on the LQs, especially the last scenario analysis question. I had anticipated my overall grade would likely fall in the B range, perhaps a B or B+. However, to my pleasant surprise, I ended up earning an A in the course.
comment_workload:
Group project: 
Origin descriptions: This group project offers you an opportunity to apply knowledge learned to real management issues presented in a reality television program – Undercover Boss. Each group will analyze an assigned episode of Undercover Boss. Each group will give a 15-minute PowerPoint presentation. At the end of each presentation, there will be a 5-minute question and answer session. We will have a random draw to determine the episode that each group will be responsible for (Actually we could make our choices).
For the group project, each team consisted of 5-6 members who were randomly assigned. Our group started prioritising our preferences 16 days before the presentation and worked on it for 2 weeks.The core requirements of the group project were to:
1. Identify and describe key management issues
2. Analyze the underlying causes of those issues
3. Generate and evaluate potential alternative actions
4. Develop a recommendation and implementation plan
Cheat sheet: The preparation of the cheat sheet for the final exam was also a significant amount of work, especially for someone like me who prefers handwriting. It took me over 15 hours to put together the cheat sheet.
Given the limitations on the number of pages allowed, I had to carefully review each set of lecture notes to ensure the content on the cheat sheet was as effective and efficient as possible.
It's also worth noting that I have a habit of taking my own additional notes after each lecture, as I believe I don't always grasp all the knowledge during the class itself. These post-lecture note-taking sessions typically take me another 2-3 hours per class.

人對於知識的追求，源於探尋世界本質的渴望。於此，人憑藉理性之光，航向未知的深藍。但海洋之奧秘豈僅封存於冰冷數據？若真理散落於雜亂無章的碎片，若傳道者之言晦澀如迷，知識的燈塔又如何照亮求索之路？
吾等修習海洋生物及環境科學，本欲窺探碧波之下生生不息的法則。然此課之荒謬，非片語能盡述。小子未歷滄桑，僅能以殘筆數行，略陳其四宗罪。
1. 資訊洪流中的迷失。 課程文件猶如遭風暴肆虐後的殘骸，數據與圖表胡亂堆疊，關鍵資訊化為圖片邊陲的螻蟻小字，彷彿刻意隱匿於視野的荒原。求知者本應循邏輯之徑漫步，在此卻被迫於文字與圖像的迷宮中匍匐尋覓，拾撿破碎的數字殘片。此非傳道授業，此乃令學者於資訊泥沼中自生自滅。
2. 語言之獄與靈感的枯竭。 講者之口，如深潛者隔著厚重面罩發出的模糊嗡鳴，其語調之平鋪直敘，足令潮汐停息、鯨歌喑啞。更甚者，其所用之語彙與邏輯，自成一種封閉的符號系統，將課堂化為僅供其一人低語的密室。縱有萬頃碧波之奇趣，在此等講述下，亦褪色為乾涸標本上的塵埃。熱忱之火，輕易便被此等冰冷與晦澀所掐滅。
3. 權威的傲慢與對話的死亡。 此課堂奉行不容置疑的「單向真理」。教授者立於講臺，彷彿手持絕對詮釋權杖，其指點之圖文縱然雜亂無章、令人費解，亦被鍍上一層「標準答案」的金漆。任何質疑與探討的嘗試，皆遭無形壁壘彈回。知識本應在對話與辯證中奔流，在此卻凝固為必須虔誠背誦的教條。學習之目的，悄然異化為破解講者心意的猜謎遊戲，而非追索客觀真實。
4. 負擔的錯位與核心價值的悖反。 通識課程，本意乃拓寬視野、調劑心神，於繁重專業課間闢一扇眺望蒼穹的窗。然此課反其道而行，以龐雜混亂的材料與專斷封閉的氛圍，織成一張最緻密的精神負擔之網。它未曾成為歇腳的綠洲，反成了需額外耗費心神去解碼、去迎合、去勉強消化的險灘。這是一種深刻的錯置，將求知的愉悅，扭曲為順從的疲憊。
而默許此等教學存續、對學生困惑置若罔聞的體系——大學本身——實與此風氣同流共棲。二者相遇，非學子之幸，乃求真路上的一片需要艱難跋涉的無光之海。
comment_teaching:
人之授業，聲調為舟，渡學生於知識之川。若舟楫雖美，其行卻滯重如陷泥淖，則再遼闊的彼岸，亦成無法抵達的困倦遠方。
講者之音，枯燥至極，雖帶標準口音，猶如精緻棺木盛放朽骨。每當於計算機課後踏入此堂，那平穩無波的聲線，便成了催眠的咒文，令人在學習共享空間中，不自覺墜入意識的深淵。
後記：Cindy之教學，較Cynthia尤為不堪。其授課恍若夢遊，言語間盡顯對所授之物的陌生與惶惑。更令人愕然者，身為教授，其英語水平竟貧瘠如中學文憑試四級之流。學術殿堂之門檻，何時淪落至此？
綜觀二者，授業無神，懶散入骨：因懶於批改，故無作業（此點或可稱幸）；因懶於批改，故僅設選擇題；因懶於安排，故無座次規劃；因懶於檢視，故無試卷覆核。授業者怠惰至此，猶如燈塔熄火、嚮導迷途，彼等何德何能，竟坐享薪俸？此非教學，乃制度豢養之懶散，蠶食學子光陰與期許的無聲災厄。
comment_grading:
此文乃考後鬱結難平所書，積憤充膺，不吐不快。
吾曾耗三日心力，焚膏繼晷，強記課件中每一細節。然試卷一展，所考竟多為投影片邊角縫隙處之微末瑣碎。平生光陰，竟虛擲於此等無謂之事，豈不悲乎？更甚者，題意曖昧不明，吾深疑出題者自身概念混沌，誤人子弟。此等課程，諸君萬勿涉足；此等考試，實乃毫無價值、徒惹憤懣之舉。
後記：期中試平均分40.56（滿分50），標準差5.24。試期為十月十六日，而成績竟遲至十一月三日夜晚方公佈，公然違背校方「兩週內回饋成績」之政策。尤有甚者，教授姿態傲慢，令人扼腕。
其試卷設計實屬詭異。專考邊角資料已令人無奈，然若溫習純熟，更會發現卷中多項選擇之措辭粗劣不堪，充滿混淆。得分遠低於自身預期，與同儕核對後更覺差距不合常理。其後，教授於公告中輕描淡寫，稱部分題目「有多於一個答案」，已「慷慨」給予分數，卻斷然拒絕覆核查卷。矛盾之處在於：既自知試卷錯漏百出，需不斷修正答案，又何以確信自己已全然更正？不讓學生查卷、不聽取回饋，又如何得知改卷確無謬誤？此乃傲慢與無知之結合體。課堂上常聞其言：「網上資訊雖多，然我等永遠正確，故只須參考本課筆記。」原以為是戲言，豈料處理正事時竟真抱此心態。如今面對不明不白之分數，無端承受低劣等級…或可歸咎於本人平庸，然在不允許覆核的前提下，我連此點亦無法確認。唯一可肯定者，乃教授之狂妄自大，與評核過程之極度不透明。我並非斷言考試必然不公，然從我的視角觀之，此可能性確實存在。是否要以學業前途作賭注，諸君請自行決斷。
期末考紀實：
整份試卷幾乎全然超出課程綱要，多道題目所涉內容我從未見過，大量詞彙不知所云，溫習過後仍須猜測近半答案。忠告諸君：不必為期末考溫習，因其荒唐程度更甚期中——期中所考至少課堂曾有提及，期末所問則根本無跡可尋。與同窗查證後發現，此次重點不在投影片邊角，而在投影片內圖片之中——那些編排混亂、無人能解其意的圖片，其上印有極細小文字，竟成為主要考題，而我對此一無所知。請相信，無論你起初多有熱忱，在閱讀期中後（即Cindy負責部分）的投影片五分鐘內，所有動力必將熄滅。欲強記所有無謂內容實屬不可能，而將如許光陰虛耗於一門通識課程，只為背誦謬誤，更毫無價值——我曾核對網上可靠資源，發現其投影片內容實有謬誤，然他們始終強調「我等永遠正確」，學生必須遵從。是故，我們作答並非基於事實，而是基於他們自以為是的認知，研習此科根本毫無意義。此外，他們從不提供練習題目，我開始懷疑他們是否每年沿用同一試卷，並在收回試題後便可隨心所欲，更不設覆核查卷環節，使學生再也無法重溫題目或提出異議。他們所定之答案，即成最終答案，無從驗證真偽。此實為我平生所遇最惡劣之考試，五十題中僅確信二十一題，餘者皆須猜度。整個課程，實是一場自欺欺人的猜謎遊戲。我衷心不推薦任何人修讀，無論你的背景或興趣為何，因為他們將竭盡所能，摧毀你的一切熱情。
再者，此科雖是我最早考畢的一科，卻是最後一科收到成績的科目——而它僅包含選擇題。這再度證明了教學團隊的怠惰與無能，因這是我唯一完全無法申請覆核查卷的課程。至此，對其評級我已無話可說，惟因此科給了我本學期最差的成績。哈哈。
客觀而論，以我在此科投入的微薄努力（期中溫習三日，期末溫習四小時，得B+），此成績或許不算太壞（可悲的是，我大抵已是B+的最高分之一）。然而，實情是：即便投入更多時間溫習，我的分數也未必提升，此乃我親見期末試卷後的結論。我僅是幸運而已。亦不知是直覺抑或僥倖，我猜對了近半題目，然此「策略」恐難複製。坦率而言，我全然不知應如何為此科備考，故將其評為「E」——因努力與成績之間的關聯，在此科低得可憐。
若閣下欲測試自身運勢，歡迎一試。
comment_workload:
此處吾以為存有變數，僅四次課堂參與評核與機械背誦（雖痛苦，卻非綿延不絕之痼疾）。然則，任憑汝如何皓首窮經，期末考場之上，必有至少十五道題目，攜前所未見之詞彙，如伏兵驟出，令汝措手不及。
吾嘗言，最上之策，乃付以最低限度之努力，而後寄望於天意（期末考前夕，吾溫習不足一日，蓋因課件令人啞然，實不知從何入手……）。然終決意予其「劣等」之評，聊以加劇此課評分之惡。吾實不解，何以眾人皆言此課易取佳績，更競相薦於同儕？此乃求學生涯中最深之幻妄，一場集體的迷思。

comment_content:
Syllabus before mid-term is all about animals and biodiversity, including habitats and different biomes. Very interesting and easy to memorize if you are a nature lover, but the lectures may be boring and long if you are not. After midterm the syllabus includes population, health, environmental concerns which are more statistical.

A. the wind
B. the water currents 
C. the polar bears)
comment_teaching:

No questions or discussions required. You will receive little to no help if you struggle, but on the bright side you can sleep through the entire lecture without being noticed.
Bonus: The professor is nice enough to send me the first two lecture recordings since I joined the course late.
comment_grading:

Attendance not required.

Midterm and finals are both only MC, but finals are slightly longer. Syllabus are not cumulative.
comment_workload: Only workload is trying to stay awake during class. No assignments, no reading, no papers, no canvas quiz, no projects, no presentations. Turn up for the biweekly quizzes, midterms and finals and you'll be fine.

comment_content:
Overall: B (3.28)
Course outline (40%): A-
Quality of course material (60%): B
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
📙 Syllabus:
Chapter 1: A Modern View of the Universe
Chapter 2: Discovering the Universe for Yourself
Chapter 3: The Science of Astronomy
Chapter 4: Making Sense of the Universe: Understanding Motion, Energy, and Gravity
Chapter 5-6: Light and Matter: Reading messages from the Cosmos; Telescopes: Portals of Discovery
Chapter 14: Our Star
Chapter 15: Surveying the Stars
Chapter 16-17: Star Birth and Star Stuff
Chapter 18: The Bizarre Stellar Graveyard
Chapter 19: Our Galaxy
Chapter 20-21: Galaxies and the Foundation of Modern Cosmology; Galaxy Evolution
Chapter 22-23: The Birth of the Universe; Dark Matter, Dark Energy, and the Fate of the Universe
--- Final Exam (All topics) ---
Textbook: "The Cosmic Perspective" Bennett, Donahue, Schneider, Voit, Seventh Edition, Pearson New International Edition
📚 From Chapter 1 to 6, it mainly talks about astronomy, which focuses on how we look at the universe from the Earth to explain different scientific phenomenon, like solar eclispe, phases of Moon and how do we know the orbit of Earth around the Sun is elliptical.
📚 From Chapter 14 to 23, it mainly talks about space science covering a wide range of topics, such as different types of star Birth and death, different types of galaxies, black holes, Big Bang and dark matter.
✅ If you are interested in learning astronomy and space science, this course is suitable for you.
✅ You don't need to buy a textbook. I even did not use the textbook throughout the whole semester.
⚠️ However, if you don’t like learning physics concepts, formulas and doing calculations, please avoid this course as the exam contains a lot of conceptual and calculations questions.
Ch.1-2:
It starts by introducing a lot of basic astronomical concepts like different types of stars, look back time, astronomical unit (AU), which are fundamental of astronomy. They are quite boring if you don’t like to learn about physics concepts.
Then you have to imagine the sky as a big sphere called celestial sphere. The sphere is used to explain different astronomical concepts and phenomenon like zenith, zodiac, constellations, altitude and latitude and causes of seasons. If you are good at constructing 3D images in your head, these topics would be quite easy for you. Otherwise, you would be quite frustrating. The only solution for those who are not good at imagining is to memorize different facts and results, which is a pain in the butt.
After that, solar eclipse and lunar eclipse would be taught, including different phases and reasons. Again, if you are good at picturing the relative positions of Earth, Moon and Sun, you would be fine. Otherwise, you need to spend more efforts in understanding the concepts.
Ch.3:
It will introduce different astronomical models and concepts built in the history, from ancient Greek, Ptolemaic model, Copernican model, discoveries by Galileo to Kelper’s laws. While most of them are conceptual, you also need to perform calculations regarding to the Kelper’s laws. Therefore, you should pay efforts to familiarize with those concepts and calculations. Most of the topics in this chapter are covered in DSE Physics E1, so you would have great advantage if you have studied them before.
Ch.4:
This chapter is the MOST PHYSICS chapter as it introduces a lot of physics concepts, mostly with formulas. This includes Newton’s three laws of motion, circular motion, conservation of momentum, conservation of energy, gravitational potential energy, escape speed and tidal locking. 90% of this chapter is covered in DSE Physics ‘Force and Motion’ and E1, so if you have studied them before, you can easily handle them. Otherwise, it is quite difficult to handle all of them.
Ch.5:
In the first part, you will be introduced to the properties of light and thermal radiation, including v=fλ, absorption, emission and continuous line spectrum and fingerprints, stefan-boltzmann law, properties of blackboard radiation. Most of the content is covered in DSE Physics E1 and CHEM 1012 Ch.2. If you have studied them before, it is much easier to understand them, although these concepts are not too difficult for new learners.
In the second part, it talks about Doppler effects, which is again covered in DSE Physics E1 or PHYS 1111/1112. After that, it talks about angular resolving power, diffraction limit and different types of teloscopes with pros and cons. These contents are in fact quite boring, but they are not too deep in depth, so it would not be difficult to understand them.
Ch.14:
It talks about our Sun, including the structure of the Sun, nuclear fusion in the Sun and solar activities. These concepts are quite easy to understand, so you would have a honeymoon time in this chapter.
Ch.15:
It first talks about using Hipparchus Magnitude Scale, apparent and absolute magnitude to measure the brightness of a star, so you should expect there would be a bunch of equations you need to use. Most of them have been covered in DSE Physics E1, except m & M equation.
Then, it talks about H-R diagram, including lifetime of main sequence stars, main sequence line, equal radius line and turn-off line. Also, it introduces mass-luminosity relationship, luminosity class, different types of star clusters and binary systems. While some concepts have been taught in E1, you should spend some time to understand these concepts before the final exam.
Ch.16-17:
It first briefly introduces different types of nebula, and focus on the process of formation of a star, which involves many steps, so you should spend some time to familiarize them.
Then, it talks about the life of a low-mass, medium-mass star and high-mass star respectively. Each process involves many steps and astronomical concepts, but no calculations are required, so it is not too difficult to understand them.
Ch.18:
It mainly talks about white dwarf, supernova, black hole and neutron star. Although there are some calculations regarding to Schwarzschild radius and tidal forces of black holes, this chapter is not difficult to handle.
Ch.19:
It mainly talks about the Milky Way Galaxy, including its history, structure and characteristics. This part is quite interesting as we can learn our own galaxy. There is one calculation regarding to orbital-velocity law, which is quite easy.
Ch.20-21:
It mainly talks about different types of galaxies and how to use cosmic distance ladder to observe galaxies and stars in different distances. Also, it talks about cosmological redshift and galactical collisions between different galaxies, which relates to the future of the Milky Way Galaxy, making this part quite inspiring.
Ch.22-23:
It is the MOST ABSTRACT chapter among all chapters as this chapter mainly talks about dark matter and the future of the universe, which are something that scientists still cannot fully understand. Therefore, although this part contains many difficult concepts regarding to the dark matter, you don’t need to fully understand them to answer the questions in the exam.

title: Rewarding
comment_content:
Like other reviews mentioned, this physics course is teaching some real physics instead of teaching you constellations and astrology. But if you're not afraid of math and physics, this is one of the best science cc in ust. It allows you to understand our universe more rigorously, learning how everything (from atoms to the universe itself) works physically and where they come from. Overall a great course that can make you actually learn something and broaden your horizon, instead of making you feel "what have I learnt" after a whole semester.
For beginners like me who didn't study physics in high school, it can also be a great introduction to physics, with all topics like classical and quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, optics, electromagnetism being briefly introduced and applied. I think it's even better than 1001 which doesn't have math at all.
But indeed having science background is an advantage, think twice if you studied neither physics nor chemistry in high school.
For content in depth I've attached my cheat sheet for reference. Disclaimer: it's very messy and I might have missed some details, absolutely don’t recommend printing it out for exam
Update (2026): In my semester there were only 2 sections with 100 quota each, but I'm happy to see that now there're 3 sections with more than 450 quota in total :D
comment_teaching:
Patient and nice local prof, will answer your questions quickly and clearly. You can directly email him instead of TAs to ask questions and he'll reply in a few hours.
Teaching in lecture is decent too. For the first few chapters he often teach with Chinese culture elements (myths, poems and even 金庸), and for later chapters when the content gets technical, he's professional and can explain those difficult concepts clearly.

comment_workload:
Fairly low. 
No weekly assignments. HW are provided for practice only, still useful for revision.
- 2 SGQ (Student Generated Questions):
Before the midterm and final, students are required to write a MC question, and each lecturer will pick one to include in the exam. Basic recall / Memorization questions is valued less than comprehensive quantitative questions (i.e. Calculation-based questions). You are required to explain your solution and include at least 1 distractor (an option that seems correct on the surface but isn't).
- iPRS (Attendance/Quiz):
Each class, there are a PRS quiz in the middle of the lecture and a MCQ at the end. Both of them are just an iPRS question related to that lecture's topic, not usually too difficult. Just that you will have to attend your registered lecture sessions.
Only the top 80% of your iPRS scores are counted, so you have some room for slip-ups or absences. 
As someone who attended 2 sessions, the iPRS questions are different between lecturers, so you may want to check out the other sessions' iPRS questions for revision in addition to your own.
- Cheat Sheet Making
Midterm allows 1 doubled-sided A4 cheat sheet; Final allows 3 doubled-sided A4 cheat sheets. There is a lot of stuff you need to consider to put in or not.
For the midterms, they explicitly said there will be questions requiring you to order things in specific sequence (e.g. Order events chronologically, order size of objects, etc...). Unless you want to memorize every little detail, which there are a lot of, you will have to find a way to fit them all in.
For the finals, less sequencing, but the later slides are really dense, so you need to read through them all and put the details in. Finding enough room is not much of a concern as the midterm, just that it takes a long time (especially if you have other courses' work piling on you). Took me a few days to make mine.

comment_content:
Syllabus of the course: 
Lectures 1 & 2: Basic knowledge about the Universe
Lectures 3, 4 & 5: Constellations, Celestial Sphere, Seasons, Lunar and solar eclipses
Lecture 6: Ancient Astronomy, Kepler's Laws
Lectures 7 & 8: Motion, Newton's Laws, Momentum, Energy, Gravitation and tides
Lectures 9 & 10: Light (EM Waves), Spectrum, Doppler's effect, Microscopes
Lecture 11: Sun's structure, Energy in the sun, Gravitational contraction
Lectures 12 & 13: Luminosity, Brightness, Binary system, HR diagram
Lectures 14 & 15: Nebulae, Star formation, Life sequence and death of stars
Lectures 16 & 17: White dwarfs, Nova/Supernova, Neutron stars, Pulsars, Black holes
Lectures 18 & 19: Structure of Milky Way, Galactic recycling, Formation of galaxy
Lectures 20 & 21: Types of galaxies, Measuring galaxy distance, Hubble's Law, Galaxy evolution and collision
Lectures 22 & 23: Universe, Big Bang Theory, Dark matter, Dark energy, Final fate of the Universe
Notice that this course will not be too focused on the Solar System. 
It will be a benefit if you have studied DSE Physics Elective 1 before. However, you should always notice that this is a serious physics course, and it's completely different from the interesting and easy-understandable information and videos online. So, the knowledge in this course is very technical and deep, making the course quite difficult to understand and boring, particularly for the second half. Unless you are really an astronomy enthusiast, you should think twice before enrolling in this course, especially if you are weak at Physics.

Although sometimes he would just read the PowerPoint and sometimes monotone also, it is still fine anyway. By the way, I quite like his jokes. He would involve some jokes related to Chinese poems and songs. If you are a local student, you can get the punchlines of them.

comment_grading:
Assessment plan of the course: 
PRS questions (10%)
Tutorial MCQ questions (15%)
Student-generated question (1%)
Strip sequence test (4%)
Open-ended question report (20%)
Final exam (50%)
PRS and MCQ questions are generally the same things, which involve answering 5-choices MC questions using iPRS system. However, MCQ questions are more difficult and complicated on average. Googling the answer and searching in the lecture PowerPoint can help you deal with most of the questions (for Prof. Chen's lectures, at least). 1 mark will be given for a correct answer in every question, and 0.25 marks for a wrong answer. They will only count the best 80% of the PRS/MCQ questions. 
Here are the statistics of the course:
PRS: Mean: 8.24/10, Median: 9.46/10, My score: 10/10
MCQ: Mean: 12.8/15, Median: 15/15, My score: 15/15
Student-generated question: 
Mean: 9.38/10, Median: 10/10, My score: 10/10
Strip sequence test: 
Mean: 2.23/4, Median: 2.35/4, My score: 2.59/4
Open-ended Question Report: 
Mean: 75.63/100, Median: 78.5/100, My score: 78/100
Final Exam: Mean: 77.66/120, Median: 78/120, My score: 80/120
Final Score: Mean: 71.57%, Median: 73.38%, My score: 77.52%
My final score is just slightly above the median and I can still get a B+. The grading is not bad actually. Try to do your best in PRS/MCQ questions and the report, then you can get an acceptable grade.
comment_workload:
This course has a very light workload. You don't need to submit any assignments until the end of the semester. A significant proportion of the final score will be PRS and MCQ. Just attend every lecture, answer the questions and you can get some marks. They also gave out some 'homework' but they are not assessed and completely optional.  
On the other hand, the strip sequence test and the student-generated question are just jokes. With their poor and tiny proportions in the final score, by some means, it is not worth revising for them. However, if you don't want to spend too much time studying this course before the final exam, then take them as chances for reviewing. 
Open-ended question report is quite important in contrast. You have to choose 1 question to answer among ~20 questions. The report should be in academic style, so you have to cite sources to support your statements or ideas, and need to use some specific structures. Follow what you have done in English Language courses is fine. 
The final exam mostly contained MC questions, with some short questions following. 3 A4-sized cheat sheets (6 pages in total) were allowed. Since this course has a broad syllabus, I strongly recommend jotting all important points into the cheat sheet.

Format and Grading Rules
Homework
Homework questions will be posted at the beginning of each chapter as self-learning materials. Students are not required to hand in homework solutions. Homework solutions will be provided by the instructors about one week after each chapter concludes.
Quizzes (iPRS)
Full marks for correct answers, 1/4 mark for incorrect answers, 0 mark for no answers.
The best 80% of a student’s quiz answers will be counted for the total marks of PRS and tutorial quizzes.
Marks of the PRS and MCQ quizzes conducted during the add-drop period will not be counted toward the final grade.
Late submissions or resubmissions will not be accepted.
MC and Strip-Sequence Quizzes
A strip-sequence question requires students to arrange a provided list of items in the correct order (not necessarily chronological). You can find sample questions posted in Canvas Files --> Sample Strip Sequence Questions. Points are awarded based on the number of inversions in the sequence on a linear scale, where full marks are given if all pairs are in the correct order, and zero marks are awarded if only half of the pairs are in the correct order.
For example, if a question presents 5 items, resulting in a total of 10 pairs, the marks will be allocated as follows:
Number of pairs in correct order | Marks
5 or fewer | 0%
6 | 20%
7 | 40%
8 | 60%
9 | 80%
10 | 100%
Student-Generated Question (SGQ)
Each student should generate ONE Multiple Choice (MC) question with FIVE choices (1 correct choice + 4 wrong choices) based on the contents of the lecture notes. You can find the marking scheme and two sample questions in Canvas Files --> Student-Generated Questions.
Written Report of an Open-ended Question (OEQ)
Each student has to submit an individual report and its topic must be chosen from one of the open-ended questions posted. You can find the report template and marking scheme in Canvas Files --> Open-Ended Questions --> Template and Marking Scheme.
Final Exam
Closed-book exam covering all chapters. There will be 40 – 45 MC questions and 4 – 6 short quantitative questions.
You can bring three A4-size cheat sheets (6 sides together, either hand-writing notes or electronic typing notes). The cheat sheets are only for individual-base use, no copying from other students is allowed.

title: for a well-received course, this prof is unusually bad at teaching
comment_content:
I genuinely don't know what I expected when I enrolled in this course. I knew the course material wouldn't be practical, but since my friends were saying that the course was good, I thought the content would at least be interesting.
My interest was quickly sapped by the 3rd week by all the AI generated slides / notes. (This was before I did my summer internship. Now that I've had the "joys" of using spec-driven development to do everything in my internship, I just feel numb about AI.) The prof's teaching style did not help.
From what I heard, apparently the teaching was just better in the previous semesters?
comment_teaching:
The slides are AI generated. You may have seen what a difficulty spike in a rhythm game chart looks like. But have you ever seen what a diff spike in a Powerpoint looks like? Some of the slides are so chock-full of notation and computation, that even the professor struggles to explain what is happening on the slide in a remotely comprehensible way.
The notes are AI generated. The exact same information is re-explained across multiple chapters like it's new information. At least they don't contain diff spikes (!)
I'm pretty sure the homework is also AI generated.
At this point, just replace the professor with an AI. Am I paying for a $40k / year ChatGPT subscription? Funnily enough, I think an AI would've taught better.
The prof teaches using a projector, and writing notes on paper. However, his lessons feel so desultory that it felt so hard to connect what he was saying into a coherent picture. Everything he wrote down felt like random scattered pieces of information we were supposed to memorize. Was he just improvising? Did he not have a plan? It turns out, probably:
Previous lecture: "Sorry, I don't think the lecture today was successful in any sense."
This lecture: "I think today I will restart and try to give a slightly more convincing argument and hopefully it will be simple, but it might or might not work. It's more like an experiment."
Haven't you taught this course for multiple semesters already!? Surely the content hasn't changed that much that you have to make it up on the fly.
Anyways, his voice was also a pretty good sleep aid.
I walked out during the first lecture, and watched lecture videos for around half the lectures. Even while watching at x1.25-x1.5 speed, I still wanted to fall asleep.
Please see attachments for more banger Shilin quotes. I gave teaching an E to balance the other reviews out. My original rating was a D.
comment_grading:
Homework + programming + final exam.

title: Needs Improvement in Teaching, but Nice Professor and Good Grade
comment_content:
This course focuses on Quantum Information Processing, which has the following topics:
Lecture 1-2: Brief History of Computers
Lecture 3-4: Brief Introduction to Quantum Computers, Deutsch's Algorithm
Lecture 5-6: Matrix Representation of Quantum Gates
Lecture 7-8: Quantum Circuits and Grover's Search Algorithm
Lecture 9-10: Complex Numbers, Single Qubit Gates and Bloch Sphere
Lecture 11-12: Universal Circuits and Quantum Fourier Transform
Lecture 13-14: Breaking RSA Encryption
Lecture 15-16: Quantum Cryptography and Communication (BB84 Protocol and Quantum Teleportation Circuit)
Lecture 17-18: Brief Introduction to Building Quantum Computers
Lecture 19-20: Classical Error Correction (Hamming Code)
Lecture 21-22: Quantum Error Correction (Quantum Repetition Code and 9-Qubit Shor's Code)
Since PHYS1007 is a Common Core Course, it only briefly introduces Quantum Information and Mechanics. If you want to understand more about the topic, you may take PHYS2022 since it gives you more advanced information on solving it. However, I think this is hard compared to other common cores since it requires us to have some previous knowledge of Linear Algebra and Complex Numbers. Otherwise, it is very hard to catch up on the course materials and easy to get lost. 
The hardest part for this course is those Quantum Algorithms. For example, Deutsch's Algorithm and Grover's Search Algorithm took me more than 1 week to fully understand how they work. The steps for these algorithms are very complicated, so I recommend watching some YouTube videos to get the idea of how they work.
These are the videos that help me a lot in this course:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL4wzlfHhrqQzJfrxDv2nYmLwvDBZmPb9-&si=6IPj3UySB9SyT2no
Overall, I will give the content an A since it gives us the most basic information about Quantum Mechanics, which is quite useful in understanding this topic.
comment_teaching:
Prof. Huang is a new professor teaching PHYS1007. His teaching needs improvement since his voice is not strong enough, and he also fails to explain the content clearly to catch students' attention. Especially some of his lecture notes are handwritten, so I could not fully understand the flow. I attended the first lecture, and after that, I did not come as it would easily make me fall asleep during the lectures. However, Prof. Huang will correct his mistakes after the lectures and even take his time to make new slides to help us understand the content well. He is also willing to answer students' questions via email or in person.
Meanwhile, the TAs are helpful and willing to give you advice. They will assist you even if you do not have an idea how to make the Quantum Circuit in the Lab Session.
Hence, I will give this part a B for more improvements in explaining the content, but other aspects are great throughout the semester.

教學涵蓋lecture同tutorial
Lecture方面（1小時20分鐘）：
professor主要是教公式的推導過程以及公式背後的物理意義，但考試不會叫你做公式推導。
本人DSE英文拿3，physics拿4，m2拿5。但是我覺得lecture堂公式推導的過程十分冗長和沉悶（可能因為我英文不好，上這堂課腦中要同時處理英文、物理和微積分，再加上飯後課，經常大腦過載陷入昏厥），學生必須時刻聽得懂每一步的數學推導在幹什麼，走一下神就會完全迷失，隨後完全不知道這一堂課在幹什麼。有感覺到Professor有嘗試讓這堂課變的有趣，課上會做些物理小實驗和舉一些生活化的例子。
還有lecture堂所教的calculus部分剛需m2，MATH1013到中期才學differentiation、最後幾堂課才會教integration、不會教任何vector基礎。所以上這門課之前你需要掌握的calculus的知識是：
- Differentiation（學到chain rule鏈式法則差不多了）
- Integration（學到代換積分法substitution差不多了）
- 3D vector基礎（dot / cross product只會在lecture課的公式推導和物理概念解釋,考試需要的vector知識就只是你要會分三個方向分別去d或者in）
這門課的內容會默認你已經熟悉這些calculus的知識，所以讀過m2的學生會有些許優勢
tutorial（50分鐘）
流程是先給你review一下這個星期或者上個星期的lecture學了些什麼，然後讓你做一張工作紙，做完對答案，最後會解答一題功課裡的題目。
我那個老師是個內地人，說英文很結巴，3句一小‘額...’，5句一大‘額......’，純靠語速來遮掩自己英文說不流暢的情況，這樣導致我在整堂課上都是一直再聽他額...額...額...，根本不知道再說什麼。所以lecture課的真正的流程是打開手機玩遊戲，等到老師解答工作紙答案的時候再抄，最後把工作紙交上去就結束了。

title: over-whelming workload
comment_content:
Lecture:
lecture 1-7 covers secondary-school-level content of motion, mechanical energy and momentum&impulse. There are some extensions, which are managable if you learned physics well in secondary school. 
lecture 8-11 covers the dynamics of rigid bodies. There is a short review of secondary-school-level rotational motion, with new concepts such as moment of inertia, torque, angular momentum. The lecture 11, where gyroscope is demostrated and explained, is not imprortant but extremely difficult to understand.
Lecture 12-13 covers gravitation. Some of the content is taught in secondary school with some extensions such as black hole.
Lecture 14-17 covers periodic motion and wave. The content ranges from secondary-school-level to more difficult concepts and formulas, which can be confusing for students to differentiate.   
Lecture 18-24 covers thermodynamics. Almost everything is new except equation of state. The formulas are not overly difficult, but you need to thoroughly understand the concepts and how the formulas are derived, as some exam questions may be related to these.
Tutorial:
The tutorial sessions are meant for reviewing and practicing the content covered in the lectures. Please note that attendance is taken for the tutorials by having students hand in a practice paper provided in class. Once you submit the practice paper, which usually contains 2 longer questions, your attendance will be recorded regardless of your performance on that paper.
After completing the practice paper, the TA will briefly explain the quetions and talk about 1 or 2 supplementary questions. Sometimes the TA can provide some practical methods that were not covered in the lectures. However, the tutorial sessions can be boring most of the time.
Remark: Textbook is compulsory is this course, otherwise students can't have the access code for homework.
comment_teaching:

Kirill’s slides are well-organised and comprehensive, which has been helpful for students throughout the learning process. However, his handwriting can be a bit difficult to read, especially for certain characters like 'r'. During lectures, Kirill tends to directly copy some formulas onto the whiteboard, without always providing thorough explanations. This approach can occasionally cause confusion, especially compared to how some other professors teach the material. Especially when learning periodic motion and wave, my friends and I still feeled confused about some concepts after attending lectures, we spent time reading textbook, searching online, watching recordings of other lectures, asking TA to clarify the concepts.
Tutorial:
HE is very enthusiastic in teaching and provides clear explanation although he pace can feel a bit rushed at times. In his tutorial, I learned something useful that I didn’t learn in the lecture.
comment_grading:
Tutorials         5%
Assignments 10%
Midterm      35%
Final Exam   50%
For the tutorials, students can earn the the mark simply by attending the assigned tutorial session. Attendance may not be recorded if you attend a tutorial session that you did not officially enroll in. Except for the two tutorial sessions that do not count towards the course grade, students are allowed to be absent for a maximum of 2 tutorial sessions without losing any tutorial grade.
For the assignments, there are a total of 11 homework assignments that count towards the course grade. Each assignment contains around 12 questions, with several parts to each question. Students are allowed a maximum of 6 attempts per question. Failure on MC question attempts will lead to a loss of grade, but students can attain full marks on calculation-based questions as long as they figure them out within the 6 attempts.There is also a dynamic study module for each chapter. Students can earn bonus points as compensation for their homework performance. After adding up the bonus points, the best 9 homework sets will be counted towards the final homework grade, meaning the lowest 2 sets will be dropped. Collaboration with classmates is recommended to ensure students can earn the maximum marks on the homework assignments.
The midterm exam covers content from Lectures 1-11. The mean score for the midterm was 15.5 out of 28, with a standard deviation of 5.6. The midterm consists of 28 MCs, all weighted equally. The majority of the questions require calculations using the formulas taught in the course. An interesting observation is that the midterm for this course seems to frequently conflict with midterms for other courses that many students take concurrently. For example, in the Fall 2023-2024 semester, the PHYS1112 midterm was scheduled on the same day as the COMP1021 midterm. This semester, the PHYS1112 midterm was scheduled on the same day as the MATH1014 midterm, creating a challenging weekend for students.
The final is comprehensive with 3/4 of the questions selected from the content covered in lecture 12-24. The mean is 22.5 out of 40 and the SD is 7.51.The final exam consists of 40 MCs, all weighted equally. Similar to the midterm, the majority of the questions require calculations using the formulas taught in the course. However, some questions also test the students' understanding of the conceptual derivation of the formulas and concepts. Therefore, in addition to remembering all the relevant formulas, students must also be familiar with the underlying conceptual development and derivation of the formulas covered throughout the course.
comment_workload: The high workload is a significant challenge in this course. Students are required to complete a set of weekly homework assignments, which typically take 2-3 hours to finish individually. After completing the homework, students may need to spend additional time on adaptive follow-up assignments if they score below 95% on the original homework. In addition to the homework, there is a set of supplementary questions that are similar in nature to the homework set. These supplementary questions typically require around 2 hours to complete.The dynamic study modules are relatively easier and usually take around 20 minutes to complete each set. Beyond the regular assignments, students may need to invest significant time in other learning activities to fully understand the course concepts. This can include reading the textbook, searching for explanations online, watching recordings of lectures by other instructors, and seeking clarification from TA, it's time-consuming.

comment_content:
The course covers classical mechanics very systematically and is quite comprehensive for an introductory university physics course.
Main topics covered (roughly in order):
- Kinematics (1D & 2D), forces, Newton's laws
- Friction, inclined planes, circular motion (uniform & non-uniform)
- Work, kinetic energy, potential energy, power, conservative/non-conservative forces
- Momentum, impulse, collisions (elastic & inelastic), center of mass
- Rotational kinematics, torque, moment of inertia, rotational energy
- Rolling motion, angular momentum conservation
- Gravitation (basic), simple harmonic motion (brief introduction in some years)

comment_content:
Having completed PHYS 111, I feel equipped to offer a mixed but ultimately positive review of this foundational course. As a student who entered with only a high school physics background, I found the course to be a significant but manageable step up in difficulty. The initial description was a bit confusing to decipher, mentioning pathways for both beginners and advanced students, but in practice, the course does a solid job of building from the ground up for those willing to put in the work.
The heart of the course lies in its learning outcomes. We spent a substantial amount of time mastering the use of Newton's laws to solve complex, single-body dynamics problems, which forms the bedrock of classical mechanics. The modules on conservation of energy and momentum were particularly enlightening, providing powerful tools to predict outcomes in collisions and rotational motion without getting bogged down in complex forces. The latter part of the semester, covering waves and thermodynamics, was challenging but rewarding. Learning to explain phenomena like interference, the Doppler effect, and applying the laws of thermodynamics to real-world problems genuinely changed how I see the physical world.
The prescribed textbook, University Physics by Pearson, was an indispensable resource. The lectures were crucial for understanding the concepts, but the textbook problems and examples were where the real learning happened for me. I do, however, have some critiques. Some of the learning outcome phrasing, like "use solenius language," seems to be a typo (likely meaning "scientific language"), which caused minor confusion. Furthermore, the "Review Feedback" section with HKD figures is completely irrelevant and should be removed, as it adds unnecessary clutter.
Overall, PHYS 111 is a demanding course that requires consistent effort. The mathematical prerequisite is no joke; you need to be comfortable with calculus to keep up. But for students seeking a rigorous introduction to university-level physics that successfully teaches you to analyze and solve problems systematically, this course is an excellent choice. It’s tough, but you’ll come out the other side with a much stronger understanding of how the world works.

comment_content:
The first half of the course covers basic mechanics: Newton's Laws, Kinematics, Work energy theorem and rotational/circular motion. Second half covers gravity, oscillatory motion, waves and thermodynamics.

The lecture format is good with revising the previous lecture, going over the content and then sample questions. The tutorial format is not that helpful in my opinion, it is very similar type of questions and the tutorial is very short. One good thing is the tutorial goes over the toughest homework problem.

Same for wave motion and sound, bad pacing.
Finally, thermodynamics. Totally 7 lectures, but holy hell, the amount of new content is still straight up insance.
I guess this is what college course feel likes, you are given new content that should take weeks to ponder, but the next week they teach something new again. There's just no time to breathe.

comment_teaching: Mr. Chen, TW is quite good, used to stay after class to always ask him anything I was unsure of. Personally I would have liked it if the professor was more animated during his delivery but well, every person is different and has their own style.
comment_grading:
Can't really complain about grading. The final grading scheme is:
1. Midterm: 30%
2. Homework: 15%
3. Tutorial Participation: 5%
4. Finals: 50%
The mean was around the 50th percentage of the exam total. The grading is not the toughest part and is manageable. Got a B with somewhat mild effort, could have done better if I was more diligent.
comment_workload:
The workload was not unbearable, but do not be mistaken to think 1112 would be any similar to DSE or A-Levels. Maybe the first 2-3 lectures about mechanics would give you a sense of familiarity but after that it will start becoming clear what university physics actually is. 
The homework is not that difficult, you have to input your answers on an online platform and they give you sufficient time to complete it. Tutorial attendance is not much, you just show up once a week to the tutorial and submit your in-class assignment. But if you do not develop a habit of reviewing your materials regularly, even for a few minutes per day you will be doomed. The workload is not too crazy, but not completely laxed either.

comment_teaching:
CHEN, Tian Wen can explain things with some daily examples and usually has experiments to demonstrate what he was teaching in that class, I think that is his good point.
However, since he is too clever, it is often that he will skip all the calculus steps in the lesson, and leave it for "self-study". 
Since no attendance at the lecture will be counted as grading, it is not necessary to go to every lecture, but the tutorial counts. therefore, make sure you can take every tutorial. CHEN will upload all the PowerPoint and the handwriting notes in the lecture onto the canvas, and if you need, there also be the lecture recordings. They are quite useful for your revision.

comment_content:
The course is intended for students with a background of DSE Physics and basic calculus. There are some overlap with DSE Physics curriculum, with come calculus mixed in. comment_content:
Kinematics: The study of motion and its mathematical description, including displacement, velocity, and acceleration.
Newton's Laws of Motion: The fundamental principles that describe the relationship between forces acting on an object and its resulting motion.
Work, Energy, and Power: The concepts of work, energy, and power, including the work-energy theorem and conservation of mechanical energy.
Momentum and Collisions: The study of momentum, impulse, and the conservation of linear momentum in collisions.
Rotational Motion: The principles of rotational motion, including torque, angular velocity, and angular acceleration.
Gravitation: The study of the gravitational force and the motion of objects under the influence of gravity.
Oscillations and Waves: The behavior of simple harmonic motion, oscillatory systems, and the properties of waves.
Thermodynamics, an introduction about state variables and function, 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics and their application.

comment_content:
This physics course goes much beyond 1112. It really focuses on why each physics quantity came to be and how everything is derived. E.g. instead of simply introducing momentum as mass times velocity, this content really focuses why mass times velocity was considered as a relevant quantity in the study of physics, why the sum of momentum of a system is more useful than the sum of its velocities etc. If you plan on doing a physics major, I highly recommend taking this course. Otherwise maybe don't (unless you really like physics).
That being said, none of the lecture material is really relevant in solving hw and exam problems. You could just read the standard 1112 lecture notes and be fine, as far as knowledge is concerned. Of course the problems are significantly more challenging that 1112 questions but they don't really utilise any of the content from the lecture notes of 1312. Thus, there is really a dissonance between what's taught in classes and what's assessed. 
The lectures and problems makes heavy use of vectors and calculus (even as far as multivariable calculus) and especially their relevance in physics. The mathematics used in the course doesn't feel like a copout. Often times when calculus-based questions are set in physics question, it ends up just being a math question without needing much physics (e.g. find the distance travelled when a velocity function is given; this question doesn't really test much physics knowledge but tests your integration skills). However, in this course, the calculus is never the focus of the questions even if you need to use it. All problems solved in lectures, hw and exams feel like physics questions and not just math questions.
TLDR; the lecture content goes into a lot depth about the origins and relevance of concepts in mechanics but the lecture content is very irrelevant to hw and exams. Take this course if you plan on doing a physics major, otherwise don't. Also don't take this course if you don't understand mathematics conceptually.

title: RMBI 1010
comment_content:
The lecture provided a comprehensive overview that encompassed the detailed introduction to the intricate risk management process. It delved into not only the fundamental concepts but also explored the diverse range of risks that exist within companies and society at large. Notably, the content leaned more towards the theoretical aspects, laying a solid foundation in concepts and principles rather than emphasizing complex quantitative calculations. 
On the other hand, the tutorial sessions were highly practical. They focused on equipping students with the skills to calculate Value at Risk (VaR) using the powerful tool of Excel. This involved learning various functions and techniques, along with the application of what-if analysis to understand the potential impacts of different scenarios. It was indeed a challenging learning experience, but simultaneously, it managed to spark the interest of many students due to its hands-on nature. 
For first-year students who lacked any prior business background, the overall content could prove to be quite arduous. The concepts and techniques were new and often required a significant amount of effort to grasp. However, given that it was part of the common core curriculum, the pressure to achieve a perfect understanding was somewhat alleviated. 
Nevertheless, for those in the CCC program, this particular course might not be the most advisable choice. The reason being that the examination format was rather demanding. It required students to write out their answers by hand in a closed-book setting. This placed a heavy emphasis on rote learning and the ability to recall information accurately. In contrast, if the exam were to be an open-book format, it would transform into a course where students could potentially achieve excellent grades, as they would have the freedom to refer to relevant materials and focus more on applying their knowledge rather than simply memorizing it.

title: A+ student exam tips
comment_content:
Maybe I can briefly talk about what could happen in the exam. if you cannot read Chinese, then Google Translate could help.
Many questions require common sense or understanding of the term. For example, 停火在現代代表什麼意思? and the lecture notes only mentioned: "停火可以終止敵對而且实际上終止战争". You will feel that there are two impossible answers. option one: 雙方軍隊返回自己國家. option two:只要不簽訂和平條約, 就無法實現和平. so option two is selected by common sense.  Pay special attention to the term mentioned in States and Peaceful Settlement. 
Around 10 questions require an understanding of classical cases. eg. lotus case (船隻懸掛旗幟國家管轄權vs對在公海損害他船的外國船艦的管轄權, the case result: no exclusive jurisdiction, both countries have jurisdiction), the North Sea Continental Shelf Case (公約约束力的條件: 有些立法公約聲言是普遍性的，但成员方必須表明其接受約束的意向，但是他們可能不受約束),  Anglo-Norwegian Fisheries Case (由低潮點開始至外有十二英里的領海範圍, note that the case happened before UNCLOS but we still answer using this principle), the Cofu channel case (strict responsibility on potential damage)
10-13 questions about student presentation. Most of the topics have positions and conclusions, and most people use the principles of international law to prove them. What you should do is try to connect them, and the exam will gonna ask you about how they prove this. Note that each student topic has one question only. 但係我自己做嘅topic都唔肯定答案. One tip for preparing this is to listen to what the professor asks or answers.
10-13 questions about international institutions: 有d topic 係冇case study, 所以佢地會問國際機構嘅運作機制 or 條約. Eg. 國際海底管理局如何分配海床的利益, 國際原子能組織有關建立和管理核電廠的手則是否具備约束力, 赤道國家對《1975年波哥大聲明》聲稱靜態地理位置軌道是其領土的一部分, 1979年月球條約的內容. It does NOT mean that human rights institutions or UN institutions will NOT be examined.
History will be included but not many (around 4-5 questions). eg. Bynkershock於1702年表示國家擁有離岸至一定大炮射程的海域，例如三英里.  Grotius說正義戰爭
Last type of question: the professor's answers to any questions raised by students or the conclusion drawn by the professor during the lecture. One tip is to go to the lecture and ask a question, I found 3 questions in the exam that related to what I had asked.

title: Good Grading Course for local and DSE history students
comment_content:
There are 4 non-cumulative quizzes, containing 24-26 MC and 1-2 short question(s). There are no classes, instead, you are engaged in 12 modules online. The modules contain lecture videos, readings (most of the modules) and movies (some of the modules). 
For the lecture videos, most of the questions (around 70%-80%) in the quizzes (except for quiz 4) are based on the content of the videos. Quiz 4, however, covers only around half of the questions related to the lecture videos since there are only 8 videos for module 9-12.
For the readings, questions about the readings are provided in the video and you have to answer them by reading the paper. Most of these questions have "correct" answers that are found within the readings. For the rest of them, you need to combine what you learnt in the lecture video and reading to explain your answer. 
It is unnecessary to read beyond the scope of these questions, as the instructor has not tested on material outside of this content. However, I recommend at least skimming through the abstract or introduction to grasp the core concepts of the readings.
For the movies, he will ask any content that the reporter or interviewee said. One of the MCs in a quiz has asked for the response of the neighbour of home husband, which only includes two sentences filmed in the movie. Therefore, I suggest watching the movies in details and take notes if possible. Besides, I had a concern whether the things I can see in the movies will be tested but luckily it has not been included in any quizzes. 
I highly recommend local and DSE history students to study this course.
Being a local, you will find that the content adheres closely to reality, particularly the political aspects, requiring no additional effort to learn.
As a DSE history student, I find studying this course easier due to its alignment with the 20th century developments. However, I do find the sociology component to be more time-consuming to learn.
