comment_content: acquired me with a deeper understanding of Hong Kong society, tackling complex societal and gender issues, covers Hong Kong historical and cultural background
comment_teaching:
Taking Contemporary Hong Kong Society gave me a deeper and more critical perspective on issues I used to take for granted. The course didn’t just provide facts — it challenged me to think about how Hong Kong’s social problems are connected to larger historical and structural forces.
One of the most memorable parts for me was the discussion on gender in Hong Kong. I had always assumed gender inequality was “less serious” here compared to other places, but through the readings and data, I realized how persistent workplace discrimination and cultural stereotypes still are. The debates on feminism in a local context made me reflect on how traditional values and modern ideals often clash.
The lecture on suicide and mental health was also very powerful. I appreciated that the course encouraged us to think sociologically about such a sensitive issue. Instead of framing suicide only as a personal tragedy, we examined the broader pressures — from housing, education, and family expectations — that shape people’s well-being. It reminded me that individual choices can’t be understood apart from social structures.
The historical dimension of the course also stood out. Learning about Hong Kong’s colonial past and post-1997 transformations gave me a better framework to understand today’s identity debates. It helped me see why issues like language, migration, and political participation continue to spark controversy.
Overall, I feel the course trained me to think critically about Hong Kong society by connecting theory to real-world problems. It also gave me tools — like gender theory, structural functionalism, and postcolonial perspectives — that I can use to analyze both current events and everyday life.

I found it’s not too hard to get a solid mark, but aiming for a really high score can be tricky, since the questions often test fine details or subtle differences in theory. It rewards consistent preparation rather than last-minute cramming.

title: Easy
comment_content:
hat explains Hong Kong’s phenomenal economic success? Why do a quarter of Hong Kong’s
population live below the poverty line? Why do women in Hong Kong outperform men in
education, but earn less money than men? Why do almost a thousand residents commit suicide
every year? What are the experiences of Hong Kong’s ethnically diverse minorities? How is Hong
Kong governed? What explains Hong Kong’s troubled political history? How do Hong Kong
residents see themselves in relation to the Chinese mainland? Why does Hong Kong have among
the highest divorce rates in the world? How is family life in Hong Kong changing?
The purpose of this course is to answer these questions, and more, by developing a sociological
understanding of Hong Kong society. The aim is not so much to compile facts and figures about
every conceivable aspect of Hong Kong, but to develop a sociological mindfulness with which to
understand it in new and helpful ways. We shall approach each topic by looking at the broad
questions and theories that sociologists use to understand modern life. We will then discuss their
relevance to Hong Kong and examine local studies. The course is, therefore, both an introduction
to sociological thinking and methods as well as an introduction to Hong Kong society.
The theme of the course is social change in Hong Kong from the post-war period. The focus is on
how industrialization, urbanization, globalization, and modernity affect our everyday lives,
institutions, relationships, and identities. The first two sections of the course will look at the
mechanics of these changes and selected social problems associated with them: the
transformation of community life, mental health, political, economic, and gender inequalities. The
final part will examine the implications of and responses to these problems: social movements for
democracy, experiences of discrimination, the emergence of distinct Hong Kong cultural identities,
and the search for intimacy, and family life.

In this year, SOSC1662 is delivered in pure self-paced online mode. Professor Groves release a module per week consisting 2-6 videos. There are also supplementary reading materials and videos, in which guiding questions in the lecture notes will tell you what points you should pay particular attention to.
comment_teaching:
Professor Julian Mcallister Groves is a veteran lecturer in HKUST, spending over 30 years in HKUST. As a native English speaker, his lectures should be understandable by everyone. Generally, his lecture videos follow the outline of the Powerpoint slides, though he is by no way a Powerpoint reader, so be sure to watch his videos in full!
Despite a pass in LANG 1401/2/34/1002 is required, Professor Groves had intentionally slowed down his speaking pace and used simpler words to accommodate those who have limited English proficiency. In fact, almost all unfamiliar English words are labelled with Chinese in quizzes.
Overall, I believe Professor Groves' teaching is excellent for online teaching. Perhaps things would have been different for face-to-face lectures--maybe (after all it has to be balanced between depth and workload). I'd have a few chats with him after quizzes on some related topics, and his responses are also friendly as well.

There are 3 quizzes in the course, each covering a part and consisting of MC questions and 1-2 short questions. The final exam is cumulative, and is essentially a longer version of the quizzes. The questions are generally easy, and a significant amount of them deal with the reading materials. Some questions may ask about rather trivial points in lectures (for example, [a word] comes from which language?). Be sure to look through the lecture notes, revise on the reading materials, and you should be fine.
Ultimately get an A for the course, which is fine for me. An A+ could be attained if I could score a few more points in the final exam: never mind, it's after all a course with nearly 400 students enrolled.
comment_workload:
Probably the easiest 3-credit common core course in HKUST.
The videos takes any time from within an hour to 3 days (while also working on other courses) to be finished, while I generally spend 2-4 days for quiz preparation. As I am used to write handwritten notes, your time spent on SOSC1662 lecture videos may be less, but anyways the weekly workload was much less than 3 hours.
Given by the fact that the course had 5 quizzes+1 group project in previous years, I consider this year's workload as negligible. As long as this kind of assessment is maintained, SOSC1662 would be a good choice if you want to go credit overload.

Overall Impression:
The final grade isn’t released, but the grading seems transparent and relatively fair. I ended up with an A+, which was a pleasant surprise. Compared to other cc courses, the assessment design is quite easy if you keep up with the materials.
Attendance / In-Class Quizzes (15%)
Attendance is tracked through 4 in-class quizzes(1 of them is a makeup quiz) based on short supplementary videos shown during the last 30 minutes of some lectures. Each quiz has 4 MCQs (1.5 points each), and you still get 1 point per question even if you answer incorrectly. Only your best 3 quizzes count, which helps boost the score. Most students scored full marks, but the quizzes aren’t purely memory-based—some questions are slightly tricky, so watching the videos carefully is worth your time.
Assignments (27%)
There are two problem sets. The first is very manageable (mean 91.4/100), while the second one takes a bit longer to do (mean 86.1/100) likely due to some trickier parts. The TAs give helpful feedback, and the assignments focus on applying class concepts. Read the full questions carefully before rushing into calculations.
Class Participation (3%)
This is based on how actively you engage—asking or answering questions during or after class. Prof. Ma encourages discussion and is very receptive even to basic or “silly” questions. From what I can tell, each participation counts as 1%, up to a max of 3%. Just speaking up 2–3 times is enough to secure this portion.
Final Exam (55%)
A 3-hour closed-book paper, split into:
35 MCQs (around half the exam)
1 calculation question (~10–15%)
2 short essays (~35–40%)
The MCQs mostly test your understanding of trends and patterns mentioned in class and need you to recall some of detailed points. The essays and calculation questions are straightforward if you've kept up with the course content. Time is not an issue, but you do need to be precise in your answers. Scores aren’t released, but performance on the final seems to weigh heavily on the final grade.

comment_content:
Chapter 1: Population growth and economic development: Causes, consequences, and controversies.

Chapter 3: Mortality Analysis
Chapter 4: Fertility Analysis
Chapter 5: Migration Analysis
The contents are well designed but may lack of depth. In the 5 chapters, the last one is the most important one (which is Prof. Ma's research interest). After this course, you will understand the demographic trends in China (and other developing countries), as well as the underlying reasons. You will have a big advantage if you learned some Economics and have some basic understanding of China's history (especially 1949-1992). If you are an Economic student, you will be familiar with some names in this course, e.g., G. S. Becker and J. R. Hicks. FYI: I major in MAEC and have got an A- in SOSC 1350 (Contemporary China: Continuity and Change).
comment_teaching:
Prof. Ma speaks slowly in his lectures and sometimes use Mandarin Chinese to facilitate his speech, and it may be a little bit difficult to focus on what he intends to talk as he digresses frequently. I agree with the previous comment that you should understand Mandarin Chinese to take this course. However, he is trying hard to use his own experience in explaining the historical incidents that have influenced the demographics in China. For example, he said his name 忠東 means 忠於毛澤東, which was a popular name in the early 1960s. He also recalled the fast on Tian'anmen Square in 1989 before the June 4th incident, where 沒有吃的，但是好多喝的，還有蜂王漿. It is really interesting to listen to these stories.
Prof. Ma will mention what is going to be tested in the exam, so it is useful to follow him during his lectures. The recordings will also be provided, so you can review the lectures before the final exam. Just pay attention that the quality of the recording may not be high enough that sometimes you cannot clearly hear him in the recordings. (Disclaimer: I do not guarantee that the recordings will be provided in the following semesters.)
comment_grading:
Components of Final Grade:
Attendance (in-class quizzes): 15%
Assignments: 27%
Class discussion: 3%
Final examination: 55%
In short: The final grade is not released, but I think the grading is fair (and perhaps better than most other UST courses). I get an A+ in this course, which is much beyond my expectation.
The attendance is recorded by 3 quizzes based on supplementary videos played in the last 30 minutes of some classes. Every quiz contains 4 MCQs with 1.5 points each, and you can get 1 point each even you choose the wrong answer. The final score is calculated by the best 3 out of 4 quizzes, and I think most of the students (including me) get full marks. However, the quizzes are a little bit tricky, so please spend some time on watching the videos during the lectures.
The assignments are composed of 2 problem sets with calculations. The problem sets are not difficult at all, and everyone gets high marks (median 95/100 and 88/100 for the 2 problem sets). The TAs also provide detailed feedback to the assignments. Nevertheless, I strongly recommend you to read thoroughly through the problem sets before doing the calculation parts. My overall score is around the median (99/100, 85/100) due to some careless mistakes in the second problem set.
Class discussion is also encouraged, especially raising questions during the lecture breaks. Each time a student asks or answers a question, Prof. Ma will record their participation number. Even though some students (like me) keep asking silly questions, Prof. Ma will happily answer them. I guess each record accounts for 1% of the total score, while the maximum is 3%. If this is true, I get full marks in this part.
The final examination is a 3-hour closed book exam. There are 35 MCQs (around 49%), 1 calculation problem (around 11%), and 2 short essay problems (around 40%). The scores are not disclosed. The time is fairly enough for the problems, so please write carefully to make sure you get all key points.
comment_workload: The workload is quite light. You only need to go to the lectures (or do other things during the lectures and spend 2 days to go through the recordings) to have fair understanding of the materials. There are 2 problem sets, and each problem set takes around 2-3 hours to finish. Compared to other CCCs with essays or group projects, this course is definitely a smart choice.

comment_content:
The course primarily revolves around the exploration of numerous German sociologists, which, to be honest, can be rather monotonous. A significant challenge lies in the necessity to memorize a plethora of names to perform well in the quizzes. The assessments, particularly the multiple-choice quizzes, demand rapid recall within a limited timeframe of 20 minutes. Given that these quizzes collectively contribute to 20% of the overall grade, each question holds substantial weight, making efficient recall crucial for success.
The final examination introduces a different format, adopting an essay-style approach. Students are confronted with four questions, and they must select two to craft comprehensive essays. This requires not only a profound understanding of the various sociologists discussed throughout the course but also the ability to apply this knowledge cohesively in a written format. The comprehensive nature of the final exam, encompassing a broader synthesis of the course material, adds a layer of complexity and depth to the evaluation process.
comment_teaching:
The quality of instruction in this course unfortunately falls below expectations. The considerable size of the class compounds the challenges, making it notably difficult to maintain focus and engagement. The professor's reliance on reading directly from the slides further contributes to the overall dissatisfaction with the teaching approach.
Additionally, there is a unique attendance policy in place. While attendance is a requirement for earning points, it adds a layer of complexity as the professor selectively designates specific classes for attendance tracking. To secure the maximum attendance points, students are compelled to attend these selected classes. The stipulation of needing five attendances to accumulate all possible points creates a dynamic where not only the learning experience but also strategic attendance planning becomes essential for optimal academic performance. This intricate attendance structure introduces an additional layer of challenge to an already demanding academic setting.

comment_content: This population course is incredibly fun and engaging, making it a standout academic experience. Instead of forcing students to memorize endless facts or historical dates, the professor focuses on teaching core demographic concepts through interactive, real-world examples. The required population calculations are straightforward, logic-based, and highly practical, allowing you to easily understand how societies change without getting bogged down in heavy math. Because the curriculum emphasizes deep comprehension over rote memorization, there is actually very little to memorize before exams. The professor has an amazing ability to turn complex global trends into enjoyable, bite-sized lessons, creating a lively classroom atmosphere where time flies by. You will learn how to analyze birth rates, migration patterns, and aging trends using simple formulas that make perfect sense. It is the perfect class for anyone who wants to learn valuable, high-level analytical skills in a stress-free environment. I highly recommend this course because the workload is highly manageable, the concepts are fascinating, and the professor makes the entire learning process genuinely enjoyable from start to finish.

Whether discussing global migration patterns, fertility rates, or aging societies, every lecture is structured with perfect clarity and brought to life using compelling, real-world examples. What truly sets this instructor apart is their genuine commitment to student success. They foster an inclusive and highly interactive classroom environment where questions are always welcomed and answered with immense patience. The course was taught in zoom format, around 3 hours every lecture. No lecture videos so you have to attend everyday to make sure you mark down everything, the exams test on a lot of random stuff mentioned in the lectures so its best if you mark down literally everything. The teaching itself wasn't bad, the lecturer often made jokes and applied the taught content to everyday life which made it a lot easier to understand probably, the TAs were pretty helpful in explaining the group project
But then comes the book content, each lecture had its own corresponding book chapter which you need to read on your own with no guidelines, its basically 30-35 pages of agony and despair, around 5000-6000 words worth of points for each chapter. Especially gender behavior where there were 3 pages describing sexual transition surgeries which weren't explicitly told to be out of the syllabus so you'll also need to memorize that in case it was tested on. Some of the book content and the lecture content were stating different things on the same points so you'll need to choose who to believe.

Seems the B range is pretty lenient but getting A will definitely require you to remember everything.

comment_content:
The course talks about biological and social theories about gender (across culture); history and the contents of feminism, LGBT, and MeToo movements; the concept of double bind; and how gender matters in the topics of education, language, data, media, bodies, labor, home, sexualities, pornography, violence, politics, economy, and Hong Kong migrant domestic workers. It also talks about solutions to the problems about gender inequality.
While it seems that the course content is comprehensive, it is not. It is outdated. It doesn't talk about the role of gender in the internet, social media, AI, video games, and instant messaging apps. But they are particularly important these days. Also, it exaggerates some of the gender inequality and downplays some other.
comment_teaching: I get that the professor is trying to teach well. However, he may be too old for the job, as social changes happen fast and he is still stuck to the past. He often quotes researches from the 1990s, and they are absolutely outdated now. Our textbook was first published in the 2000s. Also, I had a feeling that he was forcing us (though implicitly) to agree with what he was teaching in the classes. But he did invite an LGBT guest when teaching the topic of LGBT.
comment_grading:
I thought I would get a B grade at first. But I scored very well in the two exams (midterm and final, accounting for 35% and 40% of the final score). So I got an A.
There is also a research project accounting for 20% of the final score, which you would do it in group or individually, and I got a score of 75% (I don't know if that's a good score or not).
But there's a participation score, where you do not get it only by attending the classes, but by actively answering/asking questions in the classes. I think this discriminates against introverts and the professor said so himself that only a few [extroverts] would get the 5% participation score.
comment_workload:
The workload was way too heavy for a common core course. This workload is almost comparable to the workload of an honors course. We had two classes per week (not the problem), and before each class, there are required readings, usually one to two. Each reading typically has around 15 pages (some has around 30!), almost full of text. And the readings will be tested in the exams. I think you have to spend 1-2 hours before each class to read the required readings.
The professor said that any good social science course requires readings, and that he has tried making them simple. But I also had SOSC 1969 in the same semaster, and that course does not require any readings at all, and it has a better reputation from both myself and ust space. Also, the readings are definitely not simple. The words are hard, the grammar is complex, and for your information, I got 5** in DSE English Reading (I think the readings are harder than the hardest DSE B2 article). This should be an SOSC course, not a LANG course.
Finally, the group/individual project may also take some time to finish.

title: A Comprehensive and Relevant Introduction to Sustainability Issues
comment_content:
The course covers a wide range of sustainability issues that will be relevant for more future studies in environmental/sustainability fields. The course doesn't necessarily delve deep into each single topic, but just covering the surface to grasp basic concepts.
Through all its materials, I would say that the main objective that is expected of the students is to understand the interconnectedness of issues, and relate them to present case studies and our daily life.
For the assessments, there is no need to memorize all the scientific terms, etc. But what's most important is understanding the concepts and being able to connect and build upon them. (as someone who hates memorization, this course was quite nice!)
Course Materials:
L1 – Introduction 
L2 – Anthropogenic Impact on Natural Systems 
L3 – Planetary Boundaries 
L4 – Human Thriving within Planetary Boundaries 
L5 – Policy for Sustainability 
L6 – Sustainable Development 
L7 - Energy
L8 - Futures for Water
L9 - Design for a Circular Economy 
L10 - Sustainable Consumption
L11 - Futures Thinking
L12 - Final Presentation
comment_teaching:
Prof. Arthur is a very friendly and approachable teacher. He is quite understanding of students and is open for inputs to improve upon the course. Despite being a 3 hour lecture, there are always breaks in between, and there are many activities where we get to move around the class and do discussions -helps reduce sleepiness :")
His explanations are easy to understand and he provides many examples related to our daily lives. Sometimes the pace may be a little fast as there are many topics to cover.
Before each lecture we are recommended to do prior reading, however, the professor still does a recap at the beginning of each lecture which pretty much covers most of the reading materials anyways.
If you have struggles about certain topics, its really helpful to book office hours with the professor to discuss the materials further and avoid misunderstandings.
The TA's are mainly passive during lectures, but I believe they actively take note of students' participation. They pretty much grade most if not all our group projects.
comment_grading:
I believe the most important grade is the midterm, followed by reflection and poster presentation, then the rest of the group projects.
The SD for all group project work is very narrow so the scores are similar for everyone. However, having a nice group will be beneficial for peer evaluation.
Attendance is not mandatory, however it is crucial for getting a high class participation score. I'd also recommend doing the extra credit work (it's a single essay), especially if you're aiming for a high B to A range.
Group Project:
- Interim Report 1 = 5%
- Interim Report 2 = 10%
- Poster Presentation = 20%
Midterm: 35%
Reflection Essay: 15%
Peer Evaluation: 8%
Class Participation: 7%
Extra Credit Work: 5%
Grade Expectation (curve):
A: 20-25%
B: 30-40%
C: 30-40%
My final grade: A+
- Within upper quartile for each grade except interim report 1
- Attained highest scores for midterms, interim report 2, reflection, peer evaluation, extra credit work, and class participation
=====
Additional Comments:
- We're allowed a written/printed 2-sided A4 cheat sheet for midterms, so there's no need to memorize definitions or scientific terms.
However, the midterms are challenging as it is all essay questions and we are expected to be able to connect many concepts to give comprehensive answers.
- Same thing above also goes for our reflection essay and extra credit work. The more references and interconnectedness of concepts, the better.
*Key takeaway -> focus on understanding, interconnectedness, and broader application of class concepts!
comment_workload:
Workload is relatively high as the group project needs a lot of research from articles and journals to provide citations and references. I wouldn't recommend procrastinating on the interim reports or poster, and good workload allocation/planning within your group is necessary.
During some lectures there are group assignments that need additional time after class to complete (30 mins-1 hour if you divide tasks between members)
*Key takeaway -> having good group members will make everything better :") (it's freely chosen so you can plan ahead when enrolling in the class)
